News.title: Woman says she's 'tired' trying to prove she's alive after being declared dead by government
News.content:
Woman says she's 'tired' trying to prove she's alive after being declared dead by government

The elderly Florida widow says the mistake has repeatedly caused problems with her finances and official records, despite being told the error had already been corrected

View 2 Images The 84-year-old was told her Social Security number belonged to someone who had died (Image: WFLA News Channel 8/Youtube)

An 84-year-old woman has spent more than two years trying to prove to government agencies that she is still alive after being mistakenly declared dead.

‌



Priscilla Slack says the bizarre mix-up began after her husband died two years ago, when she was somehow also listed as deceased. The mistake seemed like a small administrative error which would quickly be resolved but two years on it has affected vital parts of her life.

‌



Her bank account was first to be affected. Priscilla said : “First they cancelled my bank account, and they cancelled my credit card. When I went to vote, I was still cancelled."

‌



View 2 Images Priscilla has been passed between government agencies for years (Image: WFLA News Channel 8/Youtube)

She initially tried to see the funny side, assuming the mistake would be quickly put right. She told NBC affiliate WFLA: “I kept my sense of humour about it early on, because we can all make mistakes and push the wrong button”

But the mix-up was not resolved as the problems continued to grow. Priscilla said the original error came from the Social Security Administration, and although she believed it had been corrected, other agencies continued to act as though she was dead.

‌



Each time she thought the issue had finally been resolved, another problem appeared. She has since faced many difficulties including holding bank accounts, paying taxes and voting, with agencies periodically requiring her to prove again that she is alive.

Most recently, Priscilla received a letter from the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) claiming she had filed a tax return using the Social Security number of someone who was deceased forcing her to prove that the number belonged to her.

Priscilla said attempts to resolve the problem have involved being repeatedly passed between the IRS and the Social Security Administration. She said: “How am I supposed to deal with these agencies who can’t deal with each other?”

Article continues below

Priscilla believes the agencies involved should now be responsible for correcting the records rather than leaving her to keep challenging the mistake.

The problems have continued for more than two years since her husband’s death, despite Priscilla previously being told the Social Security error had been corrected. She says other agencies have continued to flag her records and freeze accounts when the incorrect information resurfaces.

A spokesperson for the IRS said the matter was being escalated to an advocacy department in an effort to resolve it, according to WFLA.

News.title: Major EES update for 9 UK tourist hotspots including Portugal
News.content:
Major EES update for 9 UK tourist hotspots including Portugal

The European Union entry-exit system (EES) has caused repeated delays for Brits at major EU airports this year

View 3 Images (Image: Anadolu, Anadolu via Getty Images)

British holidaymakers heading abroad may finally be able to breathe a sigh of relief over the widely-criticised EES system. The scheme forces non-EU residents to queue at special machines in airports before gaining entry to 29 nations within the so-called Schengen area – essentially the majority of the European Union.

‌



However, there have been persistent reports of lengthy delays – some stretching to as long as four hours. A new report in the Sunday Times now reveals that the European Union has shelved the controversial entry-exit system (EES) across at least nine countries.

‌



Portugal, Italy, France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Germany, Malta, Greece and Switzerland are all understood to have been granted permission to postpone full implementation of EES. The newspaper reports that there appears to be no deadline by which these countries must adopt the scheme, which has already sparked widespread reports of enormous queues at European airports this summer in destinations such as Mallorca, Faro, the Canary Islands and Milan.

‌



The scheme has faced fierce criticism from Ryanair and others. The European Union describes the Entry/Exit System (EES) as an automated IT system designed to register non-EU nationals travelling on short stays each time they cross the external borders of participating European countries.

Following years of postponements, the system was rolled out from October 2025, with full implementation originally anticipated by the following April. However, faced with the prospect of significant border queues due to software failures, officials granted countries a 150-day grace period during which they could drop the checks to avoid travel chaos.

That rule ended on September 6. The EU previously insisted there would be no extension.

‌



View 3 Images (Image: Anadolu, Anadolu via Getty Images)

Yet the Sunday Times reports that at least nine Schengen countries are understood to have told the European Commission, which is responsible for overseeing the EES, that they would not enforce the new controls in full until the technology and systems were working correctly.

They have informally been allowed to do so with no time limits apparently in place to adopt the system, it is being reported. One of the main purposes of the system is to track whether non-EU citizens have spent more than their permitted 90 days in the bloc in a rolling 180-day period.

‌



Social media has been awash with debate about the scheme. One post on Reddit saw a traveller say: "They made a mess of it. Seems many basic things like it is hit and miss on the document scanning but also things like people walk up with hats and headphones and the machine doesn't tell them to remove them, and organisational things like if the machine errors the traveller has to back out and has no where to go.

"The right way to do this would have been progressive: start by getting some people eg 5% going through the machine lane, everyone else through normal.

"The vendor observes problems, fixes them, once machine working well, increase to 10%, then 20% and so on." Another person said: "The general lack of functionality of so many IT systems across the EU is kind of astonishing."

‌



A third added: "It's worse than that. There isn't even consistent protocol/IT support within a single EU airport."

Another put it more simply, saying: "I just miss having stamps."

'People are missing their flights'

Nadia, from Greater Manchester, told the Guardian in August she had made two trips to Schengen areas this summer. A trip to Tenerife in June was "quite straightforward", but her experience in July at Frankfurt airport where she was picking up a connecting flight home, was much less so.

‌



"The queue there was ridiculously long, and there was very limited information," she says. "People were wandering around trying to work out where they needed to go.

View 3 Images The new entry and exit system (EES) has led to huge delays for passengers, with some missing flights (Image: Getty)

"I'm very well travelled and pretty confident, but even I was slightly unsure and was thinking, is there some other queue I should be joining? There was no one nearby to check with without losing your place."

Article continues below

Eventually, her passport was checked. "He didn't actually take fingerprints then," says Nadia, who is a solicitor. "I think the queue was so long they decided to dispense with that.

"It's the efficiency of the system I question and the fact that individual member states' systems do not talk to one another. They shouldn't need to get information again if you have already gone through. It's pretty shambolic, and I think people missing their flights because of it is just not acceptable, especially when there's no recourse; it's not your fault."

Ryanair chief executive Michael O'Leary has repeatedly complained about EES. Speaking earlier this year, he said: "There's a bit of Brexit in this too. Here, you voted for Brexit - f***ing join the queue."

News.title: Trump responds to backlash over support for united Ireland and 'loves' what he said
News.content:
Trump responds to backlash over support for united Ireland and 'loves' what he said

Donald Trump, who is in Ireland this weekend, said that a unification between the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland 'is going to happen eventually"

View 2 Images Trump pictured in County Clare, Ireland (Image: Getty Images)

US President Donald Trump has said he "loves" the reaction sparked by his comments supporting Irish unification.

‌



The president, who is visiting Ireland this weekend, spoke briefly to reporters as he walked to the first tee on his golf resort in Doonbeg, County Clare. Asked about what he thought of the reaction to his comments yesterday, he said: "I love them."

‌



Further asked about the backlash to his intervention, he said: "I love my comments." The president was also asked about a timeline for Irish unity and about Scottish independence but did not comment on these matters.

‌



Trump controversially said yesterday: "I’d love to see it unified. I think it would be a great feather in everybody’s cap if that happened. It’s going to happen eventually." His comments sparked audible gasps around the room.

Sitting next to Taoiseach Micheál Martin, he added: "We’re talking about it and you got the right man over here to get it moving. But, yeah, I think it would be a fantastic thing.

View 2 Images Trump shaking hands with Irish President Catherine Connolly yesterday in Dublin (Image: Artur Widak/NurPhoto/Shutterstock)

‌



Donald Trump takes aim at Zelensky and calls for Ukraine to STOP strikes on Russia READ MORE :

Major update as one-year-old baby dies in Warwickshire and two people arrested READ MORE :

"Now the UK will have something to say about it, obviously. But I think it would be a great thing. I mean, how can it be bad?"

During a subsequent engagement at the US ambassador’s residence in Ireland, Trump did not back away from his earlier answer, stating Irish unification would be "a very cool thing".

DUP leader Gavin Robinson insisted Northern Ireland's destiny would be determined by its residents, not "commentary in London, Dublin or Washington". Traditional Unionist Voice leader Jim Allister declared: "Northern Ireland is not a pawn in Trump's fallout with the UK."

‌



However, Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald described the president's observations as "timely" and said Mr Martin "must now begin planning for a united Ireland". In England, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused the president of "shooting from the hip", stating: "This sort of loose talk about the future of democratic countries is deeply unhelpful and creates unnecessary tension."

Today is Trump's second and last day of his Ireland trip as the president, along with Mr Martin and other senior Irish government figures attend the final day of play at the Irish Open, which is hosted at Trump's Doonbeg course. The leader is expected to hand over the trophy before flying back to America.

As Trump's presence in Ireland sparked protests in Dublin and Clare, a major security operation remains in place. This includes Ireland's police service An Garda Síochána liaising with the Defence Forces and US Secret Service in the area around the resort.

Article continues below

Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly said there would be "no tolerance" for public disorder or attempts to impact "critical movements" of the US president. A small number of protesters gathered at Shannon Airport today.

News.title: Boy, 13, dies weeks before birthday after 'hay fever' symptoms were cancer
News.content:
Boy, 13, dies weeks before birthday after 'hay fever' symptoms were cancer

Jake Swinscoe underwent months of chemotherapy and proton beam radiotherapy before the rare cancer spread, leaving him to make the heartbreaking decision to stop the treatment

View 3 Images Jake told his family: "We tried out best" (Image: Lynsey Swinscoe / SWNS)

A 13-year-old boy died from an aggressive cancer after his mum initially mistook his symptoms for hay fever and end-of-term tiredness.

‌



Jake Swinscoe was diagnosed with stage 3 fusion-positive alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma in July 2023 and died just two weeks before his 14th birthday.

‌



Before doctors discovered the rare soft-tissue cancer, Jake had suffered from a stuffy nose, watery eyes and tiredness. His mum Lynsey Swinscoe had been giving him antihistamines before school, believing seasonal allergies were to blame. The family only realised something more serious could be wrong after noticing swelling across the bridge of his nose.

‌



View 3 Images Lynsey is now training to become a radiotherapist in her son's memory (Image: Lynsey Swinscoe / SWNS)

Dad given hours to live after pub roast dinner leaves him fighting for life READ MORE :

British dad to face court after two-year-old son fell 33ft from Cyprus hotel READ MORE :

Jake later underwent nine rounds of chemotherapy and 28 sessions of proton beam radiotherapy in London. But after the cancer spread and further treatment left him seriously unwell, he made the decision to stop chemotherapy.

Jake died peacefully at home on April 26, 2024. Before his death, he made one poignant request to his mum, telling her: “I want to be well-known and not forgotten.”

‌



Lynsey, 43, is now honouring that wish through charity work and by training to become a radiotherapist after being inspired by the care her son received. Looking back at the first signs that something was wrong, she said: “We thought the symptoms were nothing more than hay fever at first.

“Jake was tired, had a stuffy nose and watery eyes, and I was giving him antihistamines before school each morning, which seemed to work. So we didn’t think anything was seriously wrong. He was also tired but we thought it was the hot weather and end of term tiredness.

“Then we noticed a swelling across the bridge of his nose between his eyes. But even then he played sport and we thought he may have been hit with something. Our GP sent him to Salisbury District Hospital for an X-ray and they had found a mass in his nasal cavity.

‌



He was later referred to Southampton's children hospital to undertake further test, where the family were told it was likely to be rhabdomyosarcoma, a type of soft tissue cancer.

She added: “Up until then, Jake hadn’t looked particularly unwell, so I don’t think I’d fully grasped how serious it was.”

According to CCLG: The Children & Young People’s Cancer Association, some general common childhood cancer symptoms are: Feeling very tired and exhausted all of the time and/or noticeable skin paleness

Having lots of infections (such as ear, throat or chest) that don't go away or keep coming back

Having flu-like symptoms that don't go away (such as lethargy, high temperature, being sick)

*Unexplained or excessive bleeding such as in urine, poo or when being sick

*Bruising easily or a rash of small red spots on the skin (called 'petechiae')

*Persistent and unexplained sweating or fever especially at night

*Aches and pains that don't go away, especially in the bones, joints, back or legs, and may be worse at night

*Unexplained new limp or leg weakness

*Changes when going for a poo such as constipation, diarrhoea, pain or feeling of not having finished

*Feeling a lump, swelling or unusual firmness anywhere on the body, especially in the abdomen, neck, chest, pelvis or armpits

*Losing a significant and unexplained amount of weight in teenagers

*Slow growth in children

*Change in behaviour such as persistent crying and screaming in young children, sleeping a lot, being off food

‌



Jake underwent nine rounds of chemotherapy between August and March, as well as 28 sessions of proton beam radiotherapy in London.

After his final chemotherapy treatment, an MRI scan revealed the cancer had spread to his lymph nodes.

Lynsey added: “Further chemotherapy was offered to help manage his symptoms and prolong his life, but shortly after starting treatment he suffered severe seizures. His first seizure nearly killed him and he spent time in intensive care.

‌



“After that he told us he didn’t want any more chemotherapy because it made him feel so ill.

“Jake was incredibly calm. He simply said, ‘We tried our best.’ One of the things he said that always makes me smile was, ‘At least I won’t have to deal with the cost-of-living crisis.’”

Jake lived for another four weeks after deciding to stop treatment. During that time, his family focused on making the most of the moments he still felt well enough to enjoy.

‌



View 3 Images His mum Lynsey initially thought his symptoms were seasonal allergies (Image: Lynsey Swinscoe / SWNS)

Lynsey said: “We took him fishing, which he loved, and he finally got to see his sister catch a fish, something that had always been on his bucket list. We were also able to arrange some special experiences for him. He received messages from YouTuber Daz Games and Formula One driver Lando Norris, and he got to ride in a supercar.

“Most importantly, we spent time together as a family, rewatching his favourite TV shows and seeing loved ones.

‌



“Before he died, Jake even gave us instructions for his funeral. He wanted a blue coffin and specific songs played like Here Comes The Sun by the Beatles. It showed the kind of person he was, thoughtful and remarkably mature for someone so young.”

Lynsey, who is also mum to Ava, 19, has since secured a place to study Radiotherapy at the University of Liverpool. She has also joined forces with CCLG: The Children & Young People’s Cancer Association to promote its campaign aiming to improve early diagnosis.

Lynsey hopes to raise awareness of childhood cancer symptoms, secure better research funding and push for kinder treatments for young patients. She added: “What shocked me most was being told that the treatment Jake received had barely changed in 40 years.

Article continues below

“As a parent, that doesn’t feel good enough. We need kinder, more effective treatments for children facing this disease.”

News.title: Dad given hours to live after pub roast dinner leaves him fighting for life
News.content:
Dad given hours to live after pub roast dinner leaves him fighting for life

Udhyam's family were told he was the sickest patient in the hospital before he spent two weeks in a coma and began a long recovery that included learning how to walk again

View 4 Images Doctors warned the family Udhyam may not survive the ordeal (Image: GESH / SWNS)

A dad-of-three was given just hours to live after falling critically ill following a roast chicken dinner at his local pub.

‌



Udhyam Amin, 64, was rushed to hospital with suspected food poisoning after becoming unwell following the meal in February. Doctors later discovered he had contracted Campylobacter, a common cause of food poisoning, before his condition spiralled into sepsis and multi-organ failure.

‌



Udhyam, from Kingswood, Surrey, was still conscious and talking to relatives when he arrived at St Helier Hospital in Sutton, South London, despite complaining of severe stomach pain. But his blood pH had dropped to dangerously low levels and he was quickly taken into a resuscitation room.

‌



View 4 Images The dad-of-three is now back home (Image: GESH / SWNS)

Andy Burnham taking part in Great North Run to raise funds for homeless charity READ MORE :

His condition then deteriorated rapidly and he suffered a cardiac arrest before being transferred to intensive care and placed on a ventilator. His family were warned he was the sickest patient in the hospital, he might not survive the journey to intensive care and could have hours to live.

Udhyam’s daughter, Parisha Bains, 33, recalled: “It felt like our world had fallen apart. Nothing prepares you for hearing that the person you love may not make it through the day. We were told he had gone into sepsis and multi-organ failure. Most of his critical organs had shut down.

‌



“It’s nothing short of a miracle that he is still with us. We laugh and joke that he’s like a cat with nine lives.”

As his loved ones prepared for the worst, staff at St Helier worked through the night to keep him alive. Parisha, a surgical registrar at Epsom and St Helier University Hospitals NHS Trust, said: “They comforted us through endless uncertainty, answered every question with kindness, celebrated every tiny improvement with us and gave us hope when hope seemed impossible to find.

“But he made it through the night and that wasn’t expected. One of the first things he asked us when he woke up was what date it was because he had to submit his tax returns!”

‌



View 4 Images Udhyam had to learn to walk again after the illness (Image: GESH / SWNS)

Udhyam spent two weeks in an induced coma before beginning a long recovery. The former sub-postmaster turned businessman had to learn to walk again, speak clearly and slowly rebuild the strength he had lost.

He has since returned home to his family and is back working seven days a week. Udhyam said: “Words cannot express my gratitude for the exceptional care, compassion and dedication the medical teams showed me during the most difficult time of my life.

‌



“Their skill and commitment saved my life, and I will be forever grateful. I cannot thank them enough for giving me a second chance.”

Staff nurse Pooja Rani, who was part of Udhyam’s care team, said: “Udhyam was one of the sickest patients we cared for at that time, so seeing him make such a remarkable recovery and return home to his family is exactly why we do what we do.

“It was a privilege to be part of his journey, and we’re all delighted to see him back enjoying life again.”

‌



View 4 Images The family have raised over £37,000 to help other critically ill patients (Image: GESH / SWNS)

Udhyam and his family have now launched a fundraiser for Epsom and St Helier Hospitals Charity in support of the intensive care unit which treated him. More than £37,000 has already been raised, with the family hoping the money will help other critically ill patients and support relatives going through similarly difficult stays in hospital.

Molly Simpson, head of charity and fundraising at Epsom and St Helier Hospitals Charity, said: “Udhyam’s story is both remarkable and inspiring. We are enormously thankful to Udhyam’s family for turning their gratitude into action by raising funds to support St Helier.”

Article continues below

You can donate here

News.title: 'Our girl was murdered by boyfriend - killers like hers are getting off lightly'
News.content:
Watching pornography and looking up serial killers on the internet, sadistic Ross McCullam clearly felt no remorse. The 30-year-old lab technician had just dumped his girlfriend’s body under some bracken down a country lane, having strangled and attempted to decapitate her at his parents’ Leicestershire home.

Tomorrow night, Elaine and Anthony Newborough will once again be made to relive the horror of their daughter, 23-year-old Megan Newborough’s murder, when her story becomes the focus of an episode of Channel 4 series 999 What Happened Next. But the couple - who are staunch supporters of The Mirror’s Justice For Our Daughters campaign, which has successfully advocated for tougher sentences and system reforms to protect women from domestic violence killers - are willing participants.

For, while McCullam was convicted of murder at Leicester Crown Court in December 2022 and jailed for a minimum of 23 years, had Megan been murdered outside the home, the minimum tariff would have been 25 years. And the couple are campaigning for disparity in sentences to change.

View 7 Images Elaine and Anthony Newborough, pictured at their home in Nuneaton, Warwickshire (Image: Rowan Griffiths / Daily Mirror)

‌



Anthony, 58, senior account manager for a chemical business, says: “If a woman - because it’s mostly women - dies by the hands of her partner at home, their killer gets a more lenient sentence. It’s grossly unfair.” In the UK, murder by strangulation currently has a minimum sentence of 15 years, as does murder committed with a knife in a home setting - compared to 25 years if committed elsewhere

A breakthrough came this July, when David Lammy, then Secretary of State for Justice, announced in Parliament his decision to increase the minimum sentence for intimate partner or ex-partner murders to 25 years in England and Wales. But, with Lammy now replaced by Alex Norris, no change has yet been made and Anthony and Elaine - who met the new Secretary of State last week who promised to follow this up - are calling for action, not words.

The couple, who launched the Megan Newborough Foundation to fight to stop violence against women - as well as supporting The Dogs Trust, as she left behind her beloved pet dog Frank - also joined campaign group Killed Women to challenge sentencing disparities.

Elaine, 55, who works in an estate agency, says: ”Time is of the essence. Since Killed Women was formed [in November 2022], over 800 women have lost their lives in their homes at the hands of their partners. How many more killers will be given lenient sentences before women’s lives are seen to matter? Sometimes bodies aren’t even found. Their starting point [for a prison sentence] is 15 years. It’s unacceptable.”

‌



The Killed Women group includes Carole Gould, whose daughter Ellie was killed by her ex boyfriend in 2019; Julie Devey, whose daughter Poppy was killed by her ex boyfriend in 2018 and Gail Smith, whose daughter Elinor O'Brien was killed by her abusive partner in 2022.

View 7 Images Sadistic killer Ross McCullam clearly felt no remorse (Image: PA)

Megan, who had an older sister Claire, now 31, and a younger brother John, 26, was working in HR when she met her killer. In an impact statement at McCullam’s trial, Claire addressed the monster saying: “I hope she haunts you.”

Living with her family in Nuneaton, Warwickshire, Megan had been seeing McCullam for a few weeks when he invited her to his parents’ home in Coalville, Leicestershire, that fateful night in August 2021 and strangled her, slicing her throat seven times with a carving knife, and partially decapitating her, before using her car to dump her body in undergrowth.

‌



He then went home and texted her to say she was “amazing” and asking if she’d got home safely, to cover his tracks - having dumped his bloody clothes in a bin and thrown away her phone.

In 999 What Happened Next, police are seen rushing to locate Megan, following Anthony’s 999 call the day after she went out, concerned about her whereabouts. Detectives discovered that McCullam had killed her within 40 minutes of her arrival at his parents’ home.

View 7 Images Anthony and Elaine on Channel 4's 999 What Happened Next (Image: Curve Media)

The brute then returned home and left a fake concerned voicemail on her phone, professing his love for her and hoping she’d got home safely.

‌



Describing Megan in an earlier interview in The Mirror in February 2024, backing Justice For Our Daughters, as “somebody everyone could relate to and talk to,” Elaine continues: “Women are dying every day. Every year, on average, over 100 women are losing their lives. How is that acceptable?”

After speaking to the Law Commission about sentencing disparities, she says they are looking at ways to make changes, but have been warned this could take a decade. Impatient for reform, Elaine has a message for lawmakers, saying: “Get it sorted. Do it sooner rather than later. We understand they have to take advice, but stop dragging your feet and do it.

“Losing your child is a living hell. And having a sentence which feels low makes it worse. No sentence would bring back our daughter - but 23 years doesn’t seem like justice.”

View 7 Images Megan Newborough is missed by all who knew her. (Image: Rowan Griffiths / Daily Mirror)

‌



Anthony says of Megan’s killer: “He’ll be out in his 50s, potentially with another 30 years of life ahead of him. Yet he took Megan’s whole life away from her. It just does not seem fair.”

The week after she was killed, Megan was due to sign for a house of her own. She had her whole life ahead of her. Now her devastated parents want to make a difference in her memory.

Anthony says: “The change [to the sentencing] has been announced. But saying it and actually doing it are two very different things. We need action. And we won’t stop until it happens, for Megan’s legacy and for families of other victims like Megan.

“The world is missing a star. Megan was a bright spark. She was a force of nature. She was the glue that stuck the family together. We miss her every single day.”

‌



Elaine continues: "She had a wicked sense of humour. Nothing will bring Megan back, but we’re determined some good must come from losing her. We want to save other women and their families from going through the same thing. And I'm sure she would be so proud of us."

View 7 Images The family of Megan Newborough: brother John, mum Elaine, dad Anthony and sister Claire. (Image: Coventry Live/Tristan Potter)

Prosecution barrister John Cammegh agrees that the sentencing disparity must end. He says: “I wanted in excess of 25 [years]. He used a knife, he partially decapitated her. But because she was murdered within his property, it does not equate to taking a knife to the scene - that is something I struggle with.”

And former safeguarding minister, Jess Phillips, who has supported Elaine and lobby group Killed Women from its inception, adds: “Megan would be incredibly proud of her family and it has been an honour to work with them for many years.

‌



“The fundamental principle that domestic murder has to be considered equal to all other murders has ended a discrepancy that meant women's lives mattered less. Megan mattered.”

Meanwhile, Lord Chancellor Alex Norris, tells The Mirror: “I pay tribute to Elaine and Anthony Newborough, as well as Carole Gould and Julie Devey of Killed Women, who fought so bravely for this vital change[in sentencing] in the face of devastating loss.

View 7 Images Megan's dad Anthony said of her loss: "The world is missing a star." (Image: Rowan Griffiths / Daily Mirror)

“It’s a testament to their daughters’ legacies and their brave work, alongside the Mirror’s Justice for our Daughters campaign, will make sure future women and girls get the justice they deserve. I’m committed to closing this overdue gap in the law which will help ensure these heinous crimes are given a sentence which better reflects the catastrophic harm they cause.”

‌



*999 What Happened Next, Mondays at 9pm on Channel 4

News.title: Orlando Bloom begs for international aid at world's largest refugee camp as cuts fuel crisis
News.content:
Orlando Bloom begs for international aid at world's largest refugee camp as cuts fuel crisis

EXCLUSIVE: The Hollywood star, 49, called for action to help those on the brink of despair in the Cox's Bazar refugee camp where more than 1million Rohingya Muslims are facing a humanitarian crisis

View 5 Images More than one million refugees live in a network of 33 camps in Cox's Bazar in Bangladesh

Thousands of ramshackle homes line up row after row in the world’s largest refugee camp - as international aid cuts risk plunging fleeing Rohingya Muslims further into a humanitarian crisis.

‌



Astonishing drone footage shows the scale of the site at Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, where more than 1 million people are struggling to survive in a network of 33 squalid camps. Cuts to international aid - including an expected 40 per cent slash to UK budgets - has threatened to leave a generation of children lost.

‌



Now UNICEF is warning they are facing a £10 million funding gap, as they revealed Bangladesh alone has suffered a 56 per cent in bilateral UK aid. Today Hollywood star Orlando Bloom, 49, who visited the camp last year, urged global leaders to step up and help those most at risk of exploitation.

‌



View 5 Images UNICEF Goodwill Ambassador Orlando Bloom visited the camp at Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh, last year to meet children (Image: © UNICEF/UNI894760/Royena Rasnat. All rights reserved.)

Nigel Farage accused of trying to distract from Reform donations scandal with burka ban READ MORE :

Myanmar festival bombing: Dozens killed in horror paraglider raid at major event READ MORE :

The Pirates of the Caribbean actor told the Mirror: "The children I met in Cox's Bazar had dreams for their future. Today, those dreams are at risk. Funding cuts are pushing essential services to breaking point, leaving Rohingya children more vulnerable to illness, violence and missing out on education.

"These children have already endured unimaginable hardship. Their childhoods should not depend on political choices made thousands of miles away, including the decision to cut aid. If caring about childhood is yes in principle, it should be yes in practice.

‌



"That means investing in the health, education and protection children need not just to survive, but to thrive, fulfil their potential and become unstoppable." It is almost a decade since a brutal campaign of persecution forced more than a million Rohingya Muslims to flee Myanmar and make a terrifying journey into neighbouring Bangladesh.

View 5 Images Orlando called for investment in "the health, education and protection children need not just to survive, but to thrive" (Image: © UNICEF/UNI893958/Royena Rasnat. All rights reserved.)

Since then, they have made their homes in Cox’s Bazar, where aid agencies have battled to provide a sustainable place to live. But despite their efforts, they say more than 150,000 children are unable to access education.

‌



Elsewhere 954,616 refugees, including 290,455 children aged under five, have reported skin diseases since January 2025. More than 800 children were affected by grave violations, including abduction, recruitment, injuries and sexual violence, in the first quarter of 2026 alone.

It comes as UNICEF UK launches a new campaign, No Choice But Childhood, highlighting how conflict, extreme poverty and climate change are cutting childhood short for millions of children around the world, while aid cuts risk undermining decades of progress.

View 5 Images Aid agencies say cuts to international aid are undermining the progress being made in the world's largest refugee camp

‌



Jo Rea, UNICEF UK Director of Advocacy, said: "Extreme poverty, climate change and conflict are cutting childhood short for millions of children around the world. Yet with the right investment, a different future is possible.

"As aid cuts threaten to undermine decades of progress, UNICEF UK is calling on the UK Government to dedicate 25% of its international development budget to support and strengthen the vital services and systems that children around the world rely on every day to survive and thrive."

In 2016 the Mirror visited Banfladesh and watched as thousands of Rohingya Muslims trekked for days to escape the hell of Myanmar’s Rakhine district where they were forced out by the military. They found themselves in Cox’s Bazar – 70 miles south of Bangladesh’s financial capital Chittagong.

‌



View 5 Images In 2016 the Mirror's Dan Warburton visited the Cox's Bazar camp to see first-hand the conditions facing fleeing Rohingya Muslims (Image: Sunday Mirror)

Myanmar is overwhelmingly Bhuddist and regards the Rohingya as illegal immigrants. The clan – the world’s largest group of stateless people – have been denied citizenship.

The current cycle of misery began in 2012 when rioting left 200 dead, mainly Rohingya. Muslims were largely driven out of the cities and 130,000 set up home in camps in Bangladesh.

Article continues below

An FCDO Spokesperson said: "The UK remains committed to supporting some of the world's most vulnerable people, with over 70% of all UK geographic support allocated to the most fragile and conflict-affected states.

"Across our development work, children remain a priority, including through programmes that boost education outcomes, tackle child malnutrition, champion the rights of women and girls, support vital healthcare services and respond to the climate crisis."

News.title: Reform's £72m donations 'entirely in line with law', Jenrick says
News.content:
Robert Jenrick has said Reform UK believed that Â£72m in donations it has received from two cryptocurrency billionaires were "entirely in line with the law".

The party's economic spokesman told the BBC that he did not expect that it will have to return any of the money from Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, who are both British and have spent time living overseas.

The government is seeking to change the law on donations to UK political parties from British expats, including a Â£100,000 cap backdated to 25 March.

"These two donations are entirely in line with the law as it is and, as far as we know, the law as it's going to be in the future," Jenrick said.

As well as limiting how much British citizens can donate to political parties from overseas, the government has proposed a minimum residency period in which the Â£100,000 cap would still apply for those who move back to the UK.

This would be in place for the remainder of the calendar year and the following calendar year after the person returns.

Housing Secretary Angela Rayner told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that the rule changes would apply retrospectively and anyone not complying with them would have "to return that money".

Rayner added she was not commenting specifically on Delo and Harborne as she does not "understand" their "circumstances".

Answering questions about the donations following Rayner's remarks, Jenrick said: "It might be that Angela Rayner or the government keep trying to change the law to make it even harder for people to donate to Reform, nothing would surprise me.

"But, as it stands, we believe these are entirely in line with the law."

BBC News has been told that both Delo and Harborne have returned to the UK. Delo is understood to have been back in the country since last year.

Jenrick said Delo had returned to the UK "in part so that he can comply with the changes to the law".

In a statement after the programme, a Reform UK spokesman said: "We are 100% confident both [donations] are legal and won't ever have to handed back."

One person familiar with the government's proposed changes said the issue of whether Delo and Harborne are affected would likely come down to how ministers choose to define UK residency.

They said one way would be to adopt the same definition used in tax laws, but stressed how complex the rules around residency are.

News.title: Andy Burnham among Great North Run finishers
News.content:
The Great North Run (GNR) returned to Tyneside this weekend, with 63,000 runners taking part in the world's biggest half marathon - including Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

England star and Newcastle captain Dan Burn rang the starter's bell, with famous faces including football personality Chris Kamara and fitness coach Joe Wicks taking on the challenge.

The 13.1-mile (21km) event saw runners and wheelchair users race from Newcastle through Gateshead and South Tyneside, before finishing in South Shields.

Britons David Weir and Melanie Woods won the men's and women's elite wheelchair races respectively. Brigid Kosgei won the elite women's contest and Zouhair Talbi won the men's race.

The half marathon is in its 45th year and raises about Â£25m for charity each time.

News.title: 'Slim chance' government will hit 1.5m new homes target, Rayner tells BBC
News.content:
There is only a "slim chance" the government will meet its target of building 1.5 million homes in England by the next election, Housing Secretary Angela Rayner has told the BBC.

"Headwinds" including the Iran war and rising construction costs are making it harder to meet the key Labour manifesto pledge, Rayner told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg.

"But I'm definitely not giving it up," she said, and stressed that the government was "making a difference" through investing billions in social and affordable homes.

Data up to June this year suggested the government was behind on the rate of construction needed to meet the goal, which housebuilders have previously warned was too optimistic.

Labour promised to hit the target through building both private and social housing by the end of the current parliament, meaning summer 2029 at the latest.

This implied an average of 300,000 new properties would be needed each year - a rate of construction not seen in decades.

Rayner told the BBC on Sunday: "It's a slim chance, but I'm definitely not giving it up."

She said it was important to keep the goal - which she said had always been a "stretch target" - in place, but that she was "being honest with the public" that it would be difficult to achieve.

News.title: Trump doubles down on united Ireland comments on day two of visit
News.content:
President Donald Trump has doubled down on his support for a united Ireland.

He's on day two of a visit, which he is spending at Trump International Golf Links in Doonbeg, County Clare, for the Irish Open.

On Saturday, Trump told reporters he would love to see a united Ireland while at a meeting with the Taoiseach (Irish PM) MicheÃ¡l Martin in Dublin.

Speaking on Sunday at his Doonbeg golf resort, he said it would be natural to put Ireland and Northern Ireland "together".

He spoke to reporters after watching the tournament leader Irish golfer Shane Lowry tee off.

He described what he said about a united Ireland as "a fairly routine comment".

News.title: US embassy child abuse images suspect flown from UK before police interview
News.content:
A US embassy staffer accused of possessing indecent images of children, was detained at his south London flat and flown out of the UK in August, without being first questioned by British police.

The US Embassy confirmed to the BBC that authorities are investigating the allegations and they have reassigned the staff member to the US while inquiries continue.

"The United States government expects all personnel to adhere to the highest standards of conduct, and we take these allegations seriously," embassy officials said in a statement.

They added that they "quickly informed UK law enforcement and took swift action."

It is understood the individual worked at the US embassy in Vauxhall, south west London, and though not a diplomat, he enjoyed the umbrella of diplomatic protection.

He was flown back to the United States on a commercial flight, but their investigations are ongoing in conjunction with UK authorities.

It is also understood Home Office ministers and the Metropolitan Police are in close contact with the US embassy on this matter as investigations continue.

A UK government spokesperson said: "We expect all foreign diplomats in the UK to abide by our laws, in the same way we expect all UK diplomats to do so when posted overseas."

News.title: Tom Felton: I'm so excited to see Rupert Grint play Ron Weasley again
News.content:
Every night on Broadway, Tom Felton walks on stage to a roar from the audience. He had expected the reaction to die down after the first week, but it never did.

Almost 15 years after his final appearance as Draco Malfoy on screen, Felton has spent the past 10 months playing the character again in the Broadway production of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child.

I meet the actor in a dressing room at NBC Studios, just off Times Square in New York. He's just finished a live television appearance and in a few hours will be back on stage for his next performance.

He greets me with a hug and says he is excited to speak to BBC News because his mum and 100-year-old grandfather will see it. His family are some of his biggest supporters - his mum has seen the show five times already, while his dad is due to visit next month.

That support mirrors the enthusiasm Felton has encountered from Harry Potter fans, which he says still surprises him more than two decades after he first played Draco.

"I thought the applause would stop in the first week and it has not.

"It's very humbling and lovely to know how much the characters still mean to people now and if it brings them to the theatre, that's the best."

He is also struck by how many of the fans now approaching him were not alive when the first Harry Potter film was released.

"There are fans that approach me shouting 'Draco' who weren't even born when I was in the first film," he says.

News.title: Flattened molars and facial pain: Why are more young people grinding their teeth?
News.content:
Ella can't remember when she first started grinding her teeth at night, but she can vividly recall the excruciating jaw ache, the headaches, and being told her molars were disappearing.

"I was in so much pain," Ella says. "My face was changing shape and my teeth were at risk of breaking - I knew I had to do something about it."

The 31-year-old has bruxism, a condition which can cause regular and often intense teeth grinding, but says the treatment she's recently had has "without a doubt" changed her life.

Bruxism affects millions like Ella across the UK, external. Some studies suggest nearly one in four people experience the condition, although many may be unaware until symptoms appear.

According to the British Dental Association there is some anecdotal evidence that bruxism is becoming more common, but no specific figures. However, some dentists have told the BBC they are worried about the increasing number of young people they're seeing with dental problems caused by incessant gnashing.

"It is definitely on the rise," Dr Aditi Desai, president of the British Society of Dental Sleep Medicine (BSDSM), says. "And it's no surprise given that life itself nowadays can be so stressful."

News.title: Will the Thirlwall report change the debate about Lucy Letby?
News.content:
The quick take is this. The report won't change the narrative about Letby's guilt or innocence because it didn't examine that subject at all. That wasn't its remit.

Lady Justice Thirlwall said she had "approached the inquiry on the basis that Lucy Letby is guilty of the crimes of which she has been convicted".

She emphasised that it was not her role "to set about reviewing the convictions", telling the inquiry: "The Court of Appeal has done that, with a very clear result."

But there is also a longer, more complex answer.

Whatever the report's conclusions, Letby's convictions will stand. However, the inquiry hasn't operated in a vacuum. There are other parts of the legal system which will have an eye on its findings.

And the chairwoman of the Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC) - the only organisation with the power to send Letby's case back to the Court of Appeal - has told the BBC the CCRC will be paying close attention to Thirlwall.

Dame Vera Baird said: "We will be looking at the report with interest to assess whether it has any bearing on our review of the case."

The CCRC has given no indication of when it will make its decision.

But while questions over Letby's convictions weren't within the scope of the Thirlwall Inquiry, it didn't stop the subject making itself felt within the hearing room.

Just as the inquiry was wrapping up, the hospital's former executives applied for it to be delayed until the CCRC has made its decision.

Letters pushing for a delay were also written to the inquiry by Letby's lawyers and Sir David Davis, an MP who has campaigned on her behalf.

Sir David argued that an inquiry "predicated on the presumption that Lucy Letby's conviction is safe, when there is now a wealth of authoritative voices questioning that conviction, will only undermine the conclusions arrived at by your inquiry and potentially lead to more babies dying unnecessarily".

Lady Justice Thirlwall refused the requests to pause the inquiry. She said that she was not scrutinising Letby's actions, but those of the officials and managers who were responsible for responding to the crisis.

News.title: Europe must endure winter of hardship to keep pressure on Putin, says PM's security adviser
News.content:
Powell said "we cannot turn that into an advantage for Putin", adding that pressure on Putin was working "and that means we have to keep the pressure up".

"It will require some real hardship and difficulties on our parts," he added. "But we will have to swallow that and we have to keep the economic, military, political and diplomatic support going for Ukraine."

While admitting that things in Ukraine did "feel a bit difficult at the moment", with a lack of Patriot air defence missiles, strikes on businesses and the governments budget deficit, Powell insisted "there are strong reasons for optimism".

He said Trump â who has blown hot and cold on Ukraine â was "in a very different place".

"He sees that Ukraine is doing better and therefore he is not leaning in the direction of Putin in the way that he was previously. I think that's a really big asset."

Powell said Russia was no longer claiming the US had agreed that Ukraine should give up territory and hopes of Nato membership at last year's Trump-Putin summit in Alaska.

"The so-called Anchorage compromise is firmly dead," he said. "We can stop worrying about it. It's finished."

This meant "we can look for serious ways of getting to a negotiated settlement, rather than waiting for the Ukrainian people to hand over territory the Russians have not been able to conquer", Powell said.

Ukrainian commanders had successfully held the front line on the ground while Russia had reached 1.5 million casualties, Ukraine had increasingly struck deep within Russian territory while Europe's resolve remained solid, he noted.

"The strategy is to apply enough pressure to make [Putin] want to get into negotiation," Powell said.

"And I think that the escalation we hear talk about is not a problem - it's a sign of success, because what's happening is the pressure that we are putting on Putin is finally paying off."

Putin himself has given little sign he is feeling under pressure, telling journalists earlier this month: "I have no doubt that the enemy will crumble."

Meanwhile, Ukrainian authorities have begun evacuating some residents in Slovyansk and Kramatorsk, the biggest cities still under full Ukrainian control in the eastern Donbas region. Russia claims sovereignty over the Donbas and fully capturing it is a key objective for Moscow.

Powell said the war was "not about territory" but about "the right of Ukraine to be independent", adding that "to the extent that [Putin] gains another 10km of land or loses another 40km of land, this war is already won".

"That's the threat to him at home. There is a free, independent and European Ukraine, and people in Russia are going to notice that."

The national security adviser said it was a "mug's game" to predict when the war might end, but said Europe had to be prepared to negotiate a settlement.

"Where we least expect it, Putin will be ready to negotiate... It's all about getting him to be serious in that negotiation. And I think that strategy is beginning to work."

Powell, who helped negotiate the Good Friday Agreement in Northern Ireland, said the US and Europe should maintain contact with Putin â despite describing the Russian leader as a "terrorist".

"What we don't want is miscalculation - that they don't understand where our red lines are. That's why I think it's important the CIA went to Moscow as well."

News.title: Student loan terms to be made clearer in England following repayment row
News.content:
University applicants in England will be given clearer information about student loans before they take them out, the government has said.

Ministers said they would spell out that governments can change repayment rules and that different career choices can affect how much borrowers repay.

They agreed to some but not all of the recommendations made by MPs after an inquiry into student loans, and did not say whether they would reverse a freeze to the repayment threshold for some graduates.

The inquiry found the way loans had been presented to teenagers amounted to mis-selling, after the BBC revealed the Department for Education (DfE) had compared repayments to Â£30-a-month phone contracts.

The recent debate has centred around Plan 2 loans, which were issued in England between September 2012 and July 2023, and are still issued in Wales.

The interest rate on those loans is the Retail Prices Index (RPI) measure of inflation plus up to 3% depending on earnings, and borrowers repay at a rate of 9% of everything they earn over a repayment threshold, which is meant to rise with inflation every year. The loans are written off after 30 years.

Campaigners want a lower interest rate, a lower repayment rate and for the government to reverse a decision last year to freeze the threshold at Â£29,385 for three years in England.

Freezing that threshold means graduates start repaying their loans sooner and, once they do, they pay more than they would have done if it had risen with inflation.

MPs on the Treasury Committee called for a U-turn on that decision as part of a series of recommendations after an inquiry this summer.

The Treasury and the DfE did not say whether ministers would unfreeze the threshold in their response, but said: "We keep all aspects of the student finance system under review."

News.title: Man charged with concealing identity at protest
News.content:
A man has been charged with concealing his identity at a protest in Portsmouth, after police warned they would arrest demonstrators using face masks and coverings.

Several hundred anti-migrant protesters marched through the city centre while anti-racism groups also made their way to Guildhall Square on Saturday.

Hampshire Police said Timothy Miller, 76, of Sherwood Avenue in Hedge End was charged with wearing or using an item to conceal identity at a protest. He is due before Portsmouth magistrates on Monday.

David McNally, 33, of Winchester Road in Portsmouth, was also charged with obstructing the highway and attempted criminal damage. He is due in court on 29 October.

Hampshire Police said on Friday it would use new powers under the Crime and Policing Act to prevent protesters wearing face coverings that conceal their identity.

Both sets of demonstrators were kept apart by police when they arrived at Guldhall Square.

The city centre protests followed disorder on 6 September when police attended Eastney Marina as hundreds of demonstrators blocked roads in an attempt to stop coaches carrying 120 migrants, who had crossed the Channel in a dinghy, from leaving the city.

A 16-year-old male from Waterlooville was also arrested at Saturday's protests on suspicion of violent disorder, in relation to the events at Eastney Marina.

He has been released on bail until 12 December.

Del Leon Somerville, 42, from Paulsgrove appeared at Portsmouth Magistrates Court on Saturday charged with violent disorder and assaulting a police officer at the Eastney protest.

He was remanded in custody to appear at Portsmouth Crown Court on 16 September.

News.title: Major fire at derelict mill featured in Peaky Blinders and Downton Abbey
News.content:
Another major fire has broken out at a derelict mill complex where Peaky Blinders was filmed.

The blaze at Dalton Mills in Keighley started at about 20:00 BST on Saturday and at its peak required 12 fire engines to tackle it.

West Yorkshire Fire and Rescue Service (WYFRS) confirmed that due to the severity of the incident a number of nearby residents were evacuated and at 23:00 BST, 10 fire engines were still in attendance.

A spokesperson added: "Members of the public are still advised to avoid the area to allow emergency services to operate safely and effectively."

News.title: Garcia crushes overmatched Benn in two rounds
News.content:
Ryan Garcia crushed Briton Conor Benn with a ruthless second-round stoppage to retain his WBC welterweight crown in a world title mismatch in Las Vegas.

The American dominated from the opening bell, repeatedly punishing Benn as the 29-year-old charged forward with a wild and increasingly desperate approach.

Benn was dropped by a flush right hook in round two but managed to beat the count. before Garcia continued the onslaught with Benn backed against the ropes until the referee stepped in.

"I knew he would bring the pressure, I felt the shots and though 'I'll let him have his way', but I knew his was reckless and you can't do that with me," Garcia told DAZN.

"147lb is my division. I'm here, you can trust me as a champion."

It was a sobering - and, for many in the sport, unsurprising - conclusion to the biggest night of Benn's life in boxing.

Few gave the Essex fighter much chance, with Benn, who fell to the second defeat of his 10-year professional career, having never faced an opponent of Garcia's calibre and some questioning whether he had done enough to earn a world title shot in the first place.

Benn was fighting at welterweight for the first time in more than four years and had already said this would be his final appearance in the division, regardless of the result.

Garcia, 28, stayed true to his promise to stop Benn inside five rounds as he made a successful first defence of the title with his 26th win from 28 professional contests.

News.title: Shocked walker finds SUV blocking route on Wales Coast Path
News.content:
Stunned walker Canberk Beker could not believe his eyes when he came across a car blocking his way on the Wales Coast Path.

The 31-year-old was out for a stroll with wife Bethan Jones, also 31, when they saw the blue Kia Sportage on Saturday morning between Mumbles and Langland Bay.

The driver had managed to wedge the SUV between a concrete fence post on one side and a bench on the other.

Canberk, from Langland, in Swansea, said: "It was completely covering the path. I was looking inside the car."

South Wales Police said it did not attend the scene, while a local councillor believes the driver mistakenly drove down a walking path believing to be a road before getting stuck.

News.title: Watch: Is the Bayeux Tapestry exhibition worth the hype?
News.content:
Visitors flocked to the British Museum in London on Thursday as the Bayeux Tapestry exhibition opened its doors to the general public.

The Bayeux Tapestry is an embroidery almost 70m (230ft) in length and nearly 1,000 years old. It tells the story of the Norman conquest of England and the Battle of Hastings in 1066.

Adult tickets to see the tapestry are priced at Â£33 during peak times and Â£27 at off-peak times, with an additional Â£3.50 donation.

The BBC's Katie Razzall asked the first visitors if it was worth the price.

News.title: Gruffalo Granny illustrator says rise of AI images 'worrying'
News.content:
The illustrator for the Gruffalo books has said images created by artificial intelligence (AI) are "worrying".

Axel Scheffler said AI pictures are "a breach of copyright" and lose their charm when compared to the hand-drawn originals.

He was speaking to the BBC alongside author Dame Julia Donaldson for the launch of their new book Gruffalo Granny, with Dame Julia reading an extract.

News.title: F1 Spanish GP LIVE: Race result with Antonelli extending lead in world championship
News.content:
( Getty )

Kimi Antonelli took a major stride towards becoming the youngest Formula One world champion ever with victory at the Spanish Grand Prix.

The 20-year-old took advantage of Lance Stroll putting his Aston Martin in the wall to earn a free pit-stop during a Virtual Safety Car period before galloping to his eighth win from the 14 rounds so far.

While fortune was on Antonelli’s side, Lando Norris’ luck was out. The world champion was comfortably leading when Stroll crashed on the 14th lap.

But Norris drove past the pit-lane entry just as the VSC was deployed. Norris stopped on the next lap and a slow front-right tyre change lost the British driver even more time.

Having held a seven-second advantage over Antonelli prior to Stroll’s accident, Norris left the pits 13 seconds adrift of the Italian and, despite catching Max Verstappen, he was unable to find a way ahead of the Red Bull driver – even though he claimed the Dutchman illegally ran off the road in his defence of second place on the penultimate lap.

Verstappen finished runner-up, 4.3 sec behind Antonelli, with Norris third, just seven tenths back. George Russell crossed the line in fifth – the British driver questioning Mercedes’ decision to move him on to a unique two-stop strategy – to allow Antonelli to extend his title margin from 66 points to an eye-watering 81 with nine scheduled rounds remaining.

Follow live updates from the Spanish Grand Prix with The Independent

News.title: Man United v Man City LIVE: Team news as protests erupt ahead of crucial Manchester derby
News.content:
United vs City - Maresca faces first Manchester derby

Manchester United host Manchester City in the derby at Old Trafford as the two clubs battle for bragging rights.

Michael Carrick has endured a tough start to the season with disappointing results at newly promoted Hull City and at Everton, but a victory here would boost the mood in the red half of Manchester – as well as hopes of finishing above City for the first time in 14 years now that Pep Guardiola’s reign is over.

Enzo Maresca’s City side have not been wholly convincing either, struggling past Coventry City at the Etihad Stadium last time out, but they still have a perfect record in the Premier League and can open up an eight-point gap over United with victory at the home of their fierce rivals.

Who will triumph in the Manchester derby? Follow all the latest updates below.

News.title: Kimi Antonelli oozes composure with another F1 victory as debut Madrid race fails to fire
News.content:

Generally, there are two roads to take when assessing an inaugural Formula One grand prix. The first: the show, the core parameters by which F1’s glitzy American owners judge their events. And in this respect Madrid, with a sold-out 353,000 spectators across three days at the brand-new street circuit in the north-east of the city, has been something of a success.

Yet the race? The actual sport? It has to be said: less impressive. There were always concerns about the action out on-track on Sunday, given the narrow, twisty nature of this 22-turn circuit next to Real Madrid’s training ground. Without a significant shunt and red-flag-induced drama, overtaking proved as difficult as expected. It wasn’t a complete snooze-fest, by any means, but compared to the first Las Vegas race in 2023 – the last new track on the calendar, which enjoyed an action-packed grand prix after earlier logistical issues – the new Spanish Grand Prix in the capital failed to fire.

One person who will not care, however, is Kimi Antonelli. With every week and every event, the 20-year-old Italian is oozing composure, assuredness and looking like the champion-in-waiting. Here, starting in second, the Mercedes driver bided his time for most of the 57-lap race behind Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc, ready to pounce and grasp P1 when the Monegasque made his mandatory pit stop. Lo and behold, with six laps to go, Antonelli cruised into first place and never looked likely to relinquish his lead to Max Verstappen and Lando Norris behind.

open image in gallery Kimi Antonelli won the inaugural Spanish Grand Prix ( Reuters )

Norris can count himself mighty unfortunate. Starting quickly and keeping the lead at the start from pole position, the McLaren driver looked well-placed before a virtual safety car on lap 15 screwed his pit-stop plans. He lost bags of time in the 550-metre-long pit-lane and, ultimately, could not make it up on-track. Even Antonelli stated on team radio afterwards that he “felt bad for Lando.”

Norris had to settle for third, on a day to forget for the leading British contingent. George Russell, losing more ground in the title race, finished fifth, while Lewis Hamilton retired in the opening minutes due to a brake issue. It has been a week to forget for the Ferrari driver, a week on from his intra-team squabble in Monza.

It had all started so promisingly for Hamilton, too. Out of the top four on the grid, the seven-time world champion had the best start and looked well placed to move up to second, before the Briton was squeezed by Antonelli at the ultra-tight turn one before Verstappen slammed the window shut, cutting the chicane in the process.

“Max has to give that back,” implored Hamilton and Red Bull, to their star driver’s dismay, agreed. Verstappen, when told by race engineer Gianpiero Lambiase to drop back, was apopleptically cross. “What the f*** are you guys talking about? He would’ve shunted into me! If he crashes into me, we’d have been out of the race.”

open image in gallery Ferrari driver Lewis Hamilton retired from Sunday’s Spanish Grand Prix (David Davies/PA) ( PA Wire )

open image in gallery Hamilton clashed with Max Verstappen at the start ( Getty )

Reluctantly, Verstappen relented and dropped back on lap four. Yet a lap later, it would all prove inconsequential as Hamilton complained to his Ferrari engineer Carlo Santi – who has been on the end of a fair few punchy comments over team radio in recent weeks – about brake issues. “I can’t stop the car,” Hamilton bemoaned, as he then proved when he went off at turn 20.

Top-10 - Spanish Grand Prix 1. Kimi Antonelli (Mercedes) 2. Max Verstappen (Red Bull) 3. Lando Norris (McLaren) 4. Charles Leclerc (Ferrari) 5. George Russell (Mercedes) 6. Liam Lawson (Red Bull) 7. Franco Colapinto (Alpine) 8. Oscar Piastri (McLaren) 9. Arvid Lindblad (Racing Bulls) 10. Nico Hulkenberg (Audi)

Dropping to dead last, a retirement was inevitable and the 41-year-old, a six-time winner of this grand prix in Barcelona and three months on from his first Ferrari triumph in Catalunya in June, was out of Madrid’s inaugural event, with close friend and Real Madrid star Jude Bellingham watching on in the pit-lane.

But the game-changing flashpoint came on lap 15. To Norris’s dismay, Lance Stroll leaving the track and parking his failed Aston Martin by the wall triggered a virtual safety car and McLaren, unfortunately, fell on the wrong side of the coin. While those behind the race leader pitted, the reigning world champion stayed out and by the time he made his way to the pit-lane, green-flag conditions meant maximum speeds back on track.

In the blink of an eye, Norris had lost his lead and had dropped to fourth. To his credit, the Bristolian remained composed despite the rotten luck.

open image in gallery Lando Norris had to settle for third ( Getty )

The tone for the rest of the grand prix, with overtaking at a premium here given the lack of long straights, was now set. Leclerc opted to stay out in front, pleading for another safety car or incident which never came, with Antonelli just biding his time to pounce in second place.

His engineer, Peter Bonnington, urged the championship leader to conserve his hard tyres. And when Leclerc pitted on lap 50, Antonelli had enough rubber to cruise home to victory – his eighth triumph of an outstanding season to date. Bonnington called it a “masterclass” but Antonelli, mature beyond his years, remained calm, acknowledging that fortune fell his way. “It feels good to win but Lando deserved to win,” he said afterwards. “We take it; we had really good pace.”

With team Russell, starting on hards, opting for a two-stop strategy and ultimately losing out with a fifth-place finish, it means Antonelli now has an 81-point lead in the world championship with a scheduled nine rounds remaining. With every week, as Russell tries and fails to wrangle back some momentum, Antonelli is inching ever closer to becoming the sport’s youngest-ever champion.

Not a shoo-in just yet, but the ultimate prize is now creeping tantalisingly into view.

The White House social media team took time to lash out at a reporter after the journalist pointed out that Donald Trump’s aide Natalie Harp was among the aides following the president to his golf club in Ireland this weekend.

The Rapid Response 47 account, which is often the vessel for the White House to reprimand reporters it claims are being unfair to the president, referred to independent journalist Aaron Rupar as a “sick, deluded freak” after Rupar posted on his X account, “Look who made the trip to Ireland! #TravelWithNatalie”, using a hashtag he has used to document instances where Harp has been spotted close by the president’s side.

“President Trump does, in fact, travel with staff. Aaron, on the other hand, is a sick, deluded freak (in his 40s) who sits behind a keyboard and posts creepy things like this,” wrote the White House account.

Rupar replied: “I know being in my 40s makes me too old for the president but I’m at peace with it.”

Trump spent the weekend in Ireland at his Trump International Golf Links resort in Doonbeg, Ireland, where he is watching the Irish Open.

open image in gallery Natalie Harp boards Marine One as she traveled this weekend with Donald Trump to Ireland ( PA )

Attention has surrounded the 35-year-old Harp after the publication of media reports documenting the unconventional close relationship she has with the president turned heads in Washington circles. Harp, who has worked for Trump since 2022, was described in articles as Trump’s “Human Printer”, in charge of hauling around an actual portable printer and using it to print off positive news coverage and statements from the president’s allies praising his work in the White House. Other reports revealed that Harp has been known to leave deeply personal notes for the president, to the extent that it supposedly alarmed members of the Secret Service.

A report from the Washington Post last week also revealed that Harp was among a group of three close aides who received cash gifts of $45,000 over the holiday season last year.

open image in gallery The Washington Post reported that Harp was among three aides who received large cash gifts from the president over Christmas in 2025 ( AFP/Getty )

The White House has furiously denied that Harp has an inappropriate relationship with the president and Republicans have attacked the media for the focus on a young, female aide. Democrats, meanwhile, have leaned into lobbing attacks at the president over the reports and say they reinforce an image of corruption and unmoored behavior surrounding Trump in his second presidency.

Jon Ossoff, a Georgia senator running for re-election, kicked off a wave of controversy earlier in the summer when he quipped that Trump was focused solely on “build[ing] his ballroom and travel[ing] with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace”, referring to the Qatari-gifted Air Force One jet.

Harp has not commented publicly about the situation at all, and has shyed away from even appearances on friendly, conservative media networks and outlets since the controversy around her work began.

The president’s second term unleashed him and his allies against the media like never before. New restrictions were put on the White House press corps by the White House press team last year, and the press team now directly controls the assignments in the White House press pool, for the first time. Reporters are no longer allowed to roam parts of the White House grounds without escort, including areas around the press office.

Those restrictions were even tighter at the Pentagon, where a number of media organizations moved reporters out of the building rather than comply with demands from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth that they decline to publish nonpublic information. That dispute escalated into a lawsuit filed against the Pentagon by the New York Times, leading to Hegseth declaring the press office a classified space in an effort to spite and punish journalists, and restrict their access while evading legal blowback.

Trump’s own fury against the media has escalated in his second term, in the wake of his two impeachments and the January 6 attack on Congress. He now frequently spars with reporters in the White House pool, refusing to answer individual questions after asking reporters which outlets they work for — or, in some cases, directly hurling verbal abuse at reporters, mostly women, insulting their appearance and networks.

His most frequent target is CNN’s Kaitlan Collins, whom he often chastises in full view of the cameras for not smiling during press availabilities.

Harry Potter star Tom Felton has said that he is “not worried” for the mental health of the young actor taking on the role of Draco Malfoy in the upcoming HBO series.

The British actor was just 12 years old when he was cast opposite Daniel Radcliffe, Rupert Grint and Emma Watson in Warner Bros’ wizarding movies, playing Harry’s school tormentor Malfoy.

While Felton, 38, has stayed loyal to the franchise and is currently reprising the role in the Broadway production of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, he is handing the baton over to 14-year-old Lox Pratt in the highly anticipated TV reboot.

And though being thrust into the spotlight at such a young age was an overwhelming experience for the original Harry Potter cast, Felton has said that he isn’t concerned about the level of scrutiny the Lord of the Flies star will face.

open image in gallery 'Harry Potter' star Tom Felton has shared why he's 'not worried' about the new child stars reading 'negative comments' ( Getty )

“You just enjoy it for what it is,” he told BBC News, adding that he “saw a lot of myself” in the young actor.

“I’m not worried about that at all for him. He’s got a very good head on his shoulders and what you don’t know doesn’t hurt you. I’m sure he’s not one to scroll through negative comments.”

Describing Pratt as a “charming young man and fabulous actor”, Felton said that his mum had spoken to the child star’s own mother to share advice, while Felton had imparted his own wisdom too.

“I’m encouraging him to be as cheeky as possible – but professional first,” he said.

While Pratt already has on-screen experience, having played Jack Merridew in Jack Thorne’s Lord of the Flies adaptation earlier this year, Harry Potter marks a major step-up for the actor and his fellow young stars.

open image in gallery Lox Pratt as Malfoy in the HBO series ( PA )

Earlier this year, it was reported that the three lead actors – Dominic McLaughlin as Harry, Alastair Stour as Ron and Arabella Stanton as Hermione – will each receive £500,000 for starring in the first season of the show.

In comparison, Radcliffe received £1 million for the first film, with the number rising to £15 million by film number six.

However, Radcliffe has spoken frankly in the past about the realities of “growing up in the spotlight”, saying in 2016 that the “hardest” part was not the drugs or the “strange, pandering world you enter into”.

“The difficulty is trying to work out who you are while constantly coming up against a perception of yourself that everybody else already has,” he said.

“I think it’s very important, especially when you become famous young, to work out who you are without fame and without that as part of your identity, because that will go. Fame does not last forever. For anyone.”

Harry Potter season one arrives on HBO Max on 25 December.
