World.title: From the archive: Are Mexicans really always late?
World.content:
The goal of our “From the Archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article — originally published in December 2024 — is a humorous look at a stereotype regarding Mexicans and punctuality.

Before we get into the nuts and bolts regarding Mexican punctuality — or lack thereof — it’s important to clarify one thing. Mexicans are not actually always late.

That said, all stereotypes have to come from somewhere, don’t they? But like everything in life, there’s nuance to it.

Just like people all over the world, there’s room for a great deal of variety. Some people are always on time, and some people never are. Most people are punctual for certain activities, and unpunctual for others.

My dad, for instance, has never been punctual; I remember my mother saying she was terrified he wouldn’t make it to their wedding on time. My ex-husband also has challenges with punctuality, as does one of my best friends; I’ve spent great chunks of my adult life waiting hours.

I’m always super duper on time for everything, though I might let myself get to a party up to an hour late. My kid is leaning unpunctual, but I’m doing my damnedest to lecture it out of her. Because if there’s one thing kids love and respond to, it’s a good lecture.

Linguistic flexibility

One of the problems about even defining “late” is the language around defining time. For a deep dive into this, check out Joseph Sorrentino’s excellent piece on this specific type of vocabulary. Ahorita, al ratito, mañana … None of these words specify an actual time, you see? So “ahorita” could mean right this minute, and it could mean in five hours, or never. Al ratito (in a while) might mean in a couple of hours, or it might mean in a few years, depending on who’s saying it. You get the idea.

And really, this kind of language is useful because it allows for flexibility. In this way at least, Mexico is a flexible country.

Really, it has to be. Things come up that need tending to. Public transportation can be unpredictable. The opportunity to have a meal or talk to a pretty girl might come up. Your mom tells you to go fetch some things from the store, and you don’t tell her, “Sorry, I have plans.” Really, you just never know what can happen!

Life is unpredictable, and Mexicans have a fairly high tolerance for it being unpredictable, which is lucky for all of us.

Sometimes, though, there are things you must be on time for. And a good indicator of what those things are is whether or not there’s a specific time attached to them.

The meaning of ‘tolerancia’

School is one of those things. At my daughter’s school, for example, 8 a.m. is the official time kids have to be in the door. As a courtesy to the perpetually-late parents, there’s a “tolerance” of 10 minutes. To me, this means my daughter must be there before 8 a.m. if we’re not to be seen as rude and irresponsible. To others, it means 8:10 or even 8:11 is the limit. If kids aren’t in by that time, they must wait to enter the 9 a.m. class.

It was like this when I taught school here, too; some things, I suppose, are non-negotiable.

The same goes for official appointment times, even if the official or doctor you’re meeting isn’t exactly on time. So if you have a meeting with, say, immigration, you’d better be there at your appointment time! Some places will let you know that they have a tolerancia (literally, tolerance) of 10-15 minutes. This means that if you’re more than that amount of time late, you lose the appointment!

For other things, usually involving celebrations, arrival and start times are more flexible. This is especially true of parties, to which you can show up rather late without causing a fuss. Unless you’ve promised to bring something essential for the party, they’re just glad to have you there at some point. This doesn’t mean they’ll wait for you to start in on the cake and piñatas, though, so beware!

Clocks vs. cultural norms

Concerts and plays typically start within 15 to 30 minutes of their “official” start time; rock concerts might start hours after they’re meant to. Oh, well!

And if you’re meeting friends, it might depend on the specific circumstances. Are you meeting someone busy who only has a few minutes? Are you meeting them alone? In my group of mom friends, we always know that things can come up. “I’ll text you when I leave” is a good, flexible bridge that keeps people updated but keeps plans flexible.

In my own conservative and somewhat strict view, being on time means showing respect for the other person. If you are not on time, then you do not care about them or their time. And if you are on time, not only are you showing respect for them, but you’re making things easier for yourself, avoiding fluster. My cultural chauvinism is showing, I know.

But for plenty of people here, that’s a ridiculous notion. Why stress so much about being on time when literally anything can happen to make you not on time? Perhaps there’s a message here too about avoiding blame and responsibility. “Se me durmió el gallo” (The rooster went to sleep on me; as in, the rooster didn’t wake me up).

But that’s for another article. For now, I’ll leave you with a cute little proverb, as well as its juxtaposed, more truthful meme:

“Al que madruga, Dios le ayuda.” (The one who rises early receives God’s help.) It rhymes!

“Al que madruga, encuentra todo cerrado.” (The one who rises early finds everything closed.)

Truer words were never spoken.

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, https://sarahedevries.substack.com/

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Exports and gas production hit record highs as patriotic spirit swells
World.content:
Listen to this article

Bilateral communications were front and center in Mexico the week of Sept. 7, with developments running the gamut from encouraging to combative. U.S. President Donald Trump’s remark that Mexico has “nothing” the United States needs beyond “hot tamales” and “tomatoes” caught fire over the weekend, unleashing a fresh round of provocations from Trump, Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio in the days that followed.

Mexico, however, continued to highlight trade and security collaboration with its northern neighbor, though the PISA test results and next year’s midterm elections sparked more conversations at home. Meanwhile, the annual inflation rate ticked up to 3.26% — as expected according to Banxico, which forecasts inflation of 3.5% by the end of 2026. President Claudia Sheinbaum remained optimistic through it all, especially as her administration makes its plans for 2027. Overhead, punishing heat baked Mexico’s northern border states even as monsoon rains drenched the Pacific coast and center of the country.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

2027 budget takes shape

On Monday, Finance Minister Édgar Amador Zamora submitted a 10.6-trillion-peso (US $627.8 billion) budget proposal for 2027 to Congress, an increase of about 1% in real terms over this year. Amador framed the package around “five pillars” — economic growth, protecting government priorities, strengthening revenue, more efficient spending and fiscal discipline. The government is banking on those pillars to shrink the budget deficit to 3.9% of GDP next year from an estimated 4.1% in 2026, even as public debt climbs to 55% of GDP. No new taxes or fuel-price hikes are planned.

Health care gets a 10.9% real-terms boost to 1.1 trillion pesos, largely for IMSS-Bienestar infrastructure and medicine supply, while education rises about 7% to 1.3 trillion pesos to fund new schools. Pension and welfare programs get just over 1 trillion pesos, and debt servicing alone eats up 1.6 trillion pesos — roughly one of every seven pesos the government spends. Security agencies see an 11.6% bump to 331.4 billion pesos, while Pemex funding falls 69.2% as the state oil company pushes toward self-sufficiency.

The National Electoral Institute (INE) is the biggest percentage winner of all, with an 87.5% real-terms increase ahead of 2027 midterm elections, while the Energy Ministry, the National Human Rights Commission and the Federal Electricity Commission absorb the steepest cuts. Sheinbaum said the following day that she is “very satisfied” with the package and that growth could exceed the official forecast of 1.5-2.5%, citing anticipated stability in trade relations with the U.S. and Canada.

Homicides continue to fall

Security officials reported this week that daily homicides fell 53% in August compared to September 2024, the final month of the López Obrador administration, making it the least violent August since 2015.

More than 67,000 people have been arrested for high-impact crimes since Sheinbaum took office, though Security Minister Omar García Harfuch cautioned that “the job is not done.” Days later, from Tuxtla Gutiérrez, the president highlighted a 63% drop in Chiapas’s homicide rate since Gov. Eduardo Ramírez Aguilar took office, alongside nearly 10,000 arrests in the southern state. The same briefing revealed the discovery of a clandestine hospital the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) used to treat injured members.

Olmeca Refinery notches record month

Pemex’s Olmeca Refinery in Tabasco posted its best month yet for fuel production in July, averaging 252,498 barrels per day, a 78.8% jump over June. Gasoline output rose even more sharply, up nearly 128% month-over-month, after equipment fires forced repairs earlier in the year. Despite the milestone, the plant — which began operating approximately two years ago — is still running at roughly two-thirds of its 340,000-bpd capacity.

Fox and PRI’s Alito Moreno join forces

In a striking political reunion, former President Vicente Fox met with PRI leader Alejandro “Alito” Moreno to discuss “the need to build a strong opposition” ahead of 2027 midterms — 26 years after Fox became the first opposition candidate to sweep the once-dominant PRI out of the presidency, and years after he called the party “black vipers, vermin and tadpoles.”

Morena, for its part, dismissed the pairing as “the reorganization of the power elite,” saying in a statement that “they change the names, they invent new organizations, but behind the facade, it’s the same old faces.” The PRI, which ruled Mexico for 71 years, now holds just two of the country’s 32 governorships — the same number as the much smaller Citizens Movement (MC) party.

At her Monday press conference, Sheinbaum branded the reunion “PRIAN” politics dating to the “neoliberal” era of former President Carlos Salinas de Gortari, and called Fox a “traitor of democracy” — a jab tied to his role in Mexico’s disputed 2006 election.

Bilateral high points

Trade and security cooperation produced some of the week’s more encouraging bilateral news. Mexico’s exports to the U.S. hit a monthly record in July: US $60.55 billion worth of goods were sent north, pushing Mexico’s share of the $332.92 billion U.S. import market above 18%.

Along the border, Mexican and U.S. forces carried out “High Eagle,” a binational operation to detect and disable drones cartels use to surveil authorities near Tijuana and San Diego. And though bad weather grounded Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s flight to Mexico City on Wednesday, he and Sheinbaum still held a video call on USMCA negotiations that Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard described as “cordial” and “very useful,” with talks on steel, aluminum and automotive tariffs continuing ahead of a fourth bilateral review round.

Bilateral low points

Other exchanges were considerably more combative. Over the weekend, Trump proposed to rename New Mexico “New America,” despite having no legal authority to rename a U.S. state, drawing pushback from the state’s Democratic leaders. Later in the week, from Ecuador, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio doubled down on claims that cartels control “vast territories” of Mexico, hinting the threat may eventually have to be “confronted one way or the other.” Sheinbaum shot back on Thursday morning, telling Rubio to keep Mexico out of U.S. midterm politics and calling his remarks electorally motivated. Rounding out the week, U.S. Vice President JD Vance labeled the Mexican flag “a symbol of the far left” after a protester interrupted his convention speech in Dallas, telling the man to “get your ass over there” if he loved Mexico so much.

Poor PISA scores spark a debate over screens

New results from the OECD’s Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA), given to 7,843 students across 297 Mexican schools, showed that four in 10 15-year-olds — 41.8% — scored below the basic level in science, math and reading, more than double the 19.7% OECD average and Mexico’s worst showing since 2009.

Mexican students averaged 388 points in math, 408 in reading and 414 in science, all well below OECD averages of 463, 461 and 482, and the country has shed seven points in both math and reading since the 2022 test. The decline wasn’t unique to Mexico — the OECD’s education director called it part of a “dramatic” global drop, particularly in reading — and Mexican students still reported unusually high curiosity (80%, versus a 24% global average who called school “a waste of time”). Education International, the global teachers’ federation, pinned the broader slide on shrinking attention spans, heavy AI use and a worldwide teacher shortage. China, Singapore, South Korea, Estonia and Canada topped the rankings.

Education Minister Mario Delgado blamed excessive screen use for the drop in reading comprehension — arguing that “screens make it easy to ‘read’ or consume images” — while defending the New Mexican School curriculum model and promoting traditional games like yo-yos, marbles and spinning tops as a substitute for phone time. He conceded the PISA sample was “statistically representative” even as he questioned whether the test amounts to a comprehensive evaluation of Mexican education. Sheinbaum later told reporters Mexico will roll out new math and reading textbooks next year, including poems and short stories, and push a “return to pencil and paper,” tying the effort to new national guidelines already restricting cellphone use in schools.

Education Ministry, UNESCO team up on AI in schools

Also this week, Mexico’s Education Ministry signed a letter of intent with UNESCO to guide the “responsible” rollout of artificial intelligence in classrooms, with the U.N. body offering technical assistance, teacher training and research support. Officials said the goal is to ensure AI supports, rather than substitutes for, teaching and critical thinking, and the deal also opens the door to new rules on cellphone use in schools.

Mexico prepares for El Grito and Independence Day

With the country’s 216th independence anniversary approaching, more than 18,000 members of Mexico’s armed forces are readying for the Sept. 16 military parade through Mexico City, featuring drones, horses, dogs and a float marking the country’s World Cup hosting duties this past June and July. The holiday kicks off the night before, with Sheinbaum leading the Grito de Independencia from the National Palace balcony and Tejano band Intocable headlining a concert in the Zócalo.

Festivities and gritos will ring out from cities across the country, including in Sinaloa, whose capital city of Culicán will hold a public celebration of Independence Day for the first time in two years.

Points of 🇲🇽 pride

A 20-year-old engineering student from a Chihuahua farming family, Luis Ángel Robles Morales, won a national innovation award for an irrigation filter that is already helping 500 drought-stricken farmers use water more efficiently.

Forward Julián Quiñones and Club América’s Scarlett Camberos earned historic Ballon d’Or nominations, marking the first time two Mexican players — and a Mexican club — have featured on the shortlist for world soccer’s top individual honor.

World.title: Witnessing the explosive sledgehammer ritual in San Juan de la Vega, Guanajuato
World.content:
A door in the street cracked open just enough for a hand to slip through. A kid, maybe 15, curled his fingers toward himself: come here, come here, then pulled back into the dark. I looked around the street. Nobody. I stepped inside.

The house looked like a drug kitchen. Two folding tables stretched across the room, their surfaces dusted white and yellow. On one side, a bucket of potassium chlorate. On the other, sulfur. Three kids stood around the tables, working the powders together with their bare hands. One kid looked up at me and grinned, then went back to scooping powder into small plastic bags.

Josué was the one who had waved me in from the doorway. One of the boys had no hands. Both arms ended at the wrists. I didn’t want to ask. I asked anyway. He told me it happened during the explosions, a few years back. He said it the way someone tells you about a stolen bicycle, part of life.

Don Juan David, Josué’s father, walked into the room. He greeted me with a handshake and a smile, glanced at the tables of explosive powder where their children worked, and walked back out.

A dangerous tradition

Every year, on Shrove Tuesday, the townspeople of San Juan de la Vega pack homemade explosives onto sledgehammers, carry them to the streets and open fields, and slam them against the ground. People lose limbs. This time, something was different. For the first time in the town’s history, authorities had banned the use of explosives during the carnival.

Families wanted to talk. Each family insisted theirs was the true story. The carnival, they all agreed, celebrates San Juan de la Vega, a saint who saved the town from gold robbers centuries ago. The explosives reenact the gunshots from his battles.

Every family also wanted to make sure we knew that the big explosions, the ones the town is famous for, are not the real tradition. The real tradition is small. Modest. A respectful crack of gunpowder in honor of the saint. Kids started making bigger and bigger explosives, destroying city piping. Everything breaks, they said, shaking their own heads. This is not what we are.

A man named Aquino de la Vega was moving silver shipments by mule along the Camino Real when bandits started robbing him. He prayed to San Juan Bautista. The robbers stopped. Aquino vowed he would honor the saint every year, forever, and so would his sons.

Six families still carry that vow. Each one is tied to a barrio. The families fund the music, the food, the processions. They keep the image of the saint in their home for a year.

Adrenaline and danger

The word I heard more than any other was adrenalina. The afternoon before the carnival, I found Josué sitting on a curb outside a corner store, rolling a cigarette. He was quiet.

“I’m always scared before I do it,” he told me. “But once I blow up one, I can’t stop. The adrenaline is too strong. I want to keep going.”

I asked about the dangers, and stories came easily: a man who burned, another who was paralyzed, people who lost fingers, hands, arms, legs. Accidents happen because the explosives are powerful enough to send 25-kilogram sledgehammers flying through the air. A hammer goes up, a hammer comes down, and sometimes there is a head in the way.

“Police always try to take them away,” one man said, sitting in a plastic chair outside his house, two kids playing in the dirt beside him. “But they will never stop the tradition. Nothing will change.”

On the afternoon before the main event, the streets were empty. Doors closed. No music. No voices.

Boom. The first hammer hit the ground as soon as night fell.

The sound moved through me. The ground shook under my feet. My ears whistled, even from 100 meters away. My chest vibrated. Windows cracked. The pipes beneath the street groaned and split.

Then came another. And another.

Parades took the streets. Villagers singing, dancing, playing instruments, carrying the image of San Juanito through the town. Following them in the back, kids dressed as soldiers, some in boots and gas masks, others with no gloves, no protection of any kind. Everyone carried sledgehammers and backpacks stuffed with explosives.

Defying the ban

I found Josué in the crowd. Face covered in soot, eyes wide. He swung a hammer down and the detonation threw him sideways. He got up laughing and loaded another charge.

Around midnight, the first police cars appeared.

The crowd froze. About 10 men climbed out with SWAT gear, assault rifles and bulletproof vests. They walked toward the kids with the backpacks. The boys scattered.

I saw a grandmother crack her front door open. She let the kids shove their backpacks full of explosives through the gap; she closed the door, and she stood in front of it. When the police asked to enter, she stood immobile like a statue until they were gone.

The police confiscated what they could, caught a few guys, and left. Within minutes, the parades reformed. The hammers came back out. The explosions picked up where they had stopped.

At around 3 a.m., we walked back toward town to catch some sleep. I did not sleep. The bed shook after every boom. Even with earplugs, my ears hurt. It went on until 7 a.m.

We walked outside. Over 10 police cars patrolled the town. They had shut everything down. But beyond the edge of town, we could hear it. Boom. Boom.

We followed the sound.

Moving to the tracks

The townspeople had moved to the train tracks. Flat, open land, sand, rocks and gravel, not a piece of shade anywhere. They placed explosives on the rails and waited for trains to roll over them. Between trains, they took turns blowing up hammers on steel bars laid flat against the ground.

There, away from the police, the hammers got bigger.

It was noon. The sun was directly overhead. People packed more and more powder onto the sledgehammers and took turns. Huge hammers flew tens of meters into the air.

I watched a kid swing a hammer down. The explosion threw him back onto the ground. The hammer launched upward, spinning, and came down on his head. The ring of steel on skull. He tried to stand. Blood ran from his scalp, down his face, into his eyes. His friend pulled off his own shirt, wrapped it tight around the kid’s head, and hauled him onto the back of a motorcycle. They disappeared down the road.

Nobody stopped. The next person stepped up.

The next morning, the market opened in the square as always. People walked slowly, said good morning to each other. A dog slept in a doorway. The church bell rang at 8.

Here was Josué, down the road. He waved.

I went to say goodbye to Don Juan David. He pulled me into a hug that lasted a long time. He held on. We had barely talked. When he finally let go, his eyes were wet. He thanked me. He begged me to come back next year.

“Sí, San Juanito permite,” he said. If San Juanito allows it.

Mattia Astori and Daniele Colucci make Sacratos, a documentary project on extreme rituals with photos, interviews, articles and videos. They’ve worked in Mexico, India, Bolivia, Thailand and Italy.

World.title: Turtle power: Volunteer to protect Mexico’s sea turtles
World.content:
Turtle camps can be found all over Mexico’s coastline, including the Gulf Coast, allowing volunteers to liberate baby turtles.

With the fifth-longest coastline in all of Mexico — a country that is internationally known and beloved for its beach offerings — Veracruz is certainly a sea-loving state, boasting some 450 miles of Gulf Coast access. For the record, Baja California Sur, a peninsula surrounded by water on three sides, has the longest total coastline at more than 1,350 miles of beach.

Historically, Veracruz is celebrated for its seafood and coastal tropics, as well as being the site of Mexico’s largest and oldest port with access to the Atlantic Ocean.

But what has been lost in the greater narrative is that, as part of its cultural significance along the Gulf Coast, Veracruz has also become one of Mexico’s leading states for turtle conservation.

The legacy of turtle conservationism in Mexico

The earliest federal efforts to focus on sea turtle nesting in Mexico began in 1962, led by the National Institute of Biological and Fisheries Research on both of Mexico’s ample coasts. In 1963, the Center for Turtle Culture opened on Isla Mujeres, Quintana Roo.

Shortly after, in 1966, Rancho Nuevo — located in Tamaulipas, just north of Veracruz — was among the first turtle conservation camps to formally open in Mexico. The National Commission of Protected Natural Areas outlined the importance of these efforts from the mid-1960s; the investments significantly helped to maintain the growth of Mexico’s turtle populations by increasing local awareness and participation. During that time, the National Sea Turtles Conservation Program was founded as a result.

Rancho Nuevo, along with the other turtle conservation camps that would spring up all over Mexico’s beaches — from the Gulf to the Pacific — has become a crucial element of turtle protection efforts since then, utilizing a mix of dedicated turtle conservationists and public volunteers. Responsibilities include the protection of nesting sites via monitoring and safeguarding turtle nests, and assisting (or “liberating”) fresh turtle hatchlings to ensure they make it to the sea.

Milestones in national protection rights

Since the 1960s, Mexico has become a global leader in turtle conservancy; in 2025, Mexico was recognized as an exemplar for its turtle protection efforts. Currently, Mexico federally operates 26 turtle conservation centers, in addition to various independent organizations and nonprofits extending across 13 coastal states. Officials announced a record of more than 34 million newborn olive ridley turtles that reached the ocean in a single season, in Oaxaca’s Morro Ayuta region alone.

In 1990, federally backed turtle protection rights gained further ground when then-President Carlos Salinas de Gortari decreed an end to the commercial harvesting of all sea turtles and related products. The landmark move shifted former turtle hunting communities — such as areas in Mazunte, which had among the highest rates of turtle slaughter — into epicenters of turtle conservation. Mazunte opened the Mexican Turtle Center in 1991, aiding the area’s turtle population and ecotourism alike.

Mexico’s role as a sanctuary for sea turtles

According to a 2008 report from the Secretariat of Environment and Natural Resources (Semarnat), “Mexico is the country with the largest number of sea-turtle species worldwide. Seven of the eight species known … nest in Mexican beaches, both in the Pacific and in the Gulf of Mexico and Caribbean littorals: loggerhead turtle, white or green turtle, black turtle, hawksbill turtle, Kemp’s ridley, olive ridley and leatherback turtle. Two of them, Kemp’s ridley and black sea turtle, nest exclusively in Mexican beaches.”

A more recent investigation from 2023, published in Revista Mexicana de Biodiversidad, revealed that southeastern Mexico, including Veracruz, is the most diverse region for turtle conservation in the country: “According to our results, southeastern Mexico supports three-fourths of the families — and more than half of the genera — found nationwide in Mexico. These findings highlight southeastern Mexico as a region of high importance for the composition of land and freshwater turtles at the national level … Oaxaca, Chiapas and Veracruz stand out as the states with the highest species richness and endemism, respectively. These three states are located within the region considered the richest in total herpetofauna, a result of complex orography, diverse habitats and environments, and the biogeographic history of Mexico.”

An afternoon with turtle conservationists in Veracruz

Jeanne A. Mortimer, a world-renowned marine biologist known as “Madame Torti” who specializes in sea turtle conservationism, once wrote that “The importance of the central coast of Veracruz (for turtle nesting) may be attributed to the fact that the beaches are easily accessible from the ocean without great obstacles like rocks, pronounced slopes or coastal developments that prevent the movement of the adult females along the length and breadth of the beaches.”

It partially explains why Veracruz has been able to cultivate a long-lasting ethos and engagement around turtle protection, with civic initiatives like Fundación Yépez and the Veracruzano Center for Research and Conservation of the Sea Turtle having launched decades ago. Additionally, Veracruz boasts Veracruz Reef System National Park, which played a role in a major environmental ruling by Mexico’s Supreme Court to conserve sea turtle habitats by restricting the construction of industrial ports in endangered areas (although reports that the ruling hasn’t been properly enforced have been published).

Vida Millenaria is among Veracruz’s most prominent turtle conservation groups. The project began in Tecolutla in 1974 as a personal mission for Fernando Manzano, whom locals began to call “Papá Tortuga,” or Turtle Father. Over half a century later, his efforts have expanded to include other members.

To date, the nonprofit has protected and released thousands of baby turtles each year. Visitors arrive year-round to receive public education and help to release newborn turtles into the water along the beaches on the city’s northern outskirts, about a 20-minute drive from the town’s center, along a mostly deserted dirt path.

Camping under the stars in Tecolutla

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Kate Levasseur (@katelevass)

I personally drove out to experience it for myself. Depending on your budget, you can rent a group-sized or personal tent near the beach at a campsite that includes outdoor showers, bathrooms and a common area for campers and volunteers who arrive at different hours of the day to participate in the turtle release. The camp area is shaded by palm trees and is relatively cool due to the strong coastal breeze.

The camping experience adds a layer of memory-making, as you sleep beneath the moonlight on a private, mostly isolated beach while the waves wash ashore in the near distance. A rotation of Vida Millenaria workers takes turns patrolling the area on ATVs around the clock, mostly to keep an eye on the turtles and their nests. (Note: If you decide to camp overnight, be sure to bring plenty of supplies, water and food, as a one-way trip back into town requires more than 20 minutes of off-roading to reach the edge of Tecolutla). There, you can enjoy a paradisiacal beach to yourself, undisturbed, until the next day.

A volunteer brigade assembles

Early in the morning, around 7:30 a.m., volunteers of all ages begin to arrive and assemble at the center of camp. A local expert introduces the nonprofit’s history, and a musician plays music dedicated to sea turtles. Maps and visuals are used to show and explain a brief history of turtle conservation in the state, and an adult-sized turtle replica stands in as a faux mascot for guests to take pictures with.

Afterwards, participants are escorted to the nearby souvenir shop, where everything is turtle-related (of course) and handmade. Each purchase grants a set of baby turtles for group liberation — so the more things you buy, the more turtles you’re able to liberate (prices start around 150 pesos and include turtle plushies, stuffed animals, mugs, shirts, etc.). For breakfast, a local volovanero (a savory pastry vendor common in Veracruz) brings a freshly baked batch for about 50 pesos each.

Releasing hatchlings into the wild

Then, the finale: Everyone strolls down to the beach together, lines up, and is given baby turtles to release into the ocean together. It’s a spectacular sight to see upwards of 50 small creatures — more or less, depending on the volunteer group’s size that day — crawling their way into the waves for the first time. They are swept away, their tiny heads occasionally poking out from the shimmering waters before completely disappearing into the distance by the dozens.

Of course, if you’re nowhere near Veracruz, you can search for your nearest beach. You’ll likely discover a turtle conservation group awaiting your participation. It makes a memorable weekend trip — and most importantly, it helps to keep an essential part of Mexico’s ecosystem intact.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: MND goes all in on Mexico City: A perspective from our CEO
World.content:
Mexico City is having a long-overdue and well-deserved moment in the spotlight. People from all over the world of all ages are discovering the city and everything it has to offer. Entire neighborhoods are being influenced and transformed by the influx of new foreign residents and tourists. Some locals lament the changes, others celebrate them. We had one of our local CDMX writers reflect on it here.

As of late, I now hear from several people a week who have just visited the city for the first time and were blown away by how awesome it is. I can’t help but smile. When I first visited the city over 30 years ago, it was love at first sight — the history, the energy, the people, the contrasts. I would always tell people that it was one of my very favorite cities in the world and have gushed about it in articles and podcasts:

The team at Mexico News Daily is excited to announce that, starting this week, we will be further increasing our coverage of Mexico City. In addition to our regular daily content that very frequently covers news happening in the city, we are now going to begin a weekly MND Local CDMX feature that will give readers even more detailed news and information.

The idea behind this new weekly feature article is to provide the next level of news and information about the city. Perhaps most importantly, we are being very thoughtful in who we are writing for and what should be included. The goal is to write it for a wide audience: those currently living in the city, those considering moving to the city, or others just interested in learning more and being better informed for planning future trips. We hope to inspire first-timers to come check the city out, and those who have been there to come back again soon!

It is NOT written to help you understand what to do in the next 24 hours. It is NOT meant to replace local event calendars and local social media pages. It IS written to help you learn more about the city and better plan your time there. We will give you insight into new openings to be aware of, important events to plan for and new trends shaping the city. We hope to introduce you to new people, new places and new things to check out — all in an effort to inspire you to spend more time discovering this wonderful city.

Check out the first MND Local CDMX published earlier this week right here:

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

If You Only Go to One Place Trem de 3 at Blue Note Three senior figures of Brazilian instrumental music share one stage on Avenida Paulista. It is a single early show at 19:00, with no sell-out warning on the club’s page.

Tonight at a Glance — Trem de 3 · Blue Note Carlos Malta, Jaques Morelenbaum and Marcelo Costa. One show, 19:00.

— No sell-out flag Unlike last night, the club carried no last-tickets warning for tonight.

— Buy online The Sunday box office closes at 16:00, three hours before the show.

— Tickets Through the club’s own site and Eventim, its listed ticketing partner.

— Seating Tables are allocated by arrival order, so come early for a view.

— Monday The club takes Mondays off and returns on Tuesday at 20:00.

Tonight, Sunday 13 September 2026, São Paulo has more on than any other night this week. A festival closing day, an arena show, a free orchestral concert in the park, and a seated jazz room that starts at seven.

What’s On Tonight

Blue Note São Paulo lists tonight as Trem de 3, with Carlos Malta, Jaques Morelenbaum and Marcelo Costa. It is a single show at 19:00 rather than the usual double bill.

The three are instrumentalists with long careers behind them. Morelenbaum is a cellist and arranger, Malta a reeds and flute player, and Costa a percussionist.

Tonight carried no last-tickets or sold-out flag on the club’s programme page when we checked on 13 September. Several other September dates did, so this one is comparatively open.

There is a practical catch on a Sunday. The club’s published Sunday box-office hours are 10:00 to 16:00, which end three hours before the show starts.

Buy online rather than planning to pay at the door. Sales run through the club’s own site and through Eventim, its listed ticketing partner.

The club does not publish prices on its programme index. The individual show pages do not carry it either. The price appears only at checkout on Eventim.

The room is on the second floor of the Conjunto Nacional, at Avenida Paulista 2073. Tables are given out in arrival order rather than assigned when you book.

The Three Bigger Nights

The Coala Festival closes today at the Memorial da America Latina in Barra Funda. The programme runs from about 12:30 to 22:00.

Tom Ze plays a ninetieth-birthday set at 17:00 on the Palco Allianz. Joao Gomes follows at 17:30, Seu Jorge at 19:00 and Criolo at 20:50 with No na Orelha.

Day passes have been listed from R$179 half to R$358 full for the arena, with an open-bar Vila Coala tier from R$669 to R$848. Tickets go through Total Acesso. The metro and rail station is Palmeiras-Barra Funda.

Jamiroquai play Nubank Parque in Agua Branca. Doors at 16:00 and the show at 21:00, with tickets on Eventim from R$345 full and R$172.50 half.

The free option is Alceu Valenca with the Orquestra Ouro Preto on the open-air lawn at the Auditorio Ibirapuera. Gates at 17:00 and music at 18:30, no ticket, capacity around 9,000, gates 2 and 10.

There is also football. Corinthians are away at Flamengo in the Maracana at 17:30, on free-to-air television, so any bar with a screen will have it.

The Week Ahead

The club takes Mondays off. It returns on Tuesday with Michelle Abu and her show “Qual é o Tambor”, at 20:00, joined by Catto.

Wednesday is already gone. The Flávio Venturini night on 16 September is marked as sold out on the club’s own page.

Thursday returns to the double bill. Nelson Faria and Sandro Haick play at 20:00, followed by a Simply Red tribute at 22:30.

What We Could Not Confirm

Canto da Ema, the forró house in Pinheiros, is open tonight from 19:00 to midnight, at R$55 full and R$27 half. It publishes no band for tonight, so the floor is the draw rather than a named act.

Forró is a couples dance from the northeast of Brazil. The house usually runs a beginners’ class before the floor opens, so ring (11) 2503-2915 before crossing town.

Casa de Francisca in the historic centre runs a lunch session and an evening one today. The evening programme, called Alvoroço, starts at 19:00 with a free ticket quota on Sympla.

The Memorial da America Latina in Barra Funda, where the Coala Festival closes tonight. (Photo: “Memorial da América Latina. (47572448772)” by Governo do Estado de São Paulo, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.)

Where to Go

Blue Note São Paulo — Paulista The São Paulo branch of the New York jazz club, open since February 2019. It fills about 800 square metres of tables on the second floor of a landmark shopping centre. Tonight Trem de 3, a single show at 19:00.

Status No sell-out warning on the club’s page when checked on 13 September.

Box office Sunday hours are 10:00 to 16:00, so buy online for tonight.

Prices Not published on the programme index. Not published on the show page either. The price appears at checkout on Eventim.

Tickets Through the club’s own site and Eventim, its listed ticketing partner.

Address Avenida Paulista 2073, second floor, Consolação. Consolação station is nearest.

Money and How Paying Works

Any dollar figure here uses a rate of R$5.0918 to one US dollar. That is the Banco Central PTAX closing sell rate for Friday 11 September, the last business day before today.

Blue Note does not publish tonight’s price on its index page. Take the figure from the individual show page rather than from any third-party listing.

Food and drink are charged separately from the ticket. A service charge, called serviço, is usually added at about 10 per cent and is optional under Brazilian law.

Getting Home Safe

A show that starts at 19:00 finishes comfortably inside normal metro hours. That makes tonight one of the easiest nights of the week to get home from.

Avenida Paulista stays busy and well lit in the evening. Wait for a rideshare on the avenue rather than on a side street.

What time is tonight’s show?

Trem de 3 play a single show at 19:00. Sunday is an early night at this club, with no late set.

Can I buy at the door?

Not reliably. The published Sunday box-office hours are 10:00 to 16:00, which end three hours before the show, so buy online.

How much are tickets?

The club does not publish prices on its programme index. Each show has its own page with the price, sold through the club’s site and Eventim.

Canto da Ema publishes a Wednesday-to-Sunday week, but we could not open its agenda today. Ring (11) 2503-2915 before travelling to Pinheiros.

If You Only Go to One Place The Last Night of Rock in Rio Seven festival days end tonight at the Cidade do Rock in Barra da Tijuca. Gates open at 14:00, and Twenty One Pilots close the main stage after midnight.

Tonight at a Glance — Rock in Rio · Barra da Tijuca Final day of seven. Gates 14:00, last entry at midnight.

— Main stage Ivete Sangalo opens at 17:00, with Twenty One Pilots closing at 00:05.

— Tickets Ticketmaster is the only official seller. Check today’s status there first.

— Getting there Three special BRT lines run to the Cidade do Rock for the festival.

— Carioca da Gema · closed The Lapa house runs Tuesday to Saturday and is shut tonight.

Tonight, Sunday 13 September 2026, the city has one very large event and very little else. The festival ends in the west, and Lapa’s samba houses are dark until Tuesday.

What’s On Tonight

Rock in Rio closes its 2026 edition tonight at the Parque Olímpico in Barra da Tijuca. The festival ran across seven days across two blocks, 4 to 7 September around Independence Day and 11 to 13 September, and this is the last of them.

Gates open at 14:00, the last entry is at midnight and activities run until 03:00. The site holds six stages, so the evening is long rather than concentrated.

Brazilian outlets reporting today give the main stage order as Ivete Sangalo at 17:00 and Lola Young at 19:10. Halsey follows at 21:35, and Twenty One Pilots close at 00:05.

On the Palco Sunset, the same reports put Zara Larsson last at 22:50. Before her come Marina Sena with Céu, Joelma with Viviane Batidão, and Carol Biazin.

Treat those times as a guide rather than a timetable. The festival publishes the running order in its own app, and stage times move on the day.

Tickets and Getting There

Ticketmaster is the only official seller for the festival. Ignore any other source offering entry, however convincing the listing looks.

Today was not among the dates reported sold out earlier in the run. That was the position when we checked, so confirm the current status on Ticketmaster before travelling.

General admission, sold as a Gramado ticket, has been listed at R$870 (about US$171) full. A Comfort Zone ticket, which adds an area near the main stage, is R$1,950 (about US$383) full and R$975 (about US$192) half. The half-price rate, available to students and others who qualify, is R$435 (about US$85).

The BRT runs three special lines to the Cidade do Rock during the festival. There is also an official coach service with pick-up points around the city, booked through the festival’s own platform.

The Other Big Crowd Tonight

The festival is not the only mass event in the city. Flamengo host Corinthians at the Maracana at 17:30 in round 27 of the Brazilian championship.

Flamengo lead the table and Corinthians sit twelfth. The match is on free-to-air television, so any bar with a screen works if you are not going.

It finishes around 19:20, in the north of the city, as Rock in Rio traffic is building in the west. Allow for both if you are crossing town.

What Is Closed Tonight

Carioca da Gema in Lapa is shut. Its own events list jumps from last night straight to Tuesday, and its published opening hours cover Tuesday to Saturday only.

The next confirmed night there is Tuesday 15 September. Fernando Jovem plays with Samba Trombonado, with doors at 19:30 and entry at R$30 (about US$6).

The free roda at the Pedra do Sal is listed by Riotur on Mondays. A roda is a samba circle, and the next one falls tomorrow in the old port district.

Rio Scenarium on Rua do Lavradio publishes a week running Wednesday to Saturday. Its published week runs Wednesday to Saturday and it is closed on Sundays. The address is Rua do Lavradio 20.

The Lapa arches. The samba houses below them are shut on a Sunday and reopen on Tuesday. (Photo: “Arcos e Aquedutos Lapa” by Carlos Lucio, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)

Where to Go

Rock in Rio — Cidade do Rock, Barra da Tijuca The festival site is built inside the Parque Olímpico, on the western edge of the city. Six stages, food courts and the usual festival infrastructure. Tonight The seventh and final day of the 2026 edition.

Hours Gates 14:00, last entry midnight, activities until 03:00.

Transport Three special BRT lines, plus an official coach service booked through the festival.

Address Avenida Embaixador Abelardo Bueno 3401, Barra da Tijuca.

Carioca da Gema — Lapa, from Tuesday A two-storey samba house at the Lapa end of the Centro, open since 2000. Closed tonight, and worth knowing about for the week ahead. Tonight Closed. The house runs Tuesday to Saturday.

Tuesday Fernando Jovem with Samba Trombonado. Doors 19:30, main show 20:30.

Entry R$30 (about US$6) Tuesday to Thursday, R$35 (about US$7) Friday and Saturday.

Tickets Through Zig, linked from the venue’s own event listing.

Address Avenida Mem de Sá 79, Centro. Metro Cinelândia, then a short walk.

Money and How Paying Works

Dollar figures here use a rate of R$5.0918 to one US dollar. That is the Banco Central PTAX closing sell rate for Friday 11 September, the last business day before today.

Festival tickets are digital and tied to the buyer’s account. Buy only through Ticketmaster, and expect to show the ticket in the app at the gate.

In bars and restaurants a service charge, called serviço, is usually added at about 10 per cent. It is optional under Brazilian law.

Getting Home Safe

The rail network has been extended for the festival, so the 03:00 finish is covered. Plan the journey home before you go, not at the gate at three in the morning.

The special BRT lines and the official coach service are built for exactly this. Jardim Oceanico metro stays open 24 hours for boarding on festival days, and other stations are open overnight for exit only. VLT Line 1 also runs around the clock, with an hourly express between 23:00 and 05:00 calling at six stops. The special BRT runs until 04:00.

Rideshare surges hard around a festival exit in Barra da Tijuca. Expect to wait, and agree a meeting point with your group before you go in.

Frequently Asked Questions

What time does the festival start and end tonight?

Gates open at 14:00 and the last entry is at midnight. Activities run until 03:00, with the main stage closing at 00:05.

Can I still buy a ticket?

Today was not among the dates reported sold out earlier in the run, but that can change hourly. Ticketmaster is the only official seller, so check there and buy nowhere else.

Is anything open in Lapa tonight?

Carioca da Gema is closed, and its published week runs Tuesday to Saturday. Its next confirmed night is Tuesday, with Fernando Jovem and Samba Trombonado.

When is the next Pedra do Sal roda?

Tomorrow. Riotur lists that free street roda on Mondays, in the old port district.

World.title: Zambia Charges an Opposition Presidential Candidate With Sedition Over an Election Claim
World.content:
Zambia · POLITICS

Key Facts — What happened Zambian police formally arrested Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu on 11 September 2026 at Kabwe Central Police Station and charged them with seditious practices under Section 57 of the Penal Code, Chapter 87.

— Where they are held The two men were returned to Mukobeko Maximum Correctional Facility after the charges were filed.

— The wider pattern Gina Romero, the UN Special Rapporteur on freedom of peaceful assembly and of association, who serves independently of the United Nations, said on 2 September that Zambian authorities had intensified arbitrary arrests and disproportionate charges, including sedition, against political opponents.

— Earlier accusations Police had previously accused Mundubile and Zulu of treason, with allegations involving weapons and a suspected militia network.

— Why it matters The case sits within a broader contest over democratic space, rule of law, and the state’s use of criminal law against opposition actors in post-election Zambia.

Zambian police charged Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu with seditious practices on 11 September 2026, adding a second charge alongside the treason case they already face, a charge that international bodies say is being used to silence dissent.

Zambia charges an opposition presidential candidate with sedition over an election claim

Zambian police formally arrested Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu at Kabwe Central Police Station on 11 September 2026 and charged them with seditious practices under Section 57 of the Penal Code, Chapter 87. The two men were then returned to Mukobeko Maximum Correctional Facility, where they remain in custody.

The seditious practices charges against Mundubile and Makebi

The sedition charge marks a shift in the legal case against the two opposition figures. Earlier reports said police had initially accused them of treason, with allegations involving weapons and a suspected militia network.

The new charge under Section 57 of the Penal Code carries a different legal weight. It places Mundubile and Zulu inside a category of offences that human rights groups say has become a common tool against critics in Zambia.

Police have not released detailed evidence to support the seditious practices charges. The formal arrest at Kabwe Central Police Station came after the men were already in detention, deepening questions about the sequence of legal steps.

A post-election crackdown on opposition voices

Gina Romero, the UN Special Rapporteur on freedom of peaceful assembly and of association, who serves independently of the United Nations, said on 2 September that Zambian authorities had intensified arbitrary arrests and what it called disproportionate charges against political opponents. Sedition was among the charges the UN specifically named.

Amnesty International has also flagged a broader pattern in Zambia. The rights group says sedition and related security charges are being used against critics and opposition politicians.

That context places the Mundubile and Makebi case inside a wider national trend. Zambia is moving through a tense post-election period where domestic political control and security narratives are colliding.

A second charge on top of the treason case

The earlier treason accusations against Mundubile and Zulu were far more serious. Police had alleged a weapons link and a suspected militia network, claims that immediately raised the stakes.

The move to seditious practices charges could be read in different ways. Their lawyers say neither charge as described to them involves any act beyond the making of a statement. Police have not published a charge sheet. The treason case, in which Mundubile is charged alongside 16 others, has no trial date. Both men deny the allegations and neither has stood trial. A broader and more flexible statute.

Either way, the two men now face a charge that international observers say is being deployed with increasing frequency. The UN commentary suggests the case sits within a broader contest over democratic space and the rule of law.

International scrutiny and the rule of law

The United Nations has not named Mundubile and Zulu specifically in its early September statement. But its description of intensified arbitrary arrests and sedition charges matches the pattern of their case.

Amnesty International has gone further in separate reporting, documenting what it calls authoritarian practices in Zambia. The group has issued urgent actions calling for the release of detained opposition figures.

For investors and professionals watching Zambia, the legal environment matters. A state that uses criminal law against political opponents can create uncertainty far beyond the courtroom.

What the case means for Zambia’s political stability

Zambia has long presented itself as a stable democracy in Southern Africa. The post-election period is now testing that reputation.

The detention of opposition figures on sedition charges draws attention from donors, regional bodies and international markets. How the government handles the case will signal its tolerance for dissent.

The broader geopolitical angle is also visible. Zambia sits inside a region where competition for critical minerals and political influence is intensifying, a dynamic covered in Africa: The New Scramble.

What to watch next

The next legal step for Mundubile and Zulu will be a court appearance to answer the seditious practices charges. No date has been confirmed in the available reporting.

International bodies are likely to keep watching. The UN and Amnesty have both signalled that Zambia’s use of sedition charges against opposition figures is a live concern.

The government’s response to that scrutiny will shape how the case is understood. For now, the two men remain at Mukobeko Maximum Correctional Facility, and the legal process is only beginning.

Where are Mundubile and Zulu being held? They were returned to Mukobeko Maximum Correctional Facility after the seditious practices charges were filed. Why is the United Nations concerned about this case? The UN said in early September that Zambian authorities had intensified arbitrary arrests and disproportionate charges, including sedition, against political opponents.

World.title: Africa’s Trade Bank Has Lent Egypt US$9.5 Billion in Three Years and Is Turning Cairo Into a Hub
World.content:
Egypt · FINANCE

Key Facts — What happened Afreximbank said it provided about US$9.5 billion in financing to Egypt over the past three years.

— How big Egyptian media reported the bank has invested around US$41 billion in the country to date.

— The balance sheet Total assets and contingencies reached US$52.3 billion by 30 June 2026, up from US$48.5 billion at end-2025.

— The regional push Afreximbank launched a US$10 billion Gulf Crisis Response Programme for African imports of petroleum products and fertilizers.

— What comes next The bank will hold its 33rd Annual Meetings in El Alamein, Egypt, from 21 to 24 June 2026 in El Alamein.

Afreximbank Egypt financing is deepening fast, with about US$9.5 billion provided over three years and a much larger cumulative footprint reported at around US$41 billion. The African Export-Import Bank is using Cairo as its operational and strategic centre for trade, payments and crisis response.

Africa trade bank has lent Egypt US$9.5 billion in three years and is turning Cairo into a hub

The African Export-Import Bank, known as Afreximbank, has placed Egypt at the centre of its continental strategy. The Cairo-headquartered institution said it provided about US$9.5 billion in financing to Egypt over the past three years.

A balance sheet built around Egypt

Afreximbank reported total assets and contingencies of US$48.5 billion at the end of 2025. By 30 June 2026, that figure had climbed to US$52.3 billion.

Egyptian media put the bank’s cumulative investment in the country at around US$41 billion to date. That is far larger than the three-year financing figure and signals a long-term structural relationship.

The bank is headquartered in Cairo, which gives Egypt a direct line to one of Africa’s most important trade finance institutions. This positioning matters for investors watching where African capital is being directed.

The Gulf Crisis Response Programme

Afreximbank launched a US$10 billion Gulf Crisis Response Programme to help African countries secure imports. The focus is on petroleum products and fertilizers amid global supply-chain and shipping disruptions.

Egyptian reporting said Egypt is expected to receive a significant share of that package. The facility is designed to cushion African economies from external shocks.

This bridge is not a grant but a financing mechanism. It shows how Afreximbank is positioning itself as a lender of first resort when global markets tighten.

Payments integration and the Instapay link

Afreximbank plans deeper payments integration through the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System, or PAPSS, and Egypt’s Instapay. Links are under discussion with the United Arab Emirates, India and China.

That would connect Egyptian instant payments to three of the country’s most important trading partners. It also fits the broader South-South push that Afreximbank has championed.

For businesses moving money across borders, faster settlement reduces cost and risk. Egypt would become a clearing hub for a larger share of intra-African and intercontinental trade.

A trade hub in the New Administrative Capital

Afreximbank is backing a US$250 million African Trade Centre project in Egypt’s New Administrative Capital. The project is framed around trade facilitation, payments, logistics and small and medium-sized enterprises.

That physical footprint reinforces Egypt’s role as a gateway between Africa, the Gulf and Asia. It also aligns with the bank’s sovereignty narrative around African financial institutions.

The project matters for the wider scramble for African trade infrastructure. You can see the pattern in our pillar on Africa: The New Scramble.

Annual meetings and the sovereignty theme

Afreximbank planned its 33rd Annual Meetings in Egypt in June 2026. The theme was “Intra-African Trade and Industrialisation: Pathway to Economic Sovereignty.”

The meetings were scheduled for El Alamein from 21 to 24 June 2026 in El Alamein. Egypt’s Central Bank governor and Afreximbank’s president held a press briefing on the preparations.

The theme is explicit about economic sovereignty. It signals that African institutions want to finance their own trade rather than depend on external lenders.

What to watch next

The June 2026 meetings will likely produce new financing announcements and partnership details. Investors should watch for concrete figures on the Gulf Crisis Response Programme allocations.

Egypt’s expected share of that US$10 billion facility remains the key near-term number. The Instapay and PAPSS integration talks with the UAE, India and China are also worth tracking.

Afreximbank’s growing balance sheet gives it more room to act. The question is whether that capacity translates into faster trade settlement and cheaper import finance for Egyptian businesses.

It is a US$10 billion Afreximbank facility to help African countries import petroleum products and fertilizers during supply-chain disruptions. When are Afreximbank’s 2026 annual meetings? The 33rd Annual Meetings are scheduled for El Alamein, Egypt, from 21 to 24 June 2026 in El Alamein.

World.title: Southern Angola Joins the National Power Grid, Ending Years of Running on Diesel
World.content:
Angola · ENERGY

Key Facts — What happened Angola connected its southern region to the national electricity grid in May 2026, linking Huíla and Namibe from the Gove hydroelectric plant through a 213-km, 220 kV line.

— Who it hits More than 350,000 families in the south are expected to benefit from the end of long-running dependence on diesel generation.

— The money In 2026, Angola approved about $334 million for southern transmission strengthening, including the Huíla–Cunene interconnection.

— The context Angola’s grid had long been split into separate northern, central and southern systems, with the north supplying about 80% of the country’s power.

— What comes next Planned infrastructure includes a north-central-south backbone, with a target expansion of the grid from 3,354 km to 16,350 km by 2025.

Angola’s national electricity grid reached the country’s south in May 2026, when Huíla and Namibe were linked from the Gove hydroelectric plant. The connection ends the region’s long reliance on diesel generation and benefits more than 1 million people.

Southern Angola joins the national power grid, ending years of running on diesel

Angola has officially connected its southern region to the national electricity system, a move the government and the national transmission company RNT say will cut fuel imports and lower state power costs. The link, completed in May 2026, runs more than 213 km at 220 kV from the Gove hydroelectric plant to Huíla and Namibe.

A long-divided grid starts to merge

For years, Angola’s electricity network operated as three separate systems: northern, central and southern. The north dominated, supplying about 80% of the country’s power, according to U.S. government and World Bank material.

The south remained isolated, forcing communities and businesses to depend on diesel generators. That dependence made power expensive and unreliable, and it weighed on the state budget through fuel imports.

The new Gove–Huíla–Namibe connection changes that picture. The government and RNT framed the project as part of a broader national grid expansion meant to improve reliability in the south.

The money behind the Angola national electricity grid push

The financial scale is significant. In 2026, Angola approved about $334 million for southern transmission strengthening, including the Huíla–Cunene interconnection.

That package includes a $16 million grant from the Livable Planet Fund and an IBRD-backed financing structure. The International Bank for Reconstruction and Development is part of the World Bank Group.

Planned infrastructure also includes a north-central-south backbone. The U.S. Trade Service cited a target expansion of the grid from 3,354 km to 16,350 km by 2025.

Who gains and who loses

The clearest winners are households and businesses in Huíla and Namibe. More than 350,000 families are expected to benefit from the end of long-running diesel dependence.

The state also gains, because cheaper hydropower replaces imported diesel. That reduces fuel imports and lowers the cost of supplying power to the south.

Diesel suppliers and logistics operators may lose business as the south switches to grid electricity. The shift also strengthens state control over a strategic sector.

A South-South and multilateral play

The project deepens Angola’s financing ties with the World Bank while supporting regional power integration toward Namibia and Southern African Development Community markets. That fits a wider pattern of infrastructure diplomacy across the continent.

For investors and professionals watching frontier energy markets, the southern connection signals that Angola is serious about transmission, not just generation. It also reduces the carbon footprint of the south’s power supply.

The broader scramble for African infrastructure and critical resources is reshaping how multilateral lenders and national governments work together. Read more in our pillar on Africa: The New Scramble.

What the connection means for reliability

Grid interconnection should make power supply more stable in the south. Hydropower from Gove replaces diesel units that were costly to run and maintain.

Reliability gains matter for local businesses, clinics and schools. They also make the region more attractive for investment in agriculture and processing.

The government has described the connection as ending long-running dependence on diesel generation. That is a concrete shift, not just a planning promise.

What to watch next

The Huíla–Cunene interconnection is the next major piece of southern transmission strengthening. Angola approved the financing in 2026, with World Bank-linked support.

Beyond that, the north-central-south backbone remains the long-term goal. If completed as targeted, it would transform Angola from a fragmented grid into a single national system.

Regional integration toward Namibia and SADC markets will be the test of whether this infrastructure delivers value beyond Angola’s borders. Watch for procurement and construction milestones on the Huíla–Cunene link through 2026.

How many people benefit from the southern grid connection? More than 350,000 families in Angola south are expected to benefit from the end of long-running dependence on diesel generation. What is the next major transmission project in southern Angola? The Huíla–Cunene interconnection is the next major piece, with about $334 million approved in 2026 for southern transmission strengthening.

— The test Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna’s Linda Mwananchi movement is holding a major rally at Jacaranda Grounds in Embakasi East on Sunday 13 September 2026.

— The talks Sifuna, Siaya Governor James Orengo and Jubilee deputy party leader Fred Matiang’i met in Karen on 11 September, after earlier meetings on 24 August and 1 September.

— The counter-move Pro-Ruto figures including Prime Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi and Energy CS Opiyo Wandayi are campaigning in Western and Nyanza for the president’s re-election.

— The warning Human Rights Watch said on 11 September that organised gang attacks on opposition and civil society events have intensified ahead of the 2027 vote.

President William Ruto is moving to ringfence Nairobi and other opposition-leaning areas ahead of the 2027 election, while the Linda Mwananchi movement tests its strength at Jacaranda Grounds in Embakasi East on Sunday 13 September 2026.

Kenya’s political contest is shifting from parliament to the streets and closed-door strategy sessions. President William Ruto is consolidating his base in Nairobi while opposition leaders test whether they can turn public frustration into a national movement.

Ruto ringfences Nairobi as the 2027 countdown begins

President William Ruto is moving to consolidate his political base in Nairobi and other opposition-leaning areas ahead of the August 10, 2027 election. His allies are counter-mobilising in Western and Nyanza, where Prime Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi, Energy Cabinet Secretary Opiyo Wandayi and Kakamega Deputy Governor Ayub Savula have been campaigning for the president’s re-election.

The push is part of a wider scramble for national structures, funding and regional reach. Analysts quoted in Kenyan coverage say Ruto retains the advantage of incumbency, state machinery and a nationwide network.

Ruto is expected to seek another term in 2027. The early mobilisation suggests his camp wants to lock down key urban and regional strongholds before the opposition can build momentum.

Linda Mwananchi tests its mettle at Jacaranda Grounds

Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna’s Linda Mwananchi movement is testing its strength with a major rally at Jacaranda Grounds in Embakasi East on Sunday 13 September 2026. The gathering is a direct challenge to Ruto’s dominance in the capital, which has been a battleground in recent elections.

Sifuna’s camp says it is building support through small public donations. That grassroots funding model is meant to contrast with what opposition figures describe as the state-backed machinery behind the president.

The rally is the most visible sign yet that the opposition intends to contest Nairobi seriously. It also signals that Sifuna is positioning himself as a central figure in the anti-Ruto coalition.

Closed-door talks shape the opposition strategy

Behind the public rallies, opposition leaders are holding a series of private meetings. Sifuna, Siaya Governor James Orengo and Jubilee deputy party leader Fred Matiang’i met in Karen on 11 September, following earlier meetings on 24 August and 1 September.

The talks point to an effort to unite rival opposition factions under a single banner. The three figures bring different regional and party bases, which could broaden the coalition’s appeal.

No formal agreement has been announced. But the frequency of the meetings suggests the opposition is moving from protest politics toward a structured electoral challenge.

Security concerns and the foreign traders crackdown

The political contest is unfolding against a tense security backdrop. Human Rights Watch said on 11 September that organised gang attacks on opposition and civil society events have intensified ahead of the 2027 election.

Ruto’s government last week ordered a crackdown on foreign-owned small businesses. The move drew scrutiny from Burundi and prompted a temporary amnesty for undocumented East African nationals in Kenya.

Opposition leaders have criticised Ruto’s handling of the foreign traders crisis. The dispute adds another layer of friction to an already charged pre-election environment.

The regional and geopolitical read-through

Kenya remains East Africa’s anchor economy and a key player in regional diplomacy. Political stability in Nairobi matters for investors, for neighbouring states and for broader East African Community dynamics.

The foreign traders crackdown has already created diplomatic ripples with Burundi. That tension sits alongside the domestic power struggle as a factor to watch in the months ahead.

For global readers tracking the continent’s shifting alliances, the Kenyan contest is part of a wider pattern of pre-election positioning across Eastern Africa. The scramble for influence is playing out in party structures, street rallies and regional trade policy, as covered in our pillar on Africa: The New Scramble.

What to watch next

The Jacaranda Grounds rally on Sunday 13 September 2026 is the first real test of the opposition’s drawing power in Nairobi. A large turnout would embolden Sifuna and his allies; a weak showing would strengthen Ruto’s hand.

The next milestone is whether the closed-door talks produce a formal coalition agreement. Any deal involving Sifuna, Orengo and Matiang’i would reshape the opposition landscape.

Security will remain a central concern. Human Rights Watch’s warning about gang attacks means both domestic and international observers will be watching how the government handles opposition events in the run-up to August 10, 2027.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Linda Mwananchi movement? Linda Mwananchi is a political movement led by Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna that is testing its strength ahead of the 2027 election. When is Kenya’s next presidential election? Kenya’s next election is scheduled for August 10, 2027, and President William Ruto is expected to seek another term. Who are the key opposition figures meeting behind closed doors? Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna, Siaya Governor James Orengo and Jubilee deputy party leader Fred Matiang’i met in Karen on 11 September 2026.

World.title: Nigerian Savers Lose Millions After the Online Investment Platform PXES Stops Paying Out
World.content:
Nigeria · FINANCE

Key Facts — What happened The online investment platform PXES stopped paying investors in early September 2026 and then became inaccessible.

— The promises PXES offered returns of 25% to 50%, with some packages as high as 120%.

— Who it hits Victims report losses from tens of thousands to millions of naira, with angry investors storming PXES offices in Adamawa and Kogi states.

— The wider pattern The Securities and Exchange Commission said in 2025 that Nigerians had lost over ₦316 billion to Ponzi schemes and unlicensed fund managers.

— The bigger number The Guardian cited an estimated ₦1.7 trillion lost to Ponzi schemes over nine years since 2016.

— What comes next Regulators face pressure to act faster as digital platforms make quick-return scams easier to launch and harder to trace.

Nigerians have lost savings again after the PXES investment platform collapsed in early September 2026, leaving victims with losses from tens of thousands to millions of naira and reviving questions about regulatory gaps in Africa’s largest economy.

Nigerian savers lose millions after online investment platform stops paying out
