World.title: Le Pen kicks off presidential election campaign amid party tensions
World.content:
Back in her political stronghold in northern France, Marine Le Pen is delivering her first major campaign speech this Sunday.

 

The far-right candidate for 2027 is relaunching her presidential election campaign in Hénin-Beaumont, following a gathering of her party’s MPs in Le Touquet (Pas-de-Calais) on Saturday.

Le Pen is leading in the polls, with 34% of voters signalling their intention to vote for her in the first round, regardless of the scenario, according to a survey carried out on 8 and 9 September by OpinionWay for Les Échos.

Despite this, recent weeks have been marked by a series of mishaps, amid alleged tension with the president of the National Rally (RN) party, Jordan Bardella, controversy over aid to Ukraine and the release of a video in which a police officer, a volunteer member of the RN’s security team, makes racist, sexist and conspiracy-theory-based remarks.

Meanwhile, Le Pen has still not reacted to the signing of an immigration pact between Bardella and Nigel Farage, the leader of the UK's hard-right, anti-immigration Reform UK party, which provides for migrants intercepted in British waters to be sent back to France if the two parties come to power.

What role will Bardella play?

Rumours are multiplying about alleged tensions between Le Pen and Bardella, the candidate for the post of prime minister.

According to the French daily Libération, the president of the National Rally is said to have declared "it’s her or me" on 31 August, while Le Pen is reported to have announced her intention to give a greater role in the campaign to her niece, Marion Maréchal, starting with a speech at the RN's parliamentary gathering in Le Touquet.

During the 2022 presidential campaign, Maréchal backed Éric Zemmour, the leader of the rival far-right party Reconquête, rather than her aunt.

Bardella has denied any tensions, telling the French broadcaster BFM-TV: "Everything is going very, very well, I assure you. I support her 2,000%."

He added that he had an "unbreakable political and personal affinity" with Le Pen while also denying that he wanted to "impose" his line on the party.

The fundamental differences between the two leading figures of the National Rally are mainly about economic policy, especially pensions.

According to Bardella, the current French pension system "is not economically sustainable."

He also seems hesitant to have his "boss" turn her proposed ban on the wearing of the veil in public spaces into a central campaign issue.

On 31 August, he insisted that the aim was not "to impose a dress code," stressing that a referendum on the issue would be held.

The president of the Patriots for Europe group in the European Parliament also appears more pro-market than Le Pen, who has traditionally been more supportive of protectionist measures.

Support for Ukraine

Beyond this, the RN is also facing disagreements over international issues.

Appearing on BFM-TV on 4 September, Louis Aliot, the party’s vice-president and mayor of Perpignan, was asked about aid to Ukraine.

"We turn off the tap. The health system, the education system, the whole economy, everything has been cut to the bone, and yet we still find money to fund more weapons (...) I’m willing to accept that, but who pays for all this? You also have to know how to stop a war," he said.

His comments quickly sparked a debate.

On X, Édouard Philippe, the centre-right Horizons party’s candidate for 2027, seized the opportunity to accuse the RN of "its support for Putin’s regime," arguing that "turning off the tap for Ukraine means serving Russia."

"Weakening Ukraine, as Marine Le Pen wants, means threatening the security of Europe and France. I will do everything to stop her," he added.

Le Pen hit back within the hour, reminding the former prime minister that he was in office when the Russian president was "received with great pomp at the Palace of Versailles and then at the Fort of Brégançon," and that he himself had welcomed Dmitry Medvedev, then Russian prime minister, to his home city of Le Havre in June 2019.

National Rally grapples with police scandal

On 8 September, French regional daily Midi Libre released a video from November 2025 showing several municipal police officers in Carcassonne making racist, sexist and conspiracy-related comments during a nighttime patrol.

The patrol leader, responsible for nearly 90% of the remarks made that evening, is a former paratrooper, but he had also volunteered for the RN's internal security service.

He notably escorted Bardella on several trips, including during the promotional tour for his book, as well as at the launch of the RN's municipal election campaign.

The officer in question was expelled from the National Rally on Wednesday. Bardella, for his part, has described his comments as "despicable."

The Carcassonne public prosecutor’s office also announced on Wednesday the suspension of the four municipal police officers who appear in the video.

World.title: Are you smarter than a 15-year-old? Test your maths, science and reading with these PISA questions
World.content:
Every three years, the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development’s (OECD)'s Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) evaluates 15-year-olds' reading, mathematics and science abilities through a standardised test.

 

The latest report, published on Tuesday, has revealed a concerning global decline in maths and reading skills in particular. Artificial intelligence (AI), smartphones and social media have been cited as contributing factors.

"The bottom line is quite simple: You don't get fit by watching sports. You get fit by doing sports," Andreas Schleicher, the founder of the OECD's renowned PISA tests, told Euronews.

"And the same is true with learning. Learning doesn't come through the consumption of content; learning comes by engaging with ideas to compare and contrast. And AI can hollow out that very process. That's what we observe."

But what about the adults? Are we any better? A 2024 study by Reading Agency found that half of the adults in the United Kingdom don't read for pleasure, while a Eurostat survey from the same year found that almost half of EU citizens have not read a single book in twelve months.

It begs the question: How much better than the 15-year-olds would we all fare?

Now's your chance to see — scroll to have a go at a sample of the OECD's questions. Answers can be found at the very bottom of the page (no cheating!)

Mathematics

Question 1: Alex drew the following pattern of red and blue triangles.

The first four rows of the pattern are shown below.

Mathematics test from PISA 2022. OECD

What percentage of the triangles in the first four rows of Alex’s pattern are blue?

A) 37.5%

B) 50.0%

C) 60.0%

D) 62.5%

Question 2: Are the statements below supported by the information shown in the graph pictured? Answer either Yes or No for each statement.

Mathematics test from PISA 2022. OECD

The number of DVDs sold declined by about 50% from 2008 through 2014

The number of DVDs sold declined by the same amount each year from 2008 through 2014

The slope of the line is the average yearly decline in DVDs sold from 2008 to 2014

Science

Question 1: Many people are concerned about the global environmental impacts of the manufacture and disposal of clothing.

Cotton fibres come from the outer layer of the cotton plant’s seeds. Compared to synthetic fibres, cotton fibres need less processing and biodegrade more easily.

The production of cotton textiles requires a lot of water, fertilisers, pesticides and other harmful chemicals. To try to solve these issues, sustainable cotton production methods are being developed.

Which of the following actions can be taken to reduce the negative environmental impacts of producing cotton textiles? Highlight all correct answers.

Use water more efficiently

Reduce the quality of the cotton textiles produced

Increase the number of staff that cotton farms employ

Use pesticides that are harmful only to the pest species being targeted

Dispose of chemical waste in areas far away from the sites involved in cotton production

Question 2: When lightning strikes, an observer immediately sees a flash of light. Thunder occurs at the same time, but the observer hears it a little later.

The time taken before an observer hears thunder depends on factors including the distance between the observer and the location of the lightning strike.

Which one of the following statements best explains why lightning is seen before thunder is heard?

The speed of light through air is faster than the speed of sound through air.

Light does not need to travel through the air to be seen, but sound does need to travel through the air to be heard.

Particles of light are not as heavy as particles of sound, so they are easier to detect

Eyes detect light faster than ears detect sound

Reading

Question 1: In this test, you will read some sentences and decide if they make sense or not. Answer YES if the sentence makes sense and NO if the sentence does not make sense.

The red car had a flat tire

Airplanes are made of dogs

The student read the book last night

Question 2: You are visiting your relatives, who recently moved to a farm to raise chickens. You ask your aunt, “How did you learn how to raise chickens?”

She says, “We talked to a lot of people who raise chickens. And, there are lots of resources on the Internet. For example, there is a Chicken Health forum that I like to visit. It was very helpful to me recently when one of my hens hurt her leg. I’ll show you the conversation I had.”

Reading test from PISA 2022. OECD

What does Ivana_88 want to know?

If she can give aspirin to an injured hen

How often she can give aspirin to an injured hen

How to contact a veterinarian about an injured hen

If she can determine the pain level of an injured hen

Financial literacy

Financial literacy test from PISA 2022. OECD

Greg buys a bike.He takes out a loan with the bike shop's in-store finance company.How much is Greg likely to pay?

Less than 600 zeds

More than 600 zeds

Exactly 600 zeds

Answers:

Mathematics 1. A, 2. Yes, No, Yes.

Science 1. ’Use water more efficiently’ and ‘Use pesticides that are harmful only to the pest species being targeted'. 2. ‘The speed of light through air is faster than the speed of sound through air.’

Reading 1. Yes, No, Yes. 2. “If she can give aspirin to my hen”.

Financial literacy 1. The second response or third response with explanation that Greg will pay additional charges.

Find the OECD's full PISA test here. https://www.oecd.org/en/about/programmes/pisa/pisa-test.html

World.title: Oktoberfest 2026: All the rules visitors need to know
World.content:
Next Saturday, when Munich Mayor Dominik Krause taps the first beer barrel on the city's Theresienwiese, the famous cry of "O'zapft is" will ring out once again as Oktoberfest 2026 kicks off.

 

From Saturday, 19 September to Sunday, 4 October, more than six million visitors are expected at Oktoberfest, Germany's world-renowned folk and beer festival.

But attendees will have to keep some important rules in mind.

Cannabis

Munich’s Oktoberfest is a cannabis-free zone.

Back in July 2024, the Bavarian state parliament passed the "Bayerische Cannabisfolgenbegrenzungsgesetz," banning the consumption of cannabis in certain places.

Anyone caught smoking cannabis on the festival grounds faces a fine of €1,500, while repeat offenders could have to shell out more than €5,000.

Cannabis simply has no place at the Wiesn Clemens Baumgärtner (CSU) Oktoberfest official for the city of Munich

In the official final report for last year, Munich police recorded a total of 27 breaches of the cannabis ban at Oktoberfest. Simply possessing cannabis is allowed, as long as adults stay within the nationwide legal limit of up to 25 grams.

Smoking tobacco is permitted on festival grounds and in beer gardens, although a strict smoking ban has been in place inside beer tents since 2010. Most tents offer designated smoking areas or balconies, however.

There are potential fines of up to €1,000 for anyone who does not follow the rules.

Rules for children

As lively as the atmosphere may be between beer steins, music and candy floss, the law does not make exceptions for the youngest visitors.

Anyone strolling across the fairground with a pram or buggy should keep an eye on the clock. From Sunday to Friday, children in prams are welcome until 6 pm. After that it gets too crowded – and therefore too dangerous. The rules are even stricter on Saturdays and on 3 October, when prams and buggies are completely prohibited for safety reasons.

When it comes to youth protection, organisers have clear boundaries.

For the very youngest, the evening in the beer tent ends at 8 pm. Children under six, even when accompanied by their parents, must leave the tents at that time. For children and teenagers under 16, the rule from 8 pm is that they are no longer allowed on the fairground without a legal guardian. Those aged 16 or 17 may stay on the site until closing time without their parents – although in certain tents such as Käfer or the Weinzelt the night ends at midnight.

Children in traditional costume at Oktoberfest Copyright 2010 AP. All rights reserved.

Anyone coming to the Wiesn by bicycle, e-scooter, scooter, skateboard or inline skates must leave them outside the entrance to the festival grounds. They are not permitted on the site itself.

Anyone who gets on an e-scooter or a bicycle afterwards should remember that the same alcohol limits apply as for motor vehicles. Starting at a blood alcohol concentration of 0.5%, you risk a €500 fine, two penalty points on your license, and a potential one-month driving ban.

Cocaine

Cocaine is among the most commonly detected illegal drugs at Oktoberfest. In 2025 alone, around 100 people were caught using it.

The Bavarian State Office of Criminal Investigation (BLKA) reported in April 2025 that the number of cocaine offences in Bavaria had risen from 2,148 in 2020 to 3,972 in 2024 – an increase of almost 85% within four years. The agency said a "cocaine surge" across Germany was also being felt in Bavaria.

The figures are also rising in Munich. In 2025, 1,396 drug offences involving cocaine or crack were recorded, up from 1,227 in 2024 – an increase of 13.8%.

Drinking contests banned

Despite all the rules, people are of course allowed to enjoy themselves at Oktoberfest – but organisers draw a clear line between a lively atmosphere and a loss of control.

Drinking contests in which guests down their Maß as quickly as possible or encourage each other on to drink to excess are not welcome. Anyone who also starts clambering around on tables or benches and puts other guests at risk may find themselves being thrown out.

Waitress carrying beer steins in the Hofbräuhaus beer tent Copyright 2024 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

Oktoberfest visitors will also have to dig deep into their wallets in 2026, as beer is becoming increasingly more expensive.

A Maß now costs between €14.80 and €15.90. This puts the average price 2.38% above last year.

Visitors are also reminded to keep their hands to themselves and follow the rules while enjoying the event as it is meant to be, with a hearty "Ein Prosit der Gemütlichkeit!"

World.title: UAE and Iran leaders meet at the BRICS summit for the first time since the war
World.content:
Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan met Iranian president Masoud Pezeshkian on Sunday during the BRICS summit in India, weeks after the UAE announced a suspension of trade and financial dealings with Tehran.

 

The talks mark the countries’ highest-level meeting since the start of the US-Israel war with Iran, as the UAE has been making it clear through presidential diplomatic adviser Anwar Gargash that "trust is the mountain we will have to climb," as "geography leaves us no alternative to engagement," but that those relations will need to be judged by actions and not words to rebuild the shattered trust.

The Abu Dhabi Media Office said the two leaders stressed the importance of supporting efforts to reduce tensions and strengthen regional stability.

On 19 August, the UAE’s foreign ministry announced that it had halted all trade and financial transactions with Iran until further notice, citing regional escalation.

The same statement reaffirmed the UAE’s commitment to dialogue and regional cooperation. Saturday’s account of the meeting did not announce a change to the trade restrictions or a specific agreement between the two countries.

Former head of Israel’s military intelligence research department Danny Citrinowicz explained in a post on X that "despite all the bad blood between Abu Dhabi and Tehran, the emerging Gulf approach, and particularly the UAE’s, is increasingly clear: manage the Iranian risk rather than push Tehran into a corner."

"This does not mean trust. Rebuilding even a basic level of confidence between the two sides will take years. But from Abu Dhabi’s perspective, maintaining channels with Tehran is itself a form of strategic hedging. The UAE has little interest in becoming a frontline state in another regional war," the Israeli security analyst said.

Calls to protect trade and energy

Both countries are members of BRICS, the group of emerging economies that includes Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa.

They backed the summit’s New Delhi Declaration, adopted on Saturday, which expressed concern over escalating tensions in the Middle East and called for “maximum restraint”.

The declaration urged the protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure, respect for national sovereignty and a lasting settlement through diplomacy. Leaders also called for cooperation to keep global trade, supply chains and energy moving, in line with international law.

Chinese President Xi Jinping urged BRICS to help bring peace to the region, saying China would work with other members towards that goal.

The declaration also criticised unilateral tariffs and sanctions and supported further work on international payments and trade using members’ own currencies.

Speaking on Sunday at the BRICS Plus outreach session, which brings members together with other invited countries, Pezeshkian said attacks on a country’s economic and energy infrastructure had consequences beyond its borders.

He said unilateral sanctions affected food security and people’s welfare, and called for greater use of national currencies and a stronger role for the New Development Bank, the lender established by BRICS countries.

Hormuz talks planned in Oman

Separately, Pezeshkian said Arab foreign ministers were due to meet in Muscat on Monday to sign an agreement establishing a joint Iran-Oman shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz, disregarding the Gulf countries' united position that the strait must be open to free international navigation.

The UAE president's diplomatic advisor Anwar Gargash underlined days ago the country's firm position that it would not accept a single state's control of the strategic Strait of Hormuz and that it was unacceptable for oil tankers to be threatened and attacked while attempting to transit the key waterway.

“Our energy exports will not be held hostage, nor will our trade and economic activity,” Gargash said.

In an interview published on Saturday, Pezeshkian said the International Maritime Organisation would then be informed of the agreement.

Iran had already announced on 5 August that it had agreed the location of a proposed shipping route with Oman.

At the time, Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said the arrangement alone could not guarantee safe navigation while the US naval blockade and other actions against Iran continued.

Pezeshkian also said in Saturday’s interview that Iran would reopen the strait when the United States ended its blockade and attacks. His remarks did not set a date for reopening the waterway.

On Sunday, Qeshm governor Amir Teymouri said one person had been killed after a merchant vessel was struck near Iran's Hengam and Qeshm islands. He did not identify the source of the strike.

World.title: Erdogan hints at larger nuclear partnership with Russia, unsettling Turkey's allies
World.content:
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan is signalling a move to expand nuclear power cooperation with Russia, just as his country’s first Russian-built nuclear station prepares to go live later this year. The deepening partnership is likely to unsettle Turkey’s western allies.

Advertising

On the sidelines of a recent gathering of regional leaders in Kyrgyzstan, Erdogan told his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, that Russia and Turkey “will take steps together to open some new power plants, along with the opening of the Akkuyu nuclear power plant”.

The Akkuyu nuclear power plant, built by Russia’s state nuclear company Rosatom on Turkey's Mediterranean coast, is due to go online later this year.

Erdogan’s announcement comes amid strained ties with Russia, as the Turkish leader has deepened relations with United States President Donald Trump.

Ozgur Unluhisarcikli, head of the Ankara office of US think tank the German Marshall Fund, describes Erdogan’s move as a “gesture” to Putin.

“Although Turkey is competing with Russia geopolitically, and although Turkey is firmly anchored in NATO and is improving its relationship with the United States, it does not intend to sever all ties with Russia,” Unluhisarcikli explained.

“Indeed, Turkey sees the Turkey-Russia relationship as a long-term strategic one. And this is, by the way, consistent with Turkey's balancing act.”

Trump tests Turkey's energy dependence on Russia with lure of US power

Nuclear lifeline

For Ankara, nuclear energy promises to help it break free from its heavy reliance on imported power. Once operational, the Akkuyu plant in southern Turkey will supply as much as 10 percent of the country’s electricity.

Rosatom owns the Akkuyu power plant and will recoup the estimated €21.5 billion construction costs by selling electricity to Turkey, generating annual income of around €2-3 billion.

Such income could be a vital tool for Moscow to mitigate tightening sanctions by both the European Union and the United States.

“The Akkuyu nuclear power plant allows Russia to build itself various state-to-state payment channels to store liquidity in Turkish banks without necessarily interfering with any sanctions regulations,” according to George Voloshin of Acams, a global organisation dedicated to anti-financial crime, training and education.

Voloshin believes that, given the project's 60- to 80-year lifespan, Turkey’s commitment to Russian nuclear power will shape bilateral ties for the long term, with consequences.

“It will be a source of scrutiny from western partners of Turkey. At the same time, nuclear energy has been so far shielded from any sanctions, so for Russia it is clearly a kind of lifeline,” he said.

The Akkuyu plant, currently under construction, will be Turkey's first nuclear power station. © AFP/Dogan News Agency/Ibrahim Mese

Turkey seeks Black Sea shipping deal as attacks threaten grain trade

Since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Ankara has maintained that it is not bound by EU or US sanctions on Moscow. Yet behind the scenes, it has quietly followed many restrictions and secured crucial waivers, especially for Russian gas.

By leveraging its pivotal location near Syria and Iran, Ankara has walked a diplomatic tightrope between its western partners and Moscow.

However, deepening nuclear cooperation with Russia threatens to complicate the already difficult balancing act.

“It would reinforce the already existing distrust between Turkey and Europe and Turkey and the United States,” warned Unluhisarcikli.

“But at the same time, Turkey is in talks with other countries, the United States and South Korea. These are the main two competitors for Russia.”

Mutual dependency

Turkey’s dependence on Russian fossil fuels has stirred unease at home, and the idea of doubling down with Russian nuclear energy only heightens the sense of anxiety. “It is a dilemma,” Unluhisarcikli conceded.

Yet with Russia willing to shoulder the hefty construction costs, cash-strapped Ankara has a strong incentive to continue the partnership.

Russia expert Zaur Gasimov of Istanbul’s Turkish-German University points out that more than a decade of joint investment makes it tough for Turkey to turn to alternative suppliers.

"It's quite a profound project,” said Gasimov, “Russia conducts the training of Turkish specialists in the field of nuclear energy, which started 15 years ago. We now have three or four waves of Turkish engineers who stayed for longer periods in Russia; they learn the Russian language for two years, and you have an infrastructure of specialists.”

However, Gasimov stresses that, given the scale of investment by both sides, it has created an important mutual dependency. “Its importance makes the two sides, somehow, at the end, interested in preserving a certain level of the relationship,” he said.

This shared reliance might help keep Turkish-Russian rivalries in check, from North Africa to the Middle East, the Caucasus and the Black Sea.

Yet any step toward deeper nuclear cooperation is bound to invite sharper scrutiny and rising suspicion from Ankara’s western allies.

World.title: Turkey: 162 arrested in LGBTQ+ raids
World.content:
Turkish authorities have arrested at least 162 people in a weekend crackdown on the country's LGBTQ+ community. Ankara says police raids on gay bars and other venues are aimed at protecting family values.

Turkish police have arrested at least 162 people and searched the offices of six LGBTQ+ associations in weekend raids designed to support the country's campaign to protect family values.

The Ankara-based LGBTQ+ rights group Kaos GL claimed that beyond arrests, the government had also cut access to dozens of websites and social media accounts belonging to associate groups and rights advocates.

Government says its fulfilling duty to 'protect families and children'

Turkish Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said investigations — prompted by accusations of prostitution and obscenity — were coordinated by prosecutors in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Aydin and Mersin and involved judicial proceedings against 162 suspects, nine associations and 13 businesses across 15 provinces.

"As per the duty to protect families and children given to the state by the constitution, no criminal organization, abuse network or illegal activity which targets children, youths or families will be tolerated!" Gurlek added in a social media post.

Authorities say they seized drugs, digital equipment, smuggled alcohol and a gun in weekend police operations targeting gay bars and night clubs as well as a hammam that was said to be a place of prostitution.

The Istanbul prosecutor's office added that it had found evidence indicating that children and minors were being inappropriately swayed on issues tied to sexual orientation and gender identity.

Rights groups say the government is unfairly targeting the LGBTQ+ community, with Kaos GL saying that it had been accused of making "posts containing obscenities" accessible to children.

Being gay in Turkey To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Erdogan scapegoats LGBTQ+ 'perverts' for falling birthrates, avoiding actual contributing factors

The weekend police operation was dubbed "My Family is Safe" by the government and was part of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's "Decade of Family and Population" scheme, which is designed to reverse plummeting birthrates in the aging country.

Authorities say it was intended to make sure that society does not see LGBTQ+ activity as "normal" and that raids were carried out to "protect children, the institution of the family, and our shared moral values."

Although same-sex relations are not illegal in the country, homophobia is rife, with President Erdogan blaming LGBTQ "perverts" for Turkey's rapidly declining birthrates.

That would seem a rhetorical diversion from the actual complexity of reasons for the decline, which Erdogan — who has ruled as the country's authoritarian president since 2014 as well as serving as its influential prime minister for 10 years before that — has called "a disaster."

Though Turkey's statistical agency, TurkStat, tracked a sharp decline in the total fertility rate between 2013 and 2023 (from 2.11 to 1.51 ), the shift brings birthrates in the country closer to those in other developed nations.

Observers say the real reasons for the drop are more likely of a structural and institutional nature rather than one chalked up to lifestyle.

Turkey's chronically worsening financial crisis, inflation, skyrocketing housing prices, family unfriendly workplace environments, limited access to affordable childcare, and higher educational and employment rates for women are all considered reasons for Turks to postpone having children, as well as for having fewer when they finally do.

World.title: Ukraine, Poland say Russia hit Warsaw-bound passenger train
World.content:
Ukrainian officials accused Russia of a "systemic attack" on its railways following drone strikes near the Polish border, including a hit on a locomotive of a passenger train headed to Warsaw.

Russia launched two drone strikes on western Ukraine, very near its border with NATO member Poland, Ukrainian and Polish authorities said on Sunday.

One of the drones hit a passenger train locomotive in Volyn, some two kilometers (1.24 miles) from the border crossing.

"The monitoring team gave the train crew advanced warning, and thanks to that, no one was injured," Ukrainian railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia said in online post.

Putin rejects Zelenskyy's G20 talks offer To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The company later said that a "systemic attack" was happening throughout Ukraine.

Separately, Poland's PKP Intercity confirmed that they have taken control of the affected train following the attack in the Ukrainian territory.

"The train is carrying 206 people. There are no Polish citizens among the passengers," the operator said online. "After completing customs clearance, it will continue its journey towards Warsaw."

Zelenskyy: Locomotive 'deliberately burned'

On Sunday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the locomotive was "deliberately burned" and a gas station damaged in Volyn.

"It is precisely to prevent these strikes from spreading further into Europe that Ukrainian men and women fight every day, give their lives, and do not allow the aggression to expand," he said.

Moscow did not immediately comment on the reports.

Falling debris set a gas station on fire near the border checkpoint in Volyn Image: Sylwester Uchanski/REUTERS

Ukrainian officials also reported another drone strike on Yahodyn overnight, some half a mile (800 meters) from the Polish border.

The border with Poland serves as essential transit point for military and humanitarian aid.

'Putin's terror 'knocking' directly on the doors' — Ukrainian foreign minister

Commenting on the Yahodyn incident, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the "barbaric" attacks were more than "just a continuation of its attacks on our state borders."

"This is Putin's terror 'knocking' directly on the doors of the EU and NATO. Russian barbarians are at your gate, dear partners," he said in an English-language post on X.

He urged Ukraine's Western allies to make Russia "feel the consequences of its terror. Not just half-decisions, but uncompromising, powerful steps. Full trade embargo. Full entry bans. Full sanctions on the military-industrial complex."

"Putin needs to understand that his barbarism will be met with decisive action that increases the cost of war for him to an unacceptable level," he added.

World.title: Russians on the Goethe-Institut: 'Hostage to politics'
World.content:
Canceled language exams, disrupted plans to study in Germany, and the disappearance of an important cultural link: DW users shared how the closure of Germany's Goethe-Institut in Russia affects their lives.

Germany's Goethe-Institut is set toclose all Russian branches by Sunday, amid one of the worst spats in the history of relations between Russia and Germany.

The Russian Foreign Ministry ordered the closure of the German cultural centers in Moscow, St. Petersburg, and Novosibirsk in response to Berlin's reaction to the attempteddrone attackat Leipzig airport in early August. The German authorities blamed Moscow for organizing the attack and announced sanctions. They include closing the Russian culture and education center in Berlin, known as the Russian House, and the Russian Consulate General in Bonn, as well tightening visa restrictions for Russian citizens.

"All employees must cease their work in Russia as of September 13, 2026," Goethe-Institut Secretary General Gitte Zschoch said in a statement. "No more books can be borrowed from our libraries, and no further training can be offered. German language teachers are losing an important source of professional training and support. For people in Russia, this further restricts access to the German language, culture and reliable information from and about Germany."

The library of the Goethe-Institut's Moscow branch won't be accessible anymore after September 13 either Image: Timur Gusarov/TASS/picture alliance

DW asked its users in Russia to share how the closure of the Goethe-Institut will affect them personally. The responses received do not constitute a representative survey. All users shared their stories on conditions of anonymity. Russian authorities labeled DW an "undesirable organization" making every cooperation with the media company a criminal offense.

'We'll have to travel to another country' for German exams

Many DW readers fear that, after the closure of the Goethe-Institut branches, they or their relatives will no longer be able to take exams in Russia for internationally recognized German language certificates.

Some readers pointed out that closing the Goethe-Institut in Russia will hit ethnic Germans willing to relocate back to Germany, or late repatriates, especially hard.

"I no longer live in Russia, having emigrated as a late repatriate, but my parents are still in Russia and were planning to take exams at the Goethe-Institut this fall or winter before submitting their resettlement documents. It looks like they'll have to take the exams in another country, which means additional stress and expenses for them," one reader said.

DW also received responses from parents whose children are learning German and plan to continue their education in Germany.

"My son attends a German school, and now we won't be able to take the exam in Russia. We'll have to travel to another country," one message said.

Germany blames Russia for attempted terror attack in Leipzig To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

It remains unclear whether exams, language courses and educational programs will continue in Russia in another format or through partner organizations. Several readers expressed hope that at least some services will remain available online.

Goethe-Institute closures hit teachers hard

The closure of the institute will affect not only those planning to move to Germany or enroll at a German university. A German language teacher from the Moscow region told DW that her school had cooperated with the Goethe-Institut for more than 15 years.

"This partnership was one of the most important pillars of our work. The institute supported us with high-quality teaching materials and provided modern books and publications about life in Germany, helping us make lessons engaging and relevant. Our students attended additional courses, and many successfully passed the Goethe certificate exams," she wrote.

"I teach German and can't find a job in Russia," another teacher told DW.

"It's terrible. I'm a German teacher, and I feel professionally stranded and lost," a third wrote.

Despite the restrictions imposed since the beginning of Russia's war in Ukraine in 2022, demand for the institute's services remained high. According to the Goethe-Institut, around 10,000 people studied German through its programs and partnerships in 2025. Before 2023, that number used to stand at around 16,000 people. The institute administered roughly 22,000 exams, and its libraries were visited by 6,700 people in 2025.

'Culture has become a hostage to political decisions'

Many readers perceive what is happening as another stage in the destruction of ties between Russia and Germany.

"We would like cultural relations between the Russian Federation and Germany not to be destroyed," one DW user responded. "It is sad to realize that culture has become a hostage to political decisions. The closure of the Goethe-Institut will affect people who have no way of influencing politicians."

Leipzig/Halle airport in Germany was the target of an attempted drone attack in August 2026 Image: Axel Schmidt/REUTERS

Some DW readers from Russia specifically draw attention to the responsibility of politicians. One reader called the decision to close the institutes another step toward isolating the country and wondered why its consequences affect ordinary citizens rather than the Russian politicians who make such decisions.

"Why can the people making decisions to isolate Russia from Europe simultaneously provide their own children and close relatives with a European education and a European way of life?" a DW user asked, proposing a ban on the education of the children and close relatives of members of Russia's top leadership at universities in Germany and other EU countries.

Part of the audience considers Moscow's decision expected.

"The closure of the branches looks like a logical response to the closure of the Russian House in Germany. Could it have been otherwise? It is a pity that cultural and humanitarian ties between the countries are becoming hostages to politics," one reader wrote.

Some Russians hold Germany responsible for deteriorating relationship

Some Russians however believe that closing the Goethe-Institut branches in Russia was the right step and blame Germany for the recent escalation of the conflict with Russia.

"German authorities have buried cultural cooperation with Russia by shutting down the Russian House. The responsibility lies entirely with the German side, " said one of the survey participants.

A bilateral intergovernmental agreement between Russia and Germany from 2011 regulates the work of the Russian House in Berlin and the Goethe-Institut's branches in Russia. It obliges both countries, on the basis of reciprocity, to ensure conditions necessary for the operation of their cultural centers. However, it does not in any way provide for the automatic closure of one country's cultural centers in response to the other country doing so.

President of the Goethe-Institut Gesche Joost called the closure of its branches in Russia "the end of an era in German-Russian cultural relations."

According to its website, the Goethe-Institut has 154 branches in 100 countries. This number includes the three branches in Russia that are now being closed.

World.title: Croatia: 'Monster' fire triggers evacuation on Brac island
World.content:
A rapidly spreading wildfire threatened homes and tourist accommodations on the Croatian island of Brac, with firefighters battling the blaze overnight.

Nearly 700 people were evacuated amid a wildfire on the Adriatic island of Brac, Croatian media outlets reported on Sunday, following a tense night which saw hundreds of firefighters defending homes and tourist accommodations from the approaching blaze.

The situation was especially dramatic near the small town of Milna on the island's western coast.

"Last night was a disaster. It was simply impossible," Milna Mayor Frane Lozic told Net.hr news outlet. "I would have not believed that [the fire] can wipe out everything in its path so quickly."

Over 220 firefighters and 69 vehicles fought the blaze overnight Image: Ivo Cagalj/Pixsell/IMAGO

The fire was first reported on Thursday, but firefighting efforts were complicated by inaccessible terrain.

Even so, Lozic said that the authorities believed they had the situation in hand by Saturday.

"We thought we got it reined in yesterday, that it is all over, and then it happened: Sea wind starts blowing at 9 p.m. and out of nowhere, there is a monster," he said.

No deaths reported in blaze

Tourist ships joined the rescue efforts overnight, with many tourists spending the night at the beach, waiting to be evacuated.

No deaths were reported due to the blaze. However, one 76-year-old Croatian woman was hospitalized in critical condition, according to Index.hr news portal. The woman is believed to have fallen off a ship during the evacuation process. A 27-year-old man required medical aid for smoke inhalation and was then released.

Authorities estimated some 3,500 hectares (8,600 acres) were affected by the fire, according to a report by the AFP news agency.

Officials confirmed some buildings were damaged, but said it was too early for a full damage assessment.

Firefighting planes active on the scene

As of Sunday morning, Croatian authorities said there were no more "open fires" but added teams were still in the field to prevent reignition. Four specialized firefighting planes are also operating in the area.

The blaze on the island of Brac was visible from Croatia's second city, Split Image: Zvonimir Barisin/Pixsell/IMAGO

Two government ministers and the head of Croatia's national firefighting service are set to attend a high-level meeting on Brac this afternoon with local officials and leaders of the local firefighting teams, after which they are expected to provide more information about the blaze.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

World.title: Vanuatu ferry capsize leaves one dead, 30 missing
World.content:
Rescue efforts have been slow after a South Pacific inter-island ferry sank in bad weather on Friday. An investigation has already begun into negligence on the part of the operator.

At least one person has died and another 30 remain missing after an inter-island ferry in Vanuatu sank in poor weather on Friday.

The South Pacific archipelagic island nation with a population of just under 350,000 is located about 1,750 kilometers (1,090 miles) east of Australia.

The vessel went down in very heavy seas somewhere between the islands of Santo and Ambae, according to authorities.

The MV Matui, operated by the Tui Shipping Agency, set sail Friday from Santo with more than 40 passengers and crew but never arrived in Ambae.

Prime Minister Jotham Napat's office on Sunday morning said that one body had been recovered, 15 passengers had been "accounted for alive" and "over 30 people are missing at sea."

Napat's office took charge of the search and rescue effort on Sunday afternoon after the prime minister expressed frustration over being unable to reach senior officials.

In a statement, Napat's office said, "Search and rescue operations are continuing," adding that the search "in open waters is being eased off whilst efforts ‌move ​toward a search along the southeast coast, where currents may have carried survivors."

"To the survivors, we pray for your strength and recovery. To ⁠the ​families of those missing and those we ​have lost, please know that the nation stands with you in this time of grief," ​the statement continued.

Napat's office also announced that an investigation into the incident had already been launched amid suspicion of negligence on the part of operator Tui.

"This loss appears to be the result of strong winds and marine warnings not being heeded," it said, "and possibly of negligence including overloading of the vessel."

Local frustration at lack of urgency from authorities

Reports of how the rescue effort began are hazy, with Vanuatu parliamentary representative Matai Seremaiah — who took part in the search — telling New Zealand public broadcaster RNZ that a crew member had swam ashore and "alerted us that the ship had capsized."

French news agency AFP cited a hotel owner on Santo who told reporters an employee of his had pulled a survivor in a life vest to shore on Saturday afternoon and authorities were immediately alerted.

It is unclear if these accounts refer to the same survivor.

"He looked like he had been in the bathtub for 25 hours — he was wrinkled up and white. He was cold," said hotel owner Ashley Beveridge.

"There was no rescue started until this guy got washed up on our beach — lucky he got washed up in an inhabited area," he added.

Beveridge told AFP that locals had expressed great frustration at the lack of urgency shown by authorities, with private citizens mobilizing cargo ships and a plane on Saturday afternoon to search for survivors on their own.

The Maritime Rescue Coordination Center (MRCC) in Noumea, New Caledonia, has said it is now assisting in the search effort.

A French Armed Forces aircraft from New Caledonia was also deployed on Sunday morning.

The MRCC said that 12 people had been located Sunday morning.

Local media reported that survivors were being treated at Northern Provincial hospital on Santo Island.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

World.title: Indonesia rescuers search for 130 people after ferry sinks
World.content:
The ship was carrying over 240 people in the Java Sea when it ran into bad weather. Officials say six people have died and 130 are still missing.

An Indonesian passenger ship carrying 243 people sank in the Java Sea on Sunday after it was hit by bad weather, local authorities said.

Officials said six people had died, while 107 were brought to safety and some 130 passengers were still missing.

"We have carried out efforts to search for victims to the fullest extent. There were passengers who ... had already been successfully evacuated by the units at the scene," I Putu Sudayana, head of the Banjarmasin Search and Rescue Office, told reporters.

The Virgo Transport 8 was traveling from Indonesia's second-largest city of Surabaya to Banjarmasin, the capital of South Kalimantan province on Borneo island.

It departed on Saturday at 10:13 a.m. local time (0330 UTC), but the ship's operator lost contact with the vessel early Sunday amid bad weather. It was scheduled to arrive in Banjarmasin at about 2 p.m. local time on (0700 UTC) Sunday.

Over 100 people have been rescued during ongoing search and rescue operations Image: Infuz/AFP

Search operation underway

Search and rescue teams launched an operation after the operator alerted authorities. Ships and a helicopter were deployed to the vessel's last known location.

"The ship's operator reported the incident to authorities after receiving information that the vessel had encountered bad weather," Sudayana said in an earlier video briefing.

The ship's last known position was in the Java Sea, roughly 148 kilometers (92 miles) from a pier in Banjarmasin, according to the Associated Press.

Sudayana added that authorities were mobilizing all available personnel and equipment given the large number of people aboard. The agency was coordinating with maritime authorities while closely monitoring weather conditions in the area, he said.

Indonesia, a nation of roughly 17,000 islands, relies heavily on ferries for transportation, with sea travel often cheaper and more accessible than flying. But safety enforcement across the country's maritime sector has been inconsistent, contributing to a comparatively high rate of accidents.

Edited by: Natalie Muller
