World.title: Iraq seizes drone launchers near Iran to stop attacks on Saudi Arabia
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi security forces have discovered drone launchers near the border with Iran, two Iraqi security sources told AFP on Saturday.

The development took place after a drone attack targeted a pipeline in Saudi Arabia, which Riyadh and Baghdad said was launched from Iraqi territory.

“Iraqi security forces found drone launchers near the Iraqi-Iranian border in the remote al-Tayeb area of ​​the southern province of Maysan,” a security source said. A second source confirmed these details.

Earlier on Saturday, Iraq decided to close its land borders with Iran and suspend flights to the country, following Saudi Arabia’s announcement that attacks on its territory originated from Iraq.

A source at Basra International Airport said that all flights to and from Iran had been suspended until further notice.

An immediate directive was issued by the General Command of the Iraqi Armed Forces to close the Shalamcheh border crossing in the southern Iraqi province of Basra and evacuate all staff, suspending the movement of travelers and goods until further notice.

Instructions were issued for similar measures at border crossings in the provinces of Maysan, Wasit, and Diyala.

Other border crossings with Iran remained open in Erbil and Sulaymaniyah, which are controlled by the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) in northern Iraq.

The decision did not include a complete closure of the Iraqi-Iranian border but rather was limited to specific border crossings as part of the security measures taken following the attacks on Saudi Arabia.

The land crossings between Iraq and Iran represent vital economic and social arteries. Their role is not limited to the movement of travelers; large quantities of goods, foodstuffs, industrial products, and building materials pass through them, in addition to the movement of pilgrims, especially during religious seasons.

Saudi Arabia announced on Friday that the East-West pipeline had been targeted by several drones launched from Iraq, resulting in injuries to workers.

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi ordered an investigation into the Maysan Operations Command and relieved its commander, Jalil al-Sharifi, of his post after it was confirmed that the attacks originated from there.

World.title: Iraq leads OPEC+’s output growth in August
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq led the increase in OPEC+ oil production in August 2026 on a monthly basis by 297,000 barrels per day.

The OPEC monthly report, released on Thursday, showed that the alliance’s production increased to 38.055 million barrels per day in August, compared to 37.757 million in July.

OPEC production increased by approximately 346,000 barrels per day last month, reaching a total of 24.081 million barrels per day, compared to 23.735 million in July 2026.

Saudi Arabia and six other OPEC+ countries decided to maintain their oil production policy unchanged through October 2026.

The seven countries successfully eliminated voluntary production cuts of 2.2 million barrels per day in September 2025 and then 1.65 million barrels per day in September 2026.

In addition to these voluntary cuts, the OPEC+ coalition has been implementing production cuts of two million barrels per day since November 2022, with plans to continue until the end of 2026.

Iraq’s crude oil production rose by about 664,000 barrels per day (bpd) in August, reaching a total of 3.378 million bpd.

Kazakhstan’s crude oil production rose by 159,000 barrels per day in August, bringing the total to 1.807 million barrels per day.

The UAE increased its oil production by approximately 54,000 barrels per day, reaching 3.835 million bpd.

The UAE’s data remains part of the OPEC report despite its withdrawal, as its membership officially continues until the end of 2026, according to internal regulations.

World.title: Iraq unveils solar-powered green taxi initiative to drive EV transition
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The Iraqi Ministries of Environment and Transport have initiated joint planning sessions to advance the rollout of electric vehicles across the country, formulating the initial framework for a pilot project designated as the Green Taxi.

The initiative focuses on the establishment of dedicated solar-powered charging plazas, designed specifically to decouple vehicle charging from the overburdened national electricity grid, curb operating expenses, and slash automotive emissions as part of a wider state policy to gradually introduce clean energy technologies into the public transport network.

Haider Al-Darraji, Director of the Carbon Economics Company under the Ministry of Environment, stated in remarks carried by the official state newspaper that the project constitutes the initial phase of a systematic national transition toward establishing the pillars of a green economy.

Al-Darraji stressed that any long-term mandate requiring the complete replacement of conventional combustion vehicles must be managed through calculated, progressive regulatory frameworks, ensuring that the ecological transition does not impose undue financial strain on private taxi operators or everyday commuters.

The scope and velocity of subsequent expansion phases will depend entirely on empirical evaluations collected throughout the initial rollout. Authorities plan to measure performance benchmarks, including the actual volume of electric vehicles deployed, operational utilization rates, grid independence, maintenance overheads, driver feedback, and verified reductions in both fuel consumption and greenhouse gas emissions.

These real-world data points will serve as the technical blueprint for drafting a broader national substitution program to phase out fossil-fuel taxis over the coming years.

Parallel consultations between the two ministries have also explored practical infrastructure adaptations across existing transport hubs. Abbas Imran Mousa, Director General of the Planning and Follow-up Department at the Ministry of Transport, confirmed that discussions are underway to utilize parking garages and terminals operated by the General Company for Private Transport Administration.

Under this framework, designated public transport bays will be retrofitted with solar-powered charging infrastructure, ensuring that clean mobility solutions can operate autonomously while firmly embedding sustainable transport infrastructure across the country.

World.title: Iraq needs over 10,000 new schools to end overcrowding, report warns
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq requires more than 10,000 new school buildings to effectively eliminate severe classroom overcrowding and cultivate a modern pedagogical environment, according to a report released on Sunday, September 13, 2026, by the economic monitor Eco Iraq.

Despite the country maintaining an operational footprint of more than 40,000 schools serving primary and secondary pupils nationwide, the observatory underscored that existing facilities remain entirely inadequate to absorb the country’s expanding student population.

The monitor highlighted that structural deficits continue to constrain daily operations across the public education system, noting that at least 8,000 new school facilities are immediately required simply to phase out multi-shift schooling and transition toward a single-shift model where each school administration operates an independent building.

Achieving an optimal learning setting free of excessive classroom density pushes that requirement well past the 10,000-facility threshold, reflecting decades of demographic growth outpacing physical infrastructure construction.

The report also drew attention to persistent disparities in building standards across rural and peripheral regions, confirming that around 200 mud-brick schools and roughly 800 caravan-style temporary classrooms remain in active use, primarily clustered across Salah al-Din and Dhi Qar governorates.

The observatory concluded by calling on the Ministry of Education to adopt decisive capital allocation programs, emphasizing that high-density demographic hubs—most critically Baghdad, Mosul, Basra, and Dhi Qar—must sit at the very top of federal school-building initiatives to dismantle the ongoing educational backlog.

World.title: US dollar reaches 157,000 IQD in Baghdad and Basra on Sunday
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Parallel market exchange rates for the U.S. dollar climbed further across Iraq’s primary commercial centers on Sunday, September 13, 2026, with selling rates touching the 157,000-dinar threshold in both Baghdad and Basra.

The latest market bulletin highlights an expanding premium over the Central Bank of Iraq’s official statutory peg of 131,000 dinars per $100, reflecting persistent cash demand across wholesale trading floors and merchant counters.

In Baghdad, wholesale and retail bureaus quoted the greenback at a selling price of 157,000 dinars against a buying rate of 156,500 dinars for every $100, extending Saturday’s upward momentum with a tight 500-dinar margin.

The southern trading hub of Basra matched the capital’s figures precisely, recording identical selling rates of 157,000 dinars and buying prices of 156,500 dinars as merchant demand held firm across the southern commercial axis.

In the northern market of Erbil, dollar valuations advanced in close synchrony, settling just slightly below the central and southern exchanges. Bureaus across the regional capital posted selling prices of 156,750 dinars per $100, alongside a buying rate of 156,500 dinars, underscoring tight trading spreads and steady liquidity flows across all three regional markets as the business week gathered pace.

World.title: Hong Kong homes flattened for US$28 bn high-tech hub
World.content:
Hong Kong – Chan Yuk-tong hoped to spend his remaining years in the row of small, blue-brick houses where he was born and raised, but the 71-year-old’s Hong Kong village home will soon be bulldozed to make way for a vast tech hub.

An area roughly a third of Hong Kong including villages, natural wetlands and farmland is being converted into the “Northern Metropolis”, an ambitious project aimed at deepening integration with the mainland, diversifying the economy and providing new homes.

“I can’t bear to leave… If not for the government developing this area, I would likely spend the rest of my life here. After all, I belong here,” Chan told AFP as he packed up belongings in his yard.

Touted as a “new economic engine” to accommodate around 2.5 million residents and provide 650,000 jobs, the project will link Hong Kong more closely with Macau and nine cities in mainland China that make up the Greater Bay Area.

But the government’s vision for a Silicon Valley-like high-tech hub in Hong Kong comes at a huge cost to the city’s wildlife, local communities and public finances, environmental and social groups warned.

“If you build a new city in a place that was well preserved before, it would inevitably be very destructive, no matter how you mitigate it,” said Brian Wong of Liber Research Community, an NGO focused on land issues.

“Do we need to build it so big? Is it too ambitious?” he added.

– Return on investment –

The Northern Metropolis project, announced five years ago, will eventually cover 30,000 hectares (74,000 acres).

Liber said at least 25 villages will be demolished to make way for it.

Government departments told AFP they aim to integrate rural areas into the development project, but that Chan’s ancestral houses were not culturally significant enough to preserve.

Plans to integrate Hong Kong with mainland China have long faced opposition in the former British colony, where critics warn such moves would erode the city’s autonomy.

But a sweeping national security law imposed by Beijing on Hong Kong in 2020 after huge pro-democracy protests has stymied dissent in the financial hub.

It “effectively put an end to the ‘one country, two systems’ framework that allowed Hong Kong a ‘high degree of autonomy’, so greater integration with the Greater Bay Area would logically follow,” Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute, told AFP.

The government says the Northern Metropolis will cost at least HK$224 billion (US$28.6 billion), while global ratings agency S&P estimates it could top HK$360 billion.

Authorities have promised a return on investment, citing bank estimates — and a rough 20-year timeline — that the project will account for 13 percent of Hong Kong’s gross domestic product.

Tech hubs across the border in mainland China, such as Alibaba’s hometown of Hangzhou, are expanding far faster, spurred by AI investors such as Deepseek and Unitree Robotics.

Hong Kong is “less relevant for China’s national tech ambitions” than mainland powerhouses like Shenzhen, said Gary Ng, a senior economist at Natixis.

But it can nevertheless provide what they cannot: international connections, university research, and deep capital markets.

– ‘Sacrifice’ –

Last month, the first large-scale land sale in the Northern Metropolis was awarded to a consortium of six companies, including Chinese state-owned enterprises and e-commerce giant JD.com, to build housing and a logistics centre in Chan’s area.

Hannah Jeong of commercial real estate firm CBRE told AFP that policy support will first attract mainland Chinese companies wanting to build research centres and take advantage of its lower taxes and talent, data and capital flows.

“With that flow, more manpower coming in, talent coming in… forefign companies will also gradually (invest),” Jeong said.

The biggest hurdle to the Northern Metropolis’ success is “how to maintain an efficient cross-border flow, and at the same time maintaining the confidence that the international community has in Hong Kong’s uniqueness”, said Wilson Chan, co-founder of the Pagoda Institute think tank.

In her village, Niki So had watched helplessly as her neighbours’ homes were torn down, waiting for the bulldozers to reach the house where her family lived for three generations.

The 42-year-old received a public housing flat in compensation, but told AFP she will miss the village where neighbours are like family.

In July, So opened her gate to dozens of lands department officials and police, who declared the area government property.

“I hope the development here will go well, that it will thrive,” So said.

“If it doesn’t turn out as expected then I think the sacrifice of this village would be quite unfortunate.”

World.title: All eyes on US Fed to tackle high inflation
World.content:
Washington – The US Federal Reserve goes into a key rate-setting meeting this week with markets expecting policymakers to pull the trigger on a rate hike to tackle persistently high inflation — and analysts say central bank chief Kevin Warsh’s credibility is on the line.

The world’s largest economy has been dealing with years of higher-than-target inflation, and prices have surged in the wake of US President Donald Trump’s war on Iran, his signature tariff policies and the ongoing AI boom.

The Fed has held rates steady since January, choosing to wait to gauge the effects of energy price shocks and to let the tariffs’ effects on prices ripple through the economy.

In recent weeks, however, several Fed policymakers — including Warsh himself — have hinted that if inflation does not show clear signs of slowing, the central bank will have to act by raising interest rates.

On Friday, new data on consumer inflation for August showed it remaining steady at 3.4 percent — no change from the month before, but still well above the Fed’s long-term two percent target.

Market expectations of a 25-basis-point rate hike on Wednesday surged in the wake of the data, with the probability at more than 85 percent according to CME’s FedWatch tool.

The Fed last raised rates three years ago, when it was fighting surging inflation in the wake of the pandemic. They currently stand at between 3.50 and 3.75 percent.

Trump has railed against the Fed over interest rates since taking office for his second term, launching unprecedented attacks on the central bank’s independence as he demands lower rates to spur economic activity.

The US president launched a criminal probe against previous Fed chair Jerome Powell, is attempting to fire another Fed governor and has even threatened to cut trade ties with certain countries if the Fed raised rates.

Warsh was appointed by Trump and analysts say this is his first real test since taking office: Will the Fed raise rates to combat inflation, or hold steady in line with what the White House prefers?

“This is the test. This is what comes with that job, and now he has to decide how to handle it,” said David Wessel, senior fellow at the Brookings Institution.

“He’s either going to completely disappoint the markets, or he runs the risk that he’s going to start to anger Donald Trump.”

The Fed’s Federal Open Market Committee, with its 12 voting members, will announce its decision after a two-day meeting on Wednesday at 2:00 pm (1800 GMT).

– ‘Costly medicine’ –

“It’s quite likely that the Fed will raise interest rates next week,” said Claudia Sahm, chief economist at investment firm New Century Advisors who previously worked at the Fed.

But “it’s not a done deal,” she cautioned in comments to AFP. “This is a difficult decision for them to make.”

Raising interest rates would increase borrowing costs across the board for the US economy, acting as a brake on further investment and consumption activity.

Sahm warned such a move was “not a magic wand and it is a costly medicine.”

She said the Fed could still hold rates steady rather than administer that medicine, but it would have to explain its decision clearly to markets.

“If they surprise markets and they can’t explain why they’re surprising markets, then Wednesday afternoon will be pretty messy,” she said.

Since taking office, Warsh has changed the way the Fed communicates about its decisions, advocating for less transparency into the process as he thinks it locks policymakers into courses of action that may need to be adjusted.

Investors have had mixed reactions to the cut in what is known as “forward guidance,” with analysts saying it has introduced more uncertainty into how financial markets price in inflation and interest rate expectations.

Warsh has advocated in the past for lower interest rates due to expected productivity gains from AI technology, but in recent weeks he has doubled down on the Fed’s mandate to bring inflation down.

“There’s always been this doubt about whether Kevin Warsh is going to be like his predecessors and do what’s right for the economy, even if it’s politically inconvenient,” said Wessel of Brookings.

“If he raises rates now and Trump goes ballistic, he will have established his credibility as an independent Fed chair for the rest of his term.”

World.title: Messi scores but Miami held by Nashville
World.content:
Miami – Lionel Messi extended his incredible scoring streak against MLS-leaders Nashville on Saturday as Inter Miami battled to a 2-2 draw in their top-of-the-table Eastern Conference clash.

Messi curled in a superb strike on 62 minutes at Miami’s Nu Stadium to fire Inter into a 2-1 lead but Nashville grabbed a share of the points after striker Sam Surridge bundled in an injury-time equaliser.

The 39-year-old Messi has now scored a remarkable 17 goals in 14 games against Nashville in all competitions since joining Miami in 2023.

And Messi could have even improved his goals record against in Saturday’s game between the first and second-placed sides in the Eastern Conference.

Messi saw a shot crash off the underside of the bar in the 50th minute and also saw a shot cannon off the post in the 78th minute. A late Messi effort was also headed clear by Nashville defender Jeisson Palacios before Surridge’s leveler.

The result leaves Inter nine points adrift of Nashville in the race for top seeding with nine regular season games remaining.

Earlier, Nashville had got off to a dream start when English striker Surridge sprang the offside trap before burying a low shot into the bottom corner in the fourth minute.

But Miami drew level midway through the half and again Messi was involved. The World Cup-winner’s wicked in-swinging corner found the head of Nashville defender Reed Baker-Whiting, who glanced in an own goal.

It looked as if Messi had grabbed the winner midway through the second half when he combined with former Argentina international team-mate Rodrigo De Paul on the edge of the area before curling a shot beyond the dive of Brian Schwake.

But Miami’s failure to extend their lead proved costly as Surridge scored from close range in injury time to steal a point.

World.title: The Uranium rush: Inside India's scramble to fuel its nuclear ambitions
World.content:
India is securing uranium fuel for its ambitious nuclear expansion plans (AI Image)

Indiaâs nuclear math

Central Asia

Australia and Canada too on Indiaâs nuclear framework

Need for fuel

Thorium bet is the longer game

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

Whatâs next for India

Last month, when Prime Minister Narendra Modi arrived in Tashkent, the headline takeaway was diplomatic. India and Uzbekistan agreed to elevate their ties to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership and set a target of $5 billion in annual bilateral trade by 2030.But tucked into the joint statement was a line that could matter far more to Indiaâs power planners than the trade target: the two countries agreed to work towards a long-term framework for uranium supplies.PM Modi had told delegates in Tashkent that India would "establish a long-term arrangement for the supply of uranium", describing it as the next step in the two countries' energy cooperation.It is easy to overlook why a single line on uranium in a joint statement matters. But it is perhaps the clearest sign yet of a scramble that has been building quietly across three continents, from Central Asia to Australia and North America, as India moves to secure the fuel needed for what could become one of the most ambitious nuclear expansion programmes of this century.Currently, the country operates 24 nuclear reactors with a combined capacity of about 8.78 gigawatts (GW).Centre's Nuclear Energy Mission, announced in the Union Budget for 2025-26, sets a target of 100 GW by 2047, more than an eleven-fold jump, with an intermediate goal of roughly 22 GW by 2031-32.That target, however, comes with a fuel problem.Industry estimates suggest a 100-GW fleet would require somewhere in the range of 18,000 to 20,000 tonnes of natural uranium a year, roughly a third of current global mine production. India's own uranium reserves, concentrated in Jharkhand, Andhra Pradesh and Meghalaya, are comparatively thin and have historically constrained, not enabled, the country's civil nuclear programme.For decades, that shortfall was managed quietly through a handful of government-to-government contracts.Now, with the expansion target locked in, it has become the organising logic behind a wave of overlapping diplomatic and commercial deals, of which the Uzbekistan framework is only the latest.India's relationship with Uzbekistan on uranium is not new. The two countries signed a contract back in January 2019 under which Uzbekistan's state-owned Navoi Mining and Metallurgical Company agreed to supply 1,100 metric tonnes of natural uranium concentrate to India through 2026.Parliamentary records show India had received about 600 metric tonnes of that contracted volume as of March 2025, meaning the current arrangement was always going to need renewing, with expiry or no expiry.What changed in Tashkent was the structure.Rather than negotiate a one-off follow-on contract, the two sides are now working toward a long-term arrangement meant to outlast the transactional cycle of the 2019 deal.Siby George, secretary (west) in the ministry of external affairs, was quoted by news agency PTI as saying that "positive discussions have happened" on a long-term uranium supply arrangement, and that the two governments were "closing in" on signing it.No new uranium-specific pact was among the eleven agreements formally signed during the visit, the framework itself is still being finalised, but both governments used the summit to signal that Uzbekistan, one of the world's largest uranium producers, will remain a fixture of India's fuel-security plan rather than a legacy supplier being phased out.Earlier in July, India finalised the Administrative Arrangement with Australia under their 2014 Civil Nuclear Cooperation Agreement.The arrangement, sealed at the Third India-Australia Annual Summit in Melbourne, operationalises a pact that paves the way for long-term Australian uranium exports to India under IAEA safeguards.Australia holds more than a third of the world's known uranium resources, by far the largest reserve base of any country, which makes the arrangement one of the more consequential fuel-security wins in India's recent diplomatic calendar.On the other side of the globe, India signed its most commercially concrete uranium deal yet, a nine-year, roughly $2.6-billion agreement between Canada's Saskatchewan-based Cameco Corporation and India's Department of Atomic Energy, for the supply of close to 22 million pounds of uranium ore concentrate between 2027 and 2035.The deal, signed earlier in March, was struck during a visit by Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and both governments described it as a cornerstone of a new India-Canada strategic energy partnership.Separately, NTPC Ltd, India's largest power producer, tasked with building roughly 30 GW of the country's 100-GW nuclear target, has issued a tender to appoint consultants who will help identify uranium mining assets it could invest in overseas, in countries including Canada, Australia, Kazakhstan and South Africa.It is a telling move as state-run India is no longer content to simply buy uranium on long-term contracts. It wants equity exposure to the mines themselves.Together, the Uzbekistan, Australia and Canada threads are not three separate stories, but rather a larger picture of a nation that spent decades under-investing in fuel security and is now compensating for lost time on every continent that has the mineral.The external hunt for fuel has a mirror image at home: a domestic policy shift that is arguably even more consequential for India's energy sector.In December 2025, Parliament passed the Sustainable Harnessing and Advancement of Nuclear Energy for Transforming India (SHANTI) Act, ending a six-decade-old state monopoly over civil nuclear power generation.Under the new law, private companies can, for the first time, build, own and operate nuclear power plants, while the government retains control over the most sensitive parts of the chain â uranium enrichment, heavy-water production, and long-term spent-fuel management.The response from India Inc. has been immediate. A tender floated by state-run Nuclear Power Corporation of India for co-developing 220 MWe "Bharat Small Reactors" has drawn interest from Reliance Industries, Adani Power, Tata Power, Hindalco Industries, Jindal Steel and Power, and JSW Energy, a roll call of India's largest industrial conglomerates, each looking to secure captive, round-the-clock power for steel, cement and data-centre operations that a coal-fired grid increasingly cannot deliver cheaply or cleanly.Tata Power has gone furthest, publicly targeting 2032-33 for commissioning what would be India's first privately built nuclear plant, with construction beginning as early as 2028 across sites being scouted in Madhya Pradesh, Odisha and Gujarat.The SHANTI Act creates the demand; Tashkent, Melbourne and Saskatchewan are where the supply is being lined up.There is another reason India's uranium scramble needs to be viewed as part of a much longer nuclear strategy.India has for decades pursued a three-stage nuclear programme designed ultimately to make greater use of its large thorium resources.The key transition is from today's uranium-fuelled reactors to fast breeder reactors and, eventually, reactors using uranium-233 produced from thorium.The Department of Atomic Energy describes thorium-232 as the material that can be converted into fissile uranium-233 for the third stage of the programme.That strategy reached an important milestone this year when the 500 MWe Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) at Kalpakkam in Tamil Nadu attained first criticality.The DAE describes the PFBR as the flagship of the second stage of India's three-stage nuclear programme and says thorium-232 can be converted into uranium-233 through transmutation, providing the fuel for the third stage.But the technology does not offer India an immediate escape from its uranium problem. The PFBR itself is part of a transition, while the large-scale nuclear expansion envisaged for 2047 still requires conventional reactors and therefore reliable access to uranium fuel.That explains the apparent contradiction at the heart of India's nuclear strategy: the country is rushing across the world for uranium today even as it develops technologies intended to make its nuclear fuel cycle more self-reliant tomorrow.The distinction matters because thorium is not a shortcut to the 100-GW target as it is a longer-term bet on the architecture of India's nuclear programme, while imported and domestically mined uranium will remain critical to the expansion now being planned.None of the deals struck so far, not Uzbekistan, not Australia, not Canada, comes close to closing the fuel gap that 100 GW by 2047 implies on its own.Each is best understood as one card in a hand India is still assembling: diversify suppliers, avoid dependence on any single country or company, and buy time for domestic reforms, the SHANTI Act, the Bharat Small Reactor programme, and a longer-term bet on thorium, of which India holds one of the world's largest reserves, to mature into an actual generation fleet.The Tashkent uranium framework, when it is finally signed, will not by itself power a single reactor.But it is a useful marker of how far India has travelled in eighteen months: from a country that mined and imported uranium exclusively through the state, to one running parallel negotiations with Central Asian suppliers, Australian miners and Canadian producers, while a queue of its largest private conglomerates waits for its first nuclear licence.The rush is real.Whether the fuel arrives fast enough to match India's reactor-building ambitions is the question the next few Budget cycles will have to answer.

World.title: ‘We will continue in Congress’: Konda Surekha rules out joining another party, eyes 2028 polls
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Former Telangana minister

, who was recently dropped from chief minister A Revanth Reddyâs Cabinet, on Sunday said she would remain with the Congress and contest the next Assembly elections in 2028.

Addressing a meeting of her supporters in Warangal, Surekha said she and her husband Konda Murali would continue working for the people irrespective of whether she held any official position.

âWe are told not to go anywhere (join any other party) and that the party will take care of us. We are telling them that we have no intention to join any other party. We will continue in Congress. We will definitely contest on behalf of Congress.

We will win and ensure Congress returns to power,â she said.

Surekha also expressed confidence that she would receive the Congress ticket to contest from the Warangal East constituency in the 2028 Assembly polls. She said she would be re-elected as an MLA and become a minister again.

Surekha says Congress leadership is in touch

Her remarks came amid reports that the Congress leadership has been reaching out to her following her removal from the state Cabinet.

Surekha said she had been receiving calls and was being told not to join any other party.





She reiterated that she had no intention of leaving the Congress.

She said she and Murali would continue to work on people's issues and ensure development in the constituency even without holding government posts.

Removed from cabinet after controversy

Surekha was dropped from the Cabinet on September 3 following a controversy over remarks made against Revanth Reddy and others by her daughter, Konda Sushmitha Patel.

Surekha had subsequently accused the chief minister of resorting to âblackmail politicsâ to secure her removal, claiming that the party high command was not in favour of the move.

In earlier remarks, Surekha had questioned the decision to remove her, saying she had neither committed corruption nor been given an opportunity to explain herself.

She had also defended her daughter, arguing that her comments were personal and should not be attributed to her.

Surekha had questioned why she should be held responsible for remarks made by her adult daughter and referred to controversial statements made by other Congress leaders while questioning the action against her.

She had also challenged the party leadership to take action against her and met Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge in Delhi as the high command considered disciplinary action.

Other changes in Telangana Congress

The disciplinary action against Surekha was also accompanied by the removal of veteran Congress leader G Chinna Reddy as vice-chairman of the Telangana Planning Board.

World.title: Altitude and attitude: How DGCA makes sure high-flying pilots don’t fly high
World.content:
How Indiaâs aviation regulator is tightening the net on pilots and crew to ensure those trusted with thousands of lives are fit to fly. (AI-generated image)

AAIB preliminary report

What happens when a pilot gets tested for drugs?

Crew perspective

The net gets wider

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

There is something inherently unsettling about flying. Thirty thousand feet above the ground, hundreds of passengers sit inside a pressurised metal tube travelling at hundreds of kilometres per hour, trusting a handful of people with their lives for the duration of the journey. Yet every day, millions of us make this decision without thinking twice.And then, once in a blue moon, an incident happens that makes us pause and wonder just how much we can actually trust those handful of people.On August 4, an Air India A320 flying from Phuket to Delhi was cruising at 36,000 feet when it suddenly climbed 372 feet before dropping nearly 300 feet. Twenty-four people on board, including passengers and crew, were injured badly enough to require hospitalisation. Twenty were discharged shortly afterwards, while four sustained serious injuries and remained hospitalised for further treatment. Many passengers also took to social media and spoke to news reporters about how frightening the experience had been.A preliminary report shows that, over those eight seconds, the aircraft lost all three of its hydraulic systems and the autopilot disengaged. The hydraulic systems recovered within seconds, and the aircraft subsequently landed normally.On the surface, it was a technical failure. But a second finding in the incident became the headline across news outlets.As part of the standard procedure following such incidents, the crew is tested on various parameters to ensure that investigators have a complete picture of what happened. In this case, both pilots underwent the mandatory psychoactive-substance test after arriving in Delhi, a requirement for flights originating outside India.The co-pilotâs sample came back negative twice. The pilot-in-commandâs report, however, raised concerns. The Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureauâs (AAIB) preliminary report used the term ânon-negativeâ to describe both the screening test and the confirmatory laboratory report.What was reported as âpositiveâ in headlines was not, in fact, the language used in the report. In aviation investigations, that distinction matters. The AAIBâs responsibility is not to point fingers, but to establish what happened and identify measures that can prevent a recurrence.The preliminary report does not conclude that substance use caused the hydraulic failure. It does, however, flag a serious concern regarding psychoactive substances and recommends that the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) take appropriate action.The DGCA is the apex regulatory body responsible for overseeing safety standards in civil aviation. Its rulebook is extensive and is regularly revised to address emerging risks and ensure that flying remains safe for passengers and crew.Alcohol testing has been mandatory since the mid-2000s. The framework was built around Rule 24 of the Aircraft Rules, 1937, which originally required that crew members not consume alcohol within 12 hours of a flight. The rule has since been revised several times. A 2023 revision, for instance, warned that medicines and other substances containing alcohol could trigger a breathalyser reading, specifically citing products such as mouthwash and tooth gel. Crew members taking medication are required to consult their company doctor before flying.For scheduled operators, flight and cabin crew are subject to pre-flight breathalyser testing at the first departure airport during a duty period. For flights originating outside India, post-flight testing is required at the first Indian airport of landing.Being fit to fly is a regulatory requirement. But while the rules around alcohol have been in place for decades, psychoactive substances present a more complicated challenge.Drug testing is relatively new. The DGCA introduced the framework based on a 2019 report by the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, which estimated that 2.8% of Indians had used cannabis in the previous year and 2.1% had used opioids. From 2019 to 2026, these numbers have only increased.These figures should not be taken as evidence that aviation personnel use drugs. Rather, they indicate the potential scale of the threat that the misuse of psychoactive substances can pose to aviation safety.The drug-testing system applies to flight crew and air traffic controllers. Testing is required before employment, following accidents, through random checks and as follow-up in previously confirmed cases.Random testing is currently designed to cover at least 10% of an organisationâs employees each year at specified airports. The testing panel is broad, covering substances including amphetamines, methamphetamines, cocaine, opioids, benzodiazepines, marijuana/hashish, MDMA and several others.The system is also designed around confirmation, rather than treating an initial screening result as conclusive. It is consequently more time- and resource-intensive than an alcohol test.A urine sample is divided into A and B portions. The initial screening is conducted under controlled conditions. If the A sample screens positive, the B sample is sent to a DGCA-authorised laboratory for confirmatory testing, with procedures in place to maintain the chain of custody.A person who returns a positive screening result is removed from safety-sensitive duties until the confirmatory report is received.If a first confirmed positive is established, the rules provide for de-addiction and rehabilitation, followed by repeat testing and clearance from a treating psychiatrist and the organisationâs chief medical officer before the person can return to active duty.A second confirmed positive, however, carries a far more severe consequence: cancellation of the licence.In other words, the regulatory system is built around two competing principles: aviation cannot afford to ignore substance use, but neither can it treat every initial test result as proof of impairment or permanently write off a person without due process.TOI spoke to aviation personnel to understand their perspective on the DGCA rules governing substance use in the industry.A senior pilot lauded the system, saying the DGCA maintains strict standards to protect the safety of the countless passengers who entrust their lives to the aviation system every day. But he said the responsibility does not rest with the regulator alone. A moral responsibility also falls on the crew entrusted with those lives.âThe number of variables when it comes to substances in the market has increased and having access to them has become easier, but that does not mean that it can be used as an excuse. A soldier at the border is stressed too, but he has a responsibility to his nation to do his duty properly and honestly. So do we,â the pilot, who did not wish to be named, said.A cabin crew member, meanwhile, said drinking after work and, in some cases, using substances is not unheard of among crew. But she said there is a clear boundary between what happens off duty and the responsibilities that come with being in the air, and that most crew understand the implications of bringing such behaviour into the workplace.At the same time, she pointed to the pressures that come with the job.âI have been grounded for acne, for weight gain, I was once even grounded because my nails were too long,â she said.For cabin crew, the demands of the job extend beyond safety procedures and passenger service. Strict appearance standards, long and irregular working hours and constant interaction with passengers can add to the pressures of a profession in which employees are expected to maintain a high standard of presentation and hospitality at all times.These pressures, however, are difficult to separate from the broader conversation around substance use.It is this tension that sits at the heart of the debate. The pressures of the job are real, and an environment that leaves people constantly stressed can create conditions in which some may turn to alcohol or other substances. But for those sitting in the cockpit, stress cannot become an explanation for abandoning the responsibility that comes with the job.The Phuket incident has already prompted the regulator to widen that net.The DGCA has directed Indian airlines to conduct a one-time psychoactive-substance test on all their pilots by July 2027. The exercise will cover the countryâs nearly 14,000 airline pilots. Air India had already begun its own one-time testing programme for about 5,000 pilots across Air India and Air India Express following the August 4 incident.The move comes as the DGCA works on a revision of its existing rules governing psychoactive-substance testing. The current framework requires random testing, with organisations expected to cover at least 10% of their employees annually. The proposed changes are expected to make the system more stringent.The senior pilot said the next step could also involve newer testing methods capable of delivering conclusive results faster, allowing airlines to test a much larger pool of crew rather than relying primarily on periodic random checks.The DGCA can test, regulate and punish. Airlines can monitor and intervene. But ultimately, the last line of defence is also the person sitting in the cockpit.

World.content:

Chinese President Xi Jinping urged Brics countries to defend sovereign equality, peaceful dispute resolution and a more inclusive global order while expanding cooperation in technology and trade.

Here are your top stories of the day.Chinese President Xi Jinping used the Brics summit in New Delhi to call for stronger Global South cooperation and a rules-based international order. Xi rejected the âmight makes rightâ approach and advocated sovereign equality, noninterference and peaceful settlement of disputes. He also proposed deeper Brics cooperation in artificial intelligence, digital industries, trade, intelligent manufacturing and science and technology. China put forward five initiatives, including an open-source Brics AI community, as Beijing seeks to expand practical cooperation within the enlarged grouping.Russia said PM Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping offered their âgood officesâ to Russian President Vladimir Putin to help resolve the Ukraine conflict during their separate discussions with him on the sidelines of the Brics summit. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Putin welcomed their readiness to assist. PM Modi and Putin also discussed strengthening India-Russia economic ties, including the Programme for Economic Cooperation 2030, as well as infrastructure, energy, technology, defence and culture.PM Modi reiterated India's support for dialogue and diplomacy to resolve conflicts.Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned that the risks posed by increasingly powerful AI systems cannot be captured through a single probability. Responding to concerns raised by former Anthropic researchers, Amodei said different development pathways could produce very different outcomes, with the wrong trajectory potentially increasing the risk of catastrophic harm. He called for companies to work together on safeguards, while warning that excessive delays in AI development could leave powerful systems in the hands of actors less committed to safety.AAP chief Arvind Kejriwal said the party would be âextra cautiousâ while selecting future Rajya Sabha nominees following a series of defections. His remarks came after Raghav Chadha and six other AAP Rajya Sabha members joined the BJP, reducing the party's strength in Parliament and prompting scrutiny of its selection strategy.AAP is also preparing for next year's Goa Assembly election, where it has announced a pre-poll alliance with the Goa Forward Party.A major search-and-rescue operation continued in Indonesia after passenger vessel Virgo Transport 8 overturned and sank in the Java Sea amid rough weather. The vessel was carrying 243 people, including 213 passengers and 30 crew, when contact was lost early Sunday. Authorities said 107 people had been rescued and six bodies recovered, leaving around 130 people missing. The ship had been travelling from Surabaya to Banjarmasin, with the captain reportedly warning of waves reaching up to three metres before the vessel began listing.

World.title: Plugging gap: Why 67,000 EV charging points aren't enough for India’s electric dreams
World.content:
When Siddharth Das, a Delhi-NCR based working professional and long-time motor enthusiast, traded in his petrol sedan for a brand-new electric SUV, he wasnât just buying a new car.

He was also trying to make his daily commute what he describes as "future-ready".

But switching to an electric vehicle brought a different kind of calculation.

"My previous petrol car cost me 10 to 12 rupees a kilometre. With an EV, even if I use commercial chargers at 15 to 21 rupees per unit, my running cost is just 3 to 3.50 rupees a kilometre. If I could charge at domestic home rates of 8 rupees a unit, it would drop to 1 rupee per kilometre."

However, Das faces a problem even before he leaves his residential building.

"I live in an apartment complex where parking is in the basement, and the society isnât allowing home chargers due to safety protocol concerns," he explains.

His experience shows one of the bigger challenges in India's shift to electric vehicles. The cars are improving quickly, but the charging system around them is still developing and can be difficult to access.





67,000 plugs down, 13 lakhs to go

According to a landmark study by Rubix Data Sciences released in September 2026, citing baseline projections from the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII), India will need 13.2 lakh EV charging points by 2030 to support the growing number of electric vehicles.

But how far is India from that target?

Data from the Ministry of Heavy Industries shows that, as of August 2026, India had 67,657 public charging points across the country including 1,139 battery-swapping station interfaces.

This is in comparison to only 5,000 public chargers in early 2022 and 29,151 in December 2025.

But even after this growth, the current network is only about 5 percent of the 13.2 lakh charging points expected to be needed by 2030.

In simple terms, India still needs to add more than 1.25 million to reach the projected requirement. This gap matters because the number of EVs on the road is also increasing, meaning charging infrastructure has to grow fast enough to keep up with vehicle sales.

There is also a major geographical imbalance. The Rubix analysis says the top 10 states, led by Karnataka, Maharashtra and Uttar Pradesh, account for 78 per cent of all public chargers in India.

As of August 2026, India had 67,657 public charging points across the country including 1,139 battery-swapping station interfaces. This is in comparison to only 5,000 public chargers in early 2022 and 29,151 in December 2025.

That means nearly four out of every five public chargers are concentrated in just 10 states. For EV users in other parts of the country, especially smaller towns and less-developed regions, finding a public charger can therefore be much harder.

Power disconnect: Built for scooters, not long-haul trips

The problem is not only the number of chargers. It is also how much power those chargers can provide.

Out of the 66,518 non-swapping fixed chargers installed across the country as of August 2026, most are on the slower side:

48,709 chargers, or about 73 percent, are rated below 30 kW.

15,753 chargers are in the 30â60 kW range.

1,513 chargers offer 61â120 kW fast charging.

Only 534 chargers provide 121â240 kW, while just nine chargers offer more than 240 kW nationwide.

These figures are important because a chargerâs power rating affects how quickly an EV can be charged. A large network may therefore look impressive on paper, but if most chargers are low-power units, drivers travelling long distances may still have to spend considerable time charging.

The current charging mix also reflects the kinds of electric vehicles being sold in India. Federation of Automobile Dealers Associations (FADA) figures cited in the study show that the switch to electric vehicles is currently strongest among three-wheelers, where EVs have a 60.77 per cent market penetration, and two-wheelers, at 8.88 per cent.

Electric four-wheeler passenger cars have a much lower penetration of 5.70 percent.

This helps explain why India has a large number of lower-powered chargers.

Low-power AC chargers can work well for e-rickshaws, electric two-wheelers and vehicles used mainly for short city trips. But the same infrastructure is less suitable for electric cars travelling long distances or for heavy commercial vehicles that need to cover hundreds of kilometres.

Divide in driver experience: Home charging vs range anxiety

For EV owners who have private parking and can install a home charger, everyday use can be relatively simple.

Bishwajeet Kumar Seth, who bought his electric SUV in April 2026, relies entirely on home charging.

"I have a 7.2 kW charger installed at home," Seth says. "My car has a real-world range of around 550 km with the AC on. When I drove from Delhi to Mathura, I didn't even need to plug in on the road. At home, it costs me 7 to 8 rupees a unit. At a highway fast charger, they were charging 19 rupees per unit. I thought, why bear double the cost when I don't need to?"

But the experience can be very different for people who do not own an EV or who rent one occasionally.

For them, "range anxiety" remains a major concern.

Mohammad Sarim, who rented an EV during a trip to Kerala, came away hesitant.

"I had the car for 12 hours to cover 150 km, but the display showed a total range of 200 km," he shares. "Being in the outskirts, I didn't spot a single charger. The anxiety of the battery running down made it feel less convenient than a petrol car"

Saad Abbasi, a commuter in the NCR region, also says the lack of infrastructure affects buying decisions.

"Unless you live in Central or South Delhi, NCR has limited infrastructure. It's fine for home-to-office daily commuting if you can charge at home, but the moment you travel away from major cities, it becomes an issue."

Operator crisis: Empty stations in tier-2, tier-3 towns

While EV buyers worry about finding a charger, charging operators face almost the opposite problem: their chargers often do not get enough customers.

Data from the Rubix Data Sciences report shows that public chargers across India currently have a utilisation rate of only 1 to 5 per cent.

This means that, for much of the time, many public chargers are sitting unused. That creates a difficult business case, particularly for operators in smaller cities and towns. They have to spend a large amount of money upfront, but may not have enough vehicles using the chargers to recover that investment quickly.

Amit Kumar Sahu, a fuel station owner who operates a public EV charging setup in Giridih, Jharkhand, explains the financial challenge faced by local businesses.

"In private dealer-owned fuel stations, the entire investment falls on the dealer," Sahu says. "Setting up a 60 kW DC charger costs around 8.5 to 9 lakh rupees for the machine alone. On top of that, buying a dedicated 63 kVA transformer takes another 5.5 to 6 lakh rupees in deposits and grid connection expenses. You end up spending 15 to 16 lakh rupees."

"In small towns like Giridih, if only 2 to 4 vehicles show up a day, you can't recover your costs," Sahu adds.

"That is why private pump dealers in Jharkhand and Bihar avoid installing them. The vehicles aren't there yet, and without footfall, nobody wants to lock in Rs 15 lakhs."

This creates a cycle that is difficult to break. EV owners need chargers before they feel confident buying electric cars, but operators are reluctant to invest in chargers until there are enough EVs using them.

To deal with low utilisation, operators are now looking at other business models.

According to the Rubix report, charge point operators (CPOs) are moving towards fleet leasing contracts, revenue-sharing arrangements with site owners and open-roaming networks. These models can help operators get more regular usage and reduce the risk of investing in chargers that remain empty.

Technical frameworks & heavy freight road ahead

India is also trying to reduce fragmentation in its charging system. Standard-setting bodies such as the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) and the Department of Science & Technology (DST) are working on charging standards and technologies that can make charging more uniform and suitable for different types of EVs.

LECCS (light electric vehicle combined charging system): Under standards such as IS 17017 Part-2 Sec-7 and IS 17017 Part-31, LECCS combines AC charging of up to 7 kW and low-voltage DC charging of up to 12 kW into one standard plug for two and three-wheelers. The aim is to make charging more consistent instead of having different systems for different vehicles.

Under standards such as IS 17017 Part-2 Sec-7 and IS 17017 Part-31, LECCS combines AC charging of up to 7 kW and low-voltage DC charging of up to 12 kW into one standard plug for two and three-wheelers. The aim is to make charging more consistent instead of having different systems for different vehicles. Universal Sockets: These are intended for destination charging at places such as urban parking complexes. They can support charging from 2 kW to 22 kW using a standard Type-2 socket with detachable smart cables. This can reduce dependence on different proprietary charging systems.

The bigger challenge will come with heavy commercial vehicles and long-distance transport. Chargers below 60 kW are generally not enough for trucks and other heavy vehicles that need to recharge quickly and get back on the road.

DST frameworks therefore include much higher-powered charging systems. These include Split-Type DC chargers, which can dynamically distribute 40 kW to 240+ kW across several charging posts; Dual-Gun 500 kW systems; Overhead Pantographs offering up to 600 kW; and Megawatt Charging Systems (MCS), which can provide up to 3.75 MW of peak power for heavy logistics fleets.

The difference in power is significant.

A system designed for a scooter or a car used for city commuting cannot simply be used as the main charging solution for a fully loaded electric truck travelling long distances. As India's electric vehicle market moves towards larger commercial vehicles, the charging network will therefore need to become not only bigger, but much more powerful.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

Bridging the divide

Indiaâs transition to electric vehicles has moved beyond its early stage.

As driver Siddharth Das prepares for his upcoming long-distance EV trip to Nepal, he is already planning his route around fast chargers, with charging stops mapped roughly every 150 km using route planners.

Reaching the projected target of 13.2 lakhs by Rubix study by 2030 will require much more than simply adding chargers in existing EV hubs.

The network will need to expand beyond major cities and states that already have a large share of the country's chargers. At the same time, operators will need easier transformer and grid connections, charging standards will need to become more consistent, and fast chargers will need to become more widely available on national highways.

For consumers, the difference could determine whether an EV remains mainly a city vehicle or becomes a practical option for longer journeys across India.

World.title: How Gujarat's villagers turned mangroves into a natural coastal shield
World.content:
In the 1980s, when much of Gujaratâs coastline was losing its mangrove cover, some coastal communities began protecting the few patches that remained. What looked like a small act of conservation would eventually become part of one of Indiaâs most striking mangrove recoveries.

Government data shows just how dramatic that transformation has been.

According to the Forest Survey of India (FSI), Gujarat had around 427 sq km of mangrove cover in 1987. By 1999, that figure had more than doubled to 1,031 sq km. It reached 1,164.06 sq km in 2023, making Gujarat home to nearly one-quarter of India's mangrove cover. In 2026, the cover has grown to 1177.27 sq km.

It attributes the growth to a combination of large-scale plantation programmes, public-private partnerships, community participation and better protection of existing forests.

Mangroves are much more than trees growing in salty mud.

Their dense network of roots holds sediment together, reduces coastal erosion and slows waves and storm surges before they can reach settlements further inland. The forests also provide breeding and nursery grounds for fish, crabs and other marine species, making them important to both coastal ecosystems and livelihoods.

The numbers also reveal how significant Gujarat's recovery has become.





The state's 1,164 sq km of mangroves in 2023 accounted for 23.66% of India's entire mangrove cover, second only to West Bengal.

But the recovery has not been a simple story of trees being planted by the government. In several parts of Gujarat, conservation efforts have involved coastal communities in protecting and regenerating mangrove areas. That local involvement matters because mangroves occupy a difficult landscape â one constantly shaped by tides, salinity, grazing, cutting and human activity.

The government has now taken the approach nationwide through MISHTI, launched in 2023 to restore and promote mangrove ecosystems along India's coast. Under the programme, mangroves are increasingly being treated as natural infrastructure â ecosystems that can perform some of the protective functions that would otherwise require expensive coastal engineering.

Gujarat's story therefore offers an unusual lesson in climate protection: sometimes the most effective coastal defence is not something built against the sea.

It is something that grows between the land and the sea.

And in Gujarat, decades after villagers began protecting those seemingly insignificant patches of mangrove, they have grown into forests spanning more than 1,100 sq km â forming a vast, living barrier along one of India's most exposed coastlines.

World.title: ‘Corruption, casteism, dynastic politics has ended’: Amit Shah hails 12 years of Modi govt
World.content:
Union home minister

on Sunday said the Narendra Modi government had moved India away from corruption, casteism and dynastic politics and ushered in an era of âpolitics of performanceâ.

Addressing a press conference to announce the âSeva Sankalp Abhiyanâ, Shah said the month-long campaign would run from September 17 to October 17 to mark Prime Minister Narendra Modiâs birthday and â25 years of Modi rule in Gujarat and Centreâ.

Taking a direct jab at the Congress, Shah claimed that Indian politics had moved away from what he described as the three major scourges of the pre-2014 era â corruption, casteism and dynastic politics â towards a âpolitics of performanceâ.

âBefore 2014, Indian politics was suffering from three scourges -- corruption, casteism and dynastic politics. In the political era from 2014 to 2026, these three have ended and the people have moved the country towards a politics of performance,â Shah said.

He added that the Modi government had also moved the country beyond what he described as âpolicy paralysis, coalition compulsions and poor decision-makingâ.





The Union Home Minister also highlighted the governmentâs foreign and defence policies, saying Indiaâs interests had been placed at the centre of decision-making.

âFor the first time in 12 years, the people have witnessed a foreign policy with a strong backbone. Whether it is our defence policy or our foreign policy, the guiding principle is âIndia First.â Indiaâs interests are paramount to us,â he said.

âRecent first-quarter data shows India leading the major economies with a GDP growth rate of 7.8%,â he said.

âWe have demonstrated this to the entire world while addressing three long-standing issuesâArticle 370, Naxalism, and the situation in the Northeastâthat had threatened the nationâs internal security for nearly five decades,â Shah said.

The âSeva Sankalp Abhiyanâ, whose slogan is âJan Seva Hi Prabhu Sevaâ (public service is service to God), will seek to promote public participation in the goal of making India a developed country by 2047, Shah said.

World.title: U.T. Khader dismisses allegations of Congress leaders complaining to ED against Minister Satish Jarkiholi
World.content:
Health Minister U.T. Khader has dismissed allegations by some BJP leaders that some Congress leaders were behind the ED searches on the house premises of Public Works Minister Satish Jarkiholi.

“These are baseless allegations. Our party has no intention of targeting anyone. All Congress leaders remain united, regardless of any malicious propaganda. Key party leaders — including Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar, Mr. Jarkiholi, former Chief Minister Siddaramaiah, and Home Minister G. Parameshwara — stand united,” said Mr. Khader in Gadag on Sunday (September 13). He was there to attend a function organised by Congress leader H.K. Patil’s family.

Responding to Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar’s statement regarding the possibility of ED searches at the houses of three or four more Ministers, Mr. Khader said that there was no need to attribute a different meaning to the Chief Minister’s words. “He was simply pointing out that the BJP is engaging in the politics of vendetta,” he said.

“The Congress party does not harbor a mindset of engaging in vendetta or target-based politics. Investigative agencies must function in accordance with the law. But the BJP is misusing such Central agencies to target anyone for political motives, which is inappropriate,’’ he said.

“About 98% of ED raids are conducted against Congress members. However, by the time investigations conclude, 90% of the cases are dropped. Convictions occur in only 10% of the cases,” he said.

On the inspections of hotels, the Minister said that it was essential for Health Department officials to conduct these inspections in the interest of public health. “The public can lodge complaints regarding food quality in hotels. There is also a facility to submit complaints via a barcode system. Upon receiving a complaint, officials will immediately visit the site, conduct an inspection, and take necessary action,” he said.

World.title: KLE Law College wins Al Ameen national moot court competition
World.content:
KLE Law College, Bengaluru, lifted the championship in the fourth Al Ameen national moot court competition organised by Al Ameen Law College, Shoranur.

The four-day competition, which concluded on Saturday on the Al Ameen Law College campus, saw law students argue complex questions relating to constitutional and digital law.

When the KLE Law College emerged champions by winning a cash prize of ₹50,000, SASTRA Deemed University (SASTRA Law School), Thanjavur, became runners-up and won a cash prize of ₹30,000.

The event featured teams from law colleges across the country. Senior legal professionals and academicians attended the valedictory function held on Saturday.

Kerala High Court judge Jayakumar K.V. delivered the keynote address. K.J. Krishnadas, N. Sriraj, Balasubramanian, and P. Lawwellman were among the prominent legal professionals who attended the programme.

Faculty member Saritha S. Menon welcomed the gathering. Sunitha P.N., Al Ameen Law College Vice-Principal, presided over the function. Student coordinators Razin Zaheer and Natasha Jaffar proposed a vote of thanks.

World.title: Kurnool all set for Ganesh idol immersion amid water shortages, says Bharath
World.content:
Industries and Commerce Minister T.G. Bharath Gupta said that all arrangements were being made to conduct the Ganesh idol immersion in Kurnool on a grand scale.

Mr. Bharath inspected the arrangements for the immersion process at Vinayaka Ghat along the K-C Canal and the Handri-Neeva tanks near Nannur toll plaza on Sunday. He enquired with officials on the availability of water, security, and infrastructure and directed them to to make all necessary arrangements.

Speaking on the occasion, Mr. Bharath noted that the water storage level at the Sunkesula Barrage is currently at a historic low of 0.288 tmcft, which has not been seen in the past 20 years. Due to this, it is not feasible to release water directly from the Sunkesula Barrage into the K-C Canal for immersion this year, the Minister said, adding that the administration has focused on alternative arrangements for immersion.

He said that walls were being constructed on both sides of the K-C Canal at the Vinayaka Ghat to create a tank-like structure for water storage. The Minister explained that measures were being taken to divert approximately 2 million litres of water, which currently goes to waste from the pump house to the K-C Canal, and store it in a specially constructed tank at Vinayaka Ghat.

Mr. Bharath said that the Kurnool Municipal Corporation (KMC) was also arranging heavy vehicles and other necessary facilities. Noting that the water flow in the Handri-Neeva project has been good so far, he mentioned that a continuous flow is likely to be maintained during the immersion as well.

The Minister suggested that members of the Vinayaka immersion committee inspect the KC- Canal and the Handri-Neeva area near the Nannur toll gate. He stated that the final plan for the immersion would be formulated based on the committee members’ inspection and their decision.

World.title: Tiruchi City Police gear up for procession, immersion of of Vinayaka idols on Sept. 16
World.content:
The Tiruchi City Police will make comprehensive security arrangements for the procession and immersion of idols of Lord Vinayaka in the Cauvery on September 16.

The police are making arrangements along the Cauvery bridge from where the idols would be immersed in the Cauvery. Over 1,000 police personnel are to be on duty at various places within Tiruchi City on September 16. A posse of manpower will deployed along the Cauvery bridge to regulate traffic.

Meanwhile, the police took out flag march from Gandhi Market arch to Anna statue on Saturday. The flag march on Sunday was conducted at Ariyamangalam to instil confidence in the minds of the people. Tiruchi District Collector Pratik Tayal, in a press release issued on Sunday, said that flying of drones in the district was prohibited on September 16.

World.title: Modi’s bilateral meetings on BRICS sidelines put defence, security cooperation in focus
World.content:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s bilateral engagements with leaders from Asia and Africa on the sidelines of the 18thBRICS Summit in New Delhi on Sunday (September 13, 2026) emphasised defence and security cooperation, alongside trade, technology and strategic partnerships, as India sought to deepen its engagement with key partners across the Global South.

Mr. Modi held separate meetings with Kazakhstan President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, Philippines President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr., Ugandan Vice President Jessica Rose Epel Alupo, Nigerian Vice President Kashim Shettima Mustapha, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa and the President of Burundi and chairperson of the African Union, Évariste Ndayishimiye.

Strategic partner

The meeting with Mr. Marcos of the Philippines assumes particular significance for India's defence outreach in Southeast Asia. The two leaders agreed to further deepen cooperation in defence and security, along with trade and investment, space, railways, fintech, education, science and technology and innovation.

The Philippines, which became a strategic partner of India in August 2025, is also a key defence partner in the region. The country has emerged as an important customer for Indian defence equipment, particularly the BrahMos supersonic cruise missile system. It is the first foreign customer for BrahMos under a $375-million deal, with deliveries and training underway.

Defence and security also figured prominently in Mr. Modi’s discussions with Kazakhstan President Tokayev, with the two sides reviewing cooperation in these fields as well as in connectivity, energy, critical minerals and emerging technologies. Kazakhstan remains an important Central Asian partner for India amid New Delhi’s efforts to expand strategic and security engagement with the region.

The defence dimension of India’s engagement with Malaysia also received attention during BRICS-related diplomacy. Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said exploratory discussions were underway on Kuala Lumpur acquiring the BrahMos missile system, though no final decision had been taken.

Defence ties with Africa

With Nigeria, Mr. Modi discussed defence and security alongside trade, investment, energy, agriculture, health and digital technologies. Both sides reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening the strategic partnership.

The broader engagements also underlined India’s push for greater security cooperation with African partners. Discussions with Uganda focused on technology partnerships, capacity building and private-sector collaboration, while the meeting with the African Union Chairperson covered development partnership and capacity building.

Taken together, the meetings highlighted New Delhi’s effort to leverage the BRICS platform to reinforce defence partnerships, capacity building and indigenous defence exports, while expanding India’s strategic footprint across the Indo-Pacific, Central Asia and Africa.

World.title: Three bonded labourers rescued at Kalasthambadi  in Tiruvannamalai district
World.content:
Three persons, who had reportedly worked as bonded labourers, were rescued at Kalasthambadi village near Chengam in Tiruvannamalai on Sunday (September 13, 2026).

Revenue Department officials said the rescued persons were K. Viji, 25, his wife V. Sasikala, 23, and his brother K. Surya, 19. The couple have a one-year-old daughter. They are residents of Kalasthambadi. “On information, Collector Vandana Garg directed Revenue Department officials and the police to rescue the workers. A team of officials conducted an inspection and found them working under inhuman conditions for the past few years,” said an official.

Initial inquiries revealed that the rescued workers were roped in by B. Jayamani, 52, a landlord, to work on five acres of farmland a few years ago. They were paid ₹8,000-₹10,000 in advance.

Officials said the rescued persons were forced to stay in small huts without proper access to drinking water and toilets and made to work for more than 15 hours a day. They told officials that the in-charge and his men would beat them up if they stood in the shade or even drank water, officials said.

They were given release certificates to help them receive financial aid and access government schemes, officials said.

World.title: Konda couple dismisses speculation over leaving party
World.content:
HYDERABAD

Dismissing speculation about quitting the party following her removal from the Telangana Cabinet, Warangal East MLA Konda Surekha made it clear that her family would remain with the Congress.

She also hoped that her husband and former MLC Konda Muralidhar Rao would soon be offered a chairman post in any one of the State corporations. The couple said that they would strive to make Rahul Gandhi the Prime Minister.

After her removal from the Cabinet following her daughter Sushmitha’s comments against Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy, Ms. Surekha and Mr. Murali held a meeting with their main followers in Warangal for the first time on Sunday.

During the meeting, Ms. Surekha continued her claim that she had not brought any disrepute to the minister's post and expressed her anguish over removal from the Cabinet for ‘no valid reason’.

She also made a veiled attack on both Warangal West MLA Naini Rajender Reddy and MLC Baswaraju Saraiah. She said that he (Saraiah) would not even win a corporator post.

Claiming that she had received phone calls from the party high command, she hoped that an official post would be offered to Mr. Murali.

She slammed the “growing opportunistic politics” too. “We are not in politics for posts, we are here to serve the people,” the former minister said.

Ms. Surekha also appealed to her followers not to be carried away by the false propaganda.

Meanwhile, Mr. Murali maintained that they would do politics by adhering to their values and cautioned his rivals against commenting on them. He stated that the Konda couple would not leave the Congress party, and expressed his commitment to ensuring that 24 corporators win in the Warangal East constituency in the upcoming Greater Warangal Municipal Corporation (GWMC) elections.

The former MLC emphasised that those who work hard will receive tickets and assured that he will protect the workers at any cost.

World.title: BRICS Summit 2026 September 13 highlights: Modi’s bilateral meetings on BRICS sidelines put defence, security cooperation in focus
World.content:
As rising geopolitical tensions adversely impact ordinary people globally, Prime Minister Narendra Modi said on Sunday (September 13, 2026) that BRICS must rise through cooperation and inclusive growth to meet these challenges and blossom for the sake of humanity.

Interview | The Security Council is paralysed, but the UN is not broken, says UNSG Guterres

In an address at the concluding session of the two-day, India-hosted BRICS summit, the prime minister also flagged serious concerns over the “weaponisation of technology and critical minerals”, warning that it could hinder shared progress and prosperity.

Chinese President ‌Xi Jinping unveiled on Sunday initiatives in areas ranging from AI to trade to deepen cooperation among the “Greater BRICS” emerging economies, as Beijing seeks to weld ⁠the grouping into a practical platform for Global South development.
