World.title: Revered sports journalist Recah Trinidad dies at 83
World.content:
Recah Trinidad dies 'peacefully in his sleep,' two years after the death of his sports journalist son Chino

MANILA, Philippines – Veteran sports journalist and columnist Ricardo “Recah” Trinidad died on Sunday, September 13. He was 83.

His death was announced by his daughter-in-law Nice, who said Trinidad passed away at around 6 am.

“After suffering a heart attack in June, dad bravely fought for the past few months and finally found his rest. He passed peacefully in his sleep, free from pain and suffering,” wrote Nice on Facebook.

One of the most revered sports journalists of his time, Trinidad wrote for multiple publications, including Daily Express, Tempo, and Malaya, and covered some of the most prestigious sporting events, including the Olympics, Asian Games, and the iconic Thrilla in Manila in 1975, where Muhammad Ali beat Joe Frazier.

He was also an award-winning writer, with his poem Rule Acrobat from Planet F winning second prize for poetry in the 1978 Palanca Awards.

Trinidad passed his passion for sports on to his son Manolo, most commonly known as Chino, who also became a sports journalist, and served as a commissioner of the Philippine Basketball League, and was one of the founding members of the Samahang Basketbol ng Pilipinas.

FAMILY. Recah Trinidad with son Chino and wife Maria Fe during the 1994 Asian Games in Hiroshima, Japan.

“Ka Recah” passed away two years after Chino died of a heart attack in 2024.

“I find comfort knowing that dad is now reunited with his beloved eldest son, kuya Chino Trinidad,” wrote Nice.

Trinidad was also known for his Bare Eye column in the Philippine Daily Inquirer, which he started in 1986 and continued writing until his final piece in 2020.

A published author as well, Trinidad wrote the book Pacific Storm, which captured the rise of Filipino boxing icon Manny Pacquiao.

In 2023, Trinidad received the Lifetime Award in Sports Journalism from the Philippine Sportswriters Association alongside many of his peers, including the late Eddie Alinea, Percy Della, Jun Engracia, Ding Marcelo, and Al Mendoza.

Trinidad is survived by his wife, Maria Fe; his sons, Paolo and Baste; daughters-in-law Nice and Babs; and six grandchildren.

“Rest peacefully, dad, No more pain. You are home. Thank you for being our dad, I love you. We love you! and We will miss you forever,” said Nice.

The public viewing for Trinidad’s remains will start on Wednesday, September 16, before his cremation on Saturday, September 19. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Inside the Newsroom] I knew you were waiting for Martin Romualdez’s mug shot
World.content:
Rappler didn’t publish former House speaker Martin Romualdez’s mugshot taken while he was lying in a hospital bed.

Rappler fact-checked a lawyer who initially circulated an image of Vice President Sara Duterte in handcuffs without disclosing that it was AI-generated.

And some of you might have been disappointed in our decision in the first case, and thought we were too grim about the second one.

I understand — “understand” being an understatement if you’ve read our commentary or watched our talk shows or followed our investigative reports.

When the national budget is supposedly plundered by way of anomalous flood control projects, or when the country’s second highest official lets out ear-piercing expletives against the President and admits to thoughts of beheading him, you are reasonably outraged (and horrified).

We are outraged (and horrified).

So why didn’t we indulge the public, who must be desperate for big, presumably untouchable, people to be made to account; who felt like seeing one official’s mugshots or another in handcuffs served some degree of swift justice?

Because we have to provide an anchor amid the waves of emotion. Journalists must presume a suspect’s innocence, avoid sensationalism, and apply standards of ethical reporting equally and consistently for every person. Publishing images that could be humiliating runs counter to those three standards I just mentioned.

We established that the police did their job of serving Romualdez the warrant by showing their photo getting his fingerprints. We cropped and blurred some parts of the photo provided by the Criminal Investigation and Detection Group. We zoomed in on just the booking process, and excluded as much as possible the medical tubes and blood pressure-cum-heartbeat monitor attached to him.

After that photo, I reminded the news desk that, consistent with our policy, we would not use the other one — of Romualdez lying in bed, a tag bearing his name and alleged crime placed atop his haggard body.

We would have followed the same standards if Sara Duterte were indeed handcuffed. No photos if the purpose was to just show a degrading spectacle.

By adhering to these editorial standards, the intention was to ensure that the focus was on the facts of the case, our rigorous and insightful reporting, and our excellent explainers.

In Romualdez’s case, we raised questions about the necessity of a hospital arrest. We laid out the inside story and the timeline that made the circumstances leading to the hospitalization — on the day the anti-graft court issued the arrest warrant — invite suspicion.

In Duterte’s case — to be clear, she was never handcuffed — we gave context to the grave threats cases and walked our audience through what to expect moving forward, and whether or not this could affect her ongoing impeachment trial. We placed her claims of untrustworthy courts and police side by side with contradicting statements she had made in the past.

We acknowledge that government officials occupy a unique position of trust. So when they are accused of violating that, the public needs to see confirmation that law enforcers process them the way they do ordinary suspects. Thus, our use of Romualdez’s finger-printing photo but not the mugshot.

With regard to handcuffs, in some newsrooms overseas, publishing photos of officials in handcuffs are now considered appropriate under certain conditions: when they are arrested on the spot in a public place (as opposed to them submitting themselves to the cops and courts), they are accused of serious abuse of power, and there is a disclaimer that the accused is not yet convicted.

We are watching these trends and will always review our standards — to serve justice and the public, not to protect politicians. (As the newsroom evolves, and some ethical guidelines are further refined, we may have missed updating or purging past contents. We would appreciate you bringing this to our attention via feedback@rappler.com.)

For now, we do our best to show state action while we also uphold the suspect’s rights and adhere to due process. We also avoid giving a platform to the drama the accused officials may have wanted to stage.

More importantly, when we take a deep breath amid the uproar, we — the press and the people — do not become like the monsters in high places we condemn and abhor. Challenging as it may be, we can only make progress as a society if we pursue justice and accountability without moral savagery.

P.S.: We draw the line, however, when an accused official weaponizes the concepts of due process, presumption of innocence, and sub judice to gag the press and prevent free public discourse on legitimate issues.

While I started writing this newsletter Friday morning, September 11, the law firm representing Martin Romualdez wrote to Rappler, seeking to stop our Rappler+ briefing on our series of investigations into multi-million-dollar properties linked to Romualdez. We went ahead with the members-exclusive program at 3 pm on Friday.

The event will not be livestreamed nor uploaded for the broader public. If you miss it, you can still become a Rappler+ member and gain access to our archives and future exclusive reports and events. – Rappler.com

Inside the Newsroom is a newsletter delivered straight to your inbox every week. Visit rappler.com/newsletters to manage your newsletter subscriptions.

World.title: [OPINION] 2026 BARMM parliamentary elections under the shadow of resurgent extremism
World.content:
The rising incidence of violence is not isolated, but part of a persistent pattern that poses an imminent threat to the legitimacy of the peace process and the democratic transition it promises

On Monday, September 14, nearly 2.4 million voters across the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) will cast their ballots in the region’s first parliamentary elections, a milestone that represents the culmination of decades of armed struggle and peace negotiations.

The election, originally scheduled for May 2022 but postponed four times due to legal, technical, and political complications, marks the transition from an appointed transitional authority to a democratically elected government.

It is a cornerstone of the political track under the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro (CAB), signed by the Philippine government and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) in 2014.

Yet as Bangsamoro communities prepare for this historic moment, the region finds itself gripped by a signaling resurgence of violent extremism.

Recent data from Conflict Climate Action shows a troubling picture: violent incidents linked to extremist groups have nearly doubled, rising 91% to 44 cases in 2025 from 23 a year earlier.

These are not isolated encounters. They are part of a persistent pattern that poses an imminent threat to the legitimacy of the peace process and the democratic transition it promises.

The evidence of resurgent extremism is stark and multifaceted. In 2026 alone, military operations in Lanao del Sur and Maguindanao have killed 10 members of Dawlah Islamiyah-Maute, the ISIS-affiliated group responsible for the 2017 Marawi siege and numerous attacks since. These operations follow similar deadly encounters in Lanao del Norte in 2024 and 2025, demonstrating a persistent and adaptive threat.

However, the military claims extremist groups have been largely neutralized, while large-scale attacks like the Marawi Siege have been prevented; sporadic but organized violence continues to plague the region.

This escalation must be seen within a longer trajectory. The 2017 Marawi siege, carried out by the ISIS-affiliated Maute group, was the longest urban conflict in the Philippines, devastating the city and displacing more than 350,000 individuals. Nine years later, post-reconstruction remains a predicament for internally displaced people who continue to live with insecurities in transitory shelters with no definitive timeline for their return. Another indication of the threat came in December 2023, when an explosion during a Catholic Mass at Mindanao State University-Marawi killed four people and injured 42. Authorities identified DI-Maute as the primary suspect.

These encounters make clear that they continue to pose an active threat across the Mindanao region as they adapt their tactics, using online channels to recruit local Moros, while remaining operationally and ideologically linked to the foreign-led Islamic State. This digital dimension of extremism makes the threat more diffuse and harder to counter through traditional military means.

The extremist threat in Bangsamoro is not purely domestic. Even after the Marawi Siege, more than 100 foreign terrorist fighters continued traveling to the Philippines to sustain conflicts across Mindanao, as the region is seen as a hub for transnational extremist networks. This is not new. Since the Al Qaeda days, the Philippines has been regarded as a “terrorism academy” in Asia, where its archipelagic setting, porous maritime borders, and historical militant groups provide a conducive environment for training activities. The ease of movement across the island chain and weak coastal surveillance have long made it easier for foreign fighters to embed themselves within local extremist groups.

The resurgence of extremism coincides with the first Bangsamoro election and threatens to undermine it.

Security preparations have been extensive: a gun ban took effect on July 16, 2026, and will last until September 29, 2026. By August 24, at least 15 people had been arrested for violating the ban, while 20 firearms had been seized. More than 24,000 security checkpoints have been established across the region, with approximately 30,000 security personnel deployed to ensure peaceful elections.

Despite these measures, election-related violence has already occurred. On August 14, a convoy carrying interim BARMM Chief Minister Macacua was fired upon by unidentified assailants in Datu Odin Sinsuat, Maguindanao del Norte, as he returned from assuming leadership of the Bangsamoro Federalist Party. While no injuries were recorded, the attack on such a high-profile figure underscores the volatile security environment.

The COMELEC has identified 105 municipalities and three cities for checkpoint implementation to enforce the gun ban. The concentration of security concerns in these areas reflects the persistent influence of armed groups and political dynasties that have historically used violence to influence electoral outcomes.

The resurgence of extremism cannot be understood in isolation from the broader fragility of the Bangsamoro peace process. The creation of the BARMM through the CAB was intended to address historical injustices against the Bangsamoro people and provide a political solution to decades of armed conflict.

Yet after eight years, the accord faces compounding threats that erode its implementation and legitimacy.

The normalization process — the critical component of the peace agreement that includes decommissioning of MILF combatants, transformation of camps, and the delivery of socioeconomic packages — remains in a state of suspension. In July 2025, the MILF Central Committee resolved to halt the decommissioning of its remaining 14,000 combatants and 2,450 weapons, citing the government’s failure to deliver “substantially on its socioeconomic commitments”.

This deadlock in normalization has profound implications for the election and the region’s future. Combatants who remain armed and without viable livelihoods represent a pool of potential recruits for extremist groups that offer alternative narratives of resistance and identity (Crisis Group, 2026). The MILF’s inability to deliver on its promises to its own fighters undermines its credibility and creates openings for more radical actors to fill the void.

Political divisions within the MILF have further complicated the landscape. The United Bangsamoro Justice Party, led by MILF senior leaders, now competes against the Bangsamoro Federalist Party, which draws support from former MILF commanders and established regional politicians. This intra-MILF competition has transformed the movement’s internal dynamics and potentially weakened its ability to present a unified front against extremist threats.

Extremist groups do not merely exploit failures in the peace process; they arise from structural gaps that it has yet to address. While political and socio-economic reforms continue, stability remains uneven after seven years of transition. Poverty rates are dropping, yet the region still has the country’s highest illiteracy rate, and development remains sluggish. Factionalism and dynastic politics remain embedded in political life in the region. The clan feuds across the region, conflicts that have claimed lives and forced families from their homes.

These horizontal conflicts create environments where extremist groups can thrive, offering protection, identity, and purpose to youth who see no future within existing political structures. The Marawi rehabilitation process exemplifies these structural challenges. Nine years after the siege, post-reconstruction remains a predicament for internally displaced persons who continue to live with insecurities in transitory shelters with no definitive timeline for return.

The efforts to prevent violent extremism in Mindanao became a government priority after the Marawi siege. Yet, these programs remain insufficient in scale, with poor interagency coordination, duplication, and uneven evaluation. Hard security measures sometimes backfire due to overly broad definitions of extremism, risk securitizing communities, and narrow civic space, blurring the line between protection and surveillance.

The convergence of the first Bangsamoro election with the resurgence of extremism creates a critical juncture for the region. The election represents more than a political transition; it is a test of whether the peace process can deliver tangible improvements in governance, security, and livelihoods. If the election proceeds peacefully and results in a government perceived as legitimate and effective, it could strengthen the peace process and undercut extremist narratives. Conversely, if the election is marred by violence, fraud, or perceived illegitimacy, it could validate extremist claims that democratic politics cannot address Bangsamoro grievances.

The challenge now is mitigating escalating threats that could lead to another bold extremist attack, not merely another humanitarian crisis, but a terminal blow to the peace process’s legitimacy. Authorities must recognize that counterterrorism alone is insufficient and often counterproductive; military operations without a peace dividend risk producing othering that sustains extremism.

In this volatile context, the central government, MILF, and other stakeholders must act decisively and in coordination. This means returning to comprehensive agreement commitments, accelerating normalization with a clear timeline, the election proceeds without further delay, and fast-tracking the socio-economic package for reintegration to restore political and moral legitimacy. The MILF must consolidate and recalibrate its forces and resist relapse to armed struggle.

The extremism in Mindanao is not merely a symptom of peace process failures; it is an alternative that feeds on them. If authorities continue framing the situation as “under control” through hard security while disregarding these signals, and MILF leaders remain consumed by frictions, these groups will only expand and grow more relevant, waiting for the next wind to fan them into flame.

The September 14 election is not just a vote; it is a referendum on whether peace through political inclusion can prevail over violence through extremist exclusion. The future of Bangsamoro hangs in the balance. – Rappler.com

Reemar B Alonsagay is Faculty Member at the Political Studies Department of Mindanao State University Main Campus. He holds a Masters in Applied Conflict Transformation Studies from the Centre for Peace and Conflict Studies in Cambodia.

World.title: [Tech Thoughts] The Jurassic Parkification of AI chatbots
World.content:
Our dinosaurs of AI Chatbots are roaming free, untethered and unbothered by lax safeguards, and we need civic action and stronger protections against them

A man named Michael Lines sued OpenAI in July after what he says was ChatGPT feeding into his religious mania and pushed delusions he was Jesus into his mind.

Ars Technica reported that weeks of ChatGPT exchanges were said to have pushed Lines, who has bipolar I disorder, into a manic spiral where he believed that he was Jesus, that ChatGPT was God, and that he should commit suicide to return to God/Jesus/ChatGPT.

Ars Technica said at the end of its report that, thanks to timely interventions and a good support system, they were able to get Lines the care he needed to break out of the spiral.

He’s now suing OpenAI to have them make changes that could help people with mental health issues into not using artificial intelligence chatbots for help. Specifically, he’s seeking an injunction that would require the company to end conversations about self-harm and delete models trained on chat sessions with vulnerable users like him, during periods when safeguards were lacking.

‘Just because you can doesn’t mean you should’

Over on the Rappler Communities app, we had a conversation on the Everyday Tech chat channel about what happened to Lines, and Gemma Mendoza, our head of strategic programs, criticized the lack of scrutiny and regulations governments are taking over AI chatbots, especially as it relates to matters of mental health.

“Even the practice of psychology is regulated,” she said.

I explained that ChatGPT was allegedly feeding Lines’ mania and religious delusions by giving him information — from scripture passages to apparent hallucinations that Lines had a past life as Jesus — on what it meant to be the son of God.

The Ars Technica report mentioned Lines began using ChatGPT in 2023, but was actively using GPT-4o as his default model in 2024. This particular model, seen as “unsafe” by researchers, was said to do more than just validate delusional claims. Researchers said GPT-4o “elaborated on them, absorbed the user’s interpretive frame as [its] own, and progressively lost the capacity to distinguish a user in crisis from a narrative to be extended.”

Mendoza, in our chat, said, “This goes to the question of business and purpose: people think the purpose of these bots is to serve as companions.”

“No, the purpose is to get people to become dependent so they will pay more,” she added.

I was more worried, meanwhile, about how governments could turn back the clock and regulate something so ambiguously harmful, and she responded with what inspired the title of today’s piece: that what’s happening with AI chatbots reminded her of Jurassic Park.

The original line taken from Jurassic Park was, “Your scientists were so preoccupied with whether or not they could, that they didn’t stop to think if they should.” But I only remembered the shorthand of “Just because you can doesn’t mean you should.”

As we know from those movies, the dinosaurs took over… and instead of thinking about simple cause and effect (clone dinos for a park/build AI chatbots — make money!) we had to factor in chaos (dinosaurs and AI killing people as an unintended consequence of their creation) that no amount of safeguards could compensate for.

Better safeguards means civic action

In our conversation, Mendoza mentioned that scrutinizing AI chatbots, especially for mental health outcomes, means civic action is needed. Various sectors need to work together to know more about the effects of chatbots on mental health.

That means getting researchers of all stripes, not just psychologists and psychiatrists, on board to study it. It also means getting legislations passed to build more stringent safeguards into AI chatbots before they’re launched, to avoid them doing things like the above.



Further, Lines and mental health experts also said people with the lived experiences of having specific mental health issues such as bipolar disorder or schizophrenia should have their perspectives incorporated into OpenAI’s crisis response.

Explained Ars Technica, “They might rate ChatGPT responses differently from clinical experts, potentially helping OpenAI detect more red flags to improve its responses, escalate crisis interventions, or terminate harmful chat sessions.”

Ultimately? Our dinosaurs of AI Chatbots are roaming free, untethered and unbothered by lax safeguards. I really don’t want to accelerate the timeline of AI chatbots turning our Jurassic world into a fallen kingdom. – Rappler.com

World.title: News Reflection: Sara Duterte does not feel safe. At all.
World.content:
The Sara Duterte who said she had enlisted a hitman to kill her foes (only in case they do her in, she insists) is the same Sara Duterte who later said she does not feel safe anywhere in this country, the same country her father, Rodrigo Duterte, ruled with drug war bloodshed not long ago.

In whichever light they are viewed, the Vice President’s words merit deep pondering. Paterno Esmaquel leads us in this week’s News Reflection, to find meaning and truth (if any) in our leader’s utterances. – Rappler.com

World.title: SM paw parks, pet changing stations: Hanna Carinna Sy wants your fur baby at the mall
World.content:
'Pet initiatives are close to home for me because I have pets myself, and I know firsthand how much fur babies are a beloved part of families,' the third-generation Sy tells Rappler

MANILA, Philippines – Ask Hanna Carinna Sy what her pet project is and — no pun intended — the answer is pets.

The third-generation Sy, now senior assistant vice president for marketing and leasing at SM Supermalls, has worked on programs ranging from children’s talent competitions to spelling bees. But the one closest to her heart involves making the family mall empire a little friendlier to fur babies.

“Pet initiatives are close to home for me because I have pets myself, and I know firsthand how much fur babies are a beloved part of families,” Sy told Rappler in an interview. “That’s really the thinking behind the SM Super Pets Club.”

Of course, behind all the fondness for our four-legged friends is a compelling business case, too.

“Regarding our customer segment size, the pet community is rapidly growing into one of the top performing groups,” Sy said.

Sy told Rappler that while SM’s active lifestyle “tribe” still generates more foot traffic, pet owners tend to spend more per visit and stay longer at the mall. That makes them one of SM’s more lucrative and fast-growing customer communities.

It only makes sense then that SM is making space for them. (READ: ‘Cookie-cutter’ no more? SM Nuvali to open November 27 with 1-hectare indoor garden)

A changing station for your fur baby

One of the newer additions is a pet changing station at The Podium, essentially a dedicated area near restrooms where owners can clean and freshen up their pets in the middle of a mall trip.

“We’ve also introduced Pet Changing Stations, which began in SM Podium, to give pet owners a space to freshen up their pets,” Sy said.

For now, The Podium serves as the flagship for the concept, but SM is already looking at possibly bringing it to their other malls. And if Sy gets her way, future versions could become a whole room rather than just a small changing area.

FRESHEN UP. The flagship pet changing station is located at The Podium, near the restrooms. Lance Spencer Yu/Rappler.

“When I first helped develop the pet program, my vision was to build an ecosystem rather than just a loyalty program,” she told Rappler on Friday, September 11.

For Sy, the programs are also a way of putting her own stamp on the family business. Carrying the Sy surname, after all, means inevitably carrying the legacy of “Tatang” — SM founder Henry Sy Sr. (READ: Dear You, and the stories of love and migration the Filipino-Chinese pass down)

“At the end of the day, I’m more than just the granddaughter of Tatang, or more than just the daughter of my dad,” Sy said during a recent fireside chat with the media. “But you know, I can also contribute in my own ways.”

SM already has 34 active Paw Parks nationwide, which are fenced-off spaces in the mall where pets can play and socialize. SM Megamall also recently revamped its Paw Park as the company continues updating the spaces.

In other news, SM has been changing its malls to suit particular communities and experiences. It now has 22 running hubs and 102 pickleball courts, while SM Aura is getting two tennis courts and will turn its grand staircase into a library. And when SM Harrison Plaza opens by the end of 2027, it will have an entire floor dedicated to Gen Zs — only fitting for a mall within walking distance of several schools, whose students SM expects will be looking for a new place to hang out after class. – Rappler.com

World.title: From Bronze Age Settlements to Medieval Cities: New Archaeological Discoveries Across Kazakhstan
World.content:
ASTANA — From Bronze Age settlements to medieval cities, archaeological research across Kazakhstan continues to reveal new details about the societies that once inhabited the Eurasian steppe.

Recent excavations have brought new findings from the ancient settlement of Zhankent in the Kyzylorda Region and a Bronze Age site near Imantau in northern Kazakhstan, while authorities are expanding efforts to protect historical and cultural monuments.

Together, these discoveries highlight the diversity of Kazakhstan’s archaeological heritage and show how excavation, scientific cooperation and modern research methods are helping researchers reconstruct different periods of the country’s past.

Zhankent: 20 years of archaeological research

One of the country’s longest-running archaeological projects is taking place at the ancient settlement of Zhankent in the Kyzylorda Region.

Systematic research at the site began in 2005. Over the past two decades, archaeologists have excavated more than 4,000 square meters and uncovered more than 25,000 artefacts, according to the Ministry of Science and Higher Education of Kazakhstan.

The finds include ceramic, metal, stone, bone and glass objects. They provide researchers with information about the daily life, crafts, economy and cultural connections of the settlement’s inhabitants.

Zhankent is particularly important for studying the history of the Oghuz. Archaeologists have investigated citadel, shahristan, residential quarters and economic structures, gradually reconstructing the layout and development of the medieval city.

The archaeological project has involved researchers from Kazakhstan and several other countries, contributing to a broader understanding of medieval settlements along the Syr Darya and the archaeological landscape of southern Kazakhstan.

Recent work at the site has focused on several areas of the ancient city, including the eastern gate complex and shahristan. Archaeologists have uncovered ceramic fragments, traditional asyks and animal remains, adding to the material evidence of everyday life at Zhankent. The settlement is also part of the Silk Roads: Fergana–Syr Darya Corridor included in Kazakhstan’s UNESCO World Heritage efforts.

Researchers are also using electrical tomography to examine underground layers and identify possible structures without excavating every part of the settlement.

Imantau: a glimpse into Bronze Age life

While Zhankent provides evidence of medieval urban civilization, archaeological research in northern Kazakhstan is taking researchers several thousand years further back. A joint expedition involving the National Museum of Kazakhstan and the National Museum of the People’s Republic of China conducted excavations at a Bronze Age settlement near Imantau in the Aiyrtau district of the North Kazakhstan Region.

According to the National Museum of Kazakhstan, the expedition was held from July 14 to Aug. 16, 2026, as part of cooperation between the two institutions. The researchers are studying the settlement to learn more about the daily life, economy and culture of ancient communities that lived in the region.

The site provides an opportunity to examine a period when communities across the Eurasian steppe were developing new forms of settlement, livestock breeding and metalworking. The expedition is part of longer-term cooperation between the two national museums.

The Imantau project adds another chronological layer to Kazakhstan’s ancient history. Archaeological work elsewhere in the country has similarly revealed evidence from different periods, including Bronze Age settlements and sites connected to the Silk Road.

Protecting what archaeology uncovers

Discovering historical sites is only one part of archaeological research. Protecting the sites themselves is equally important, particularly as ancient settlements and monuments can be vulnerable to construction, land use and natural deterioration.

In the Atyrau Region, protection zones were established for 41 historical and cultural monuments. Specialists also monitored 171 heritage sites and conducted expert assessments of 100 objects. Following the assessments, 80 objects were recommended for inclusion in the list of historical and cultural monuments.

The work covered several districts of the region and included field inspections of the condition of historical sites. The newly established protection zones add to 180 monuments in the Atyrau Region for which such zones had previously been approved.

Such measures are intended to establish clear boundaries around protected sites and reduce the risk of damage from development and other activities.

A wider archaeological picture

The discoveries at Zhankent and Imantau are part of a much broader archaeological effort taking place across Kazakhstan.

At Saraishyk, a medieval settlement associated with the Golden Horde and located in the Atyrau Region, excavations have uncovered hundreds of artefacts and architectural remains, providing new evidence about urban life in the region.

The findings included remains of residential buildings, a citadel and a caravanserai dating to the early 14th century, alongside household and decorative objects made of metal, glass, bone and ceramics.

In southern Kazakhstan, archaeological research has also revealed new evidence of the ancient Kangju state. Excavations at Kultobe have uncovered inscriptions and other artefacts that are helping researchers understand the political and cultural history of the region.

Other recent excavations have focused on earlier periods. Archaeologists in the Kostanai Region have studied Neolithic burials that provide evidence of communities living in northern Kazakhstan thousands of years ago.

These projects demonstrate the chronological depth of Kazakhstan’s archaeological heritage: from early human settlements and the Bronze Age to ancient states, Turkic monuments, Oghuz cities and Golden Horde centres.

Modern archaeology is also increasingly combining traditional excavation with laboratory analysis, geophysical methods and international cooperation. These approaches allow researchers to study not only individual artefacts but also the wider environment in which ancient communities lived.

Pottery can reveal information about technology and cultural contacts, animal remains can provide clues about diet and economic activity, while coins and other objects can help trace trade networks.

World.title: RIKO’s Škrabec: Kazakhstan’s Next Chapter Lies Beyond Resources
World.content:
ASTANA – Director and Partner of Slovenian engineering company RIKO Janez Škrabec has been coming to this part of the world for nearly four decades. His first visit to the Soviet Union was in 1988, when Kazakhstan belonged to a completely different political and economic reality. Today, he is returning to Astana, which is increasingly positioning itself as a regional center of transport, energy, investment and technological cooperation.

There is a certain value in seeing a country not at one particular moment, but across decades. Škrabec’s perspective is therefore more than that of a businessman assessing a market. He has watched the region change, institutions evolve, and Eurasia’s geography take on new economic meaning.

His visit to Kazakhstan comes as Kazakhstan-Slovenia ties build on the momentum of Slovenian President Nataša Pirc Musar’s visit in spring 2025, which placed greater emphasis on practical economic cooperation in trade, investment, energy, transport and technology. Škrabec joined the Slovenian business delegation during that visit and attended the business forum in Astana with President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev. For RIKO, the visit became a catalyst: the company has since opened a representative office in Astana and is developing projects in energy, water, transport and industrial infrastructure. The next challenge, in Škrabec’s view, is to turn political goodwill into lasting business partnerships.

In an interview with The Astana Times, Škrabec discussed where business can move faster than politics, why energy and infrastructure may become the foundation of a deeper Kazakhstan-Slovenia partnership, and why lasting economic ties ultimately depend not only on capital and technology but also on trust.

From political momentum to practical cooperation

“High-level political visits matter because they open doors, build trust and create the conditions for companies to move toward concrete projects,” Škrabec said.

For him, however, the real test of political goodwill comes after the official meetings end.

“Business can move faster than politics when there is a clear project, financing, technology and a reliable local partner. At that point, political goodwill can quickly become economic reality,” he said.

The next stage of Kazakhstan-Slovenia cooperation, he believes, should therefore focus less on declarations and more on projects in which the two sides can combine their respective strengths. That view comes from a much longer personal history with the region.

“I first came to the then Soviet Union as a young entrepreneur in 1988, and for decades RIKO was active in Russia, Belarus and Ukraine,” he said.

That experience gives Škrabec a perspective that goes beyond assessing Kazakhstan as a market. He has watched the wider region transform over several decades and has seen Astana itself emerge as one of the most visible symbols of Kazakhstan’s transformation. It is a perspective shaped as much by time as by business and one that helps explain why he sees Kazakhstan’s current trajectory not as a sudden opportunity, but as the latest stage in a much longer transformation.

Energy as a test of long-term partnership

Energy is one area where Škrabec believes this principle can be put into practice.

“Kazakhstan needs not only new generation capacity, but also modernization of transmission and distribution networks, stronger grid reliability, digitalization, integration of renewables and energy-storage solutions,” he said.

He sees opportunities across a broad part of the energy system, including “transformer and traction substations, grid modernization, hydropower, renewables, battery storage and energy efficiency.”

For Slovenian companies, Škrabec believes the opportunity lies in combining specialized engineering with technology integration and project implementation.

“Slovenian companies are strong in specialized engineering, technology integration and project implementation. RIKO, for example, has references in photovoltaics, hydropower, substations and battery energy storage,” he said.

But he also places a strong emphasis on localization, noting that the most sustainable model is not simply to export European solutions to Kazakhstan.

“For us, localization is essential. We want to work with Kazakh engineers, contractors and manufacturers and, where economically justified, develop local production or joint ventures.”

He also sees potential in the European Union’s Global Gateway initiative, “especially where Kazakhstan’s development priorities can be combined with European engineering and financial instruments.” The approach reflects a broader idea running through Škrabec’s thinking: the strongest partnerships create capacity on both sides rather than simply completing individual contracts.

What still holds European investors back

Kazakhstan, in his assessment, has become increasingly interesting to European capital for reasons that extend well beyond raw materials.

“Kazakhstan offers a powerful mix of advantages: natural resources, strategic geography, growing infrastructure and a clear ambition to modernize its industrial and technological base,” Škrabec said.

He believes European investors are increasingly looking at Kazakhstan “not only as a resource market, but as a place for infrastructure, logistics, industry, energy transition and higher-value technology.” For Slovenian companies, another advantage is familiarity with the wider region.

“Many of us have decades of experience in the wider post-Soviet region. We understand technical standards, institutional structures and the organization of large infrastructure projects,” he said.

At the same time, Škrabec is frank about what European investors continue to watch closely.

“European investors still pay close attention to regulatory predictability, procurement transparency, administrative efficiency, investment protection and geopolitical risk,” he said, noting that progress on those fronts could have a direct economic effect.

Beyond trade: building joint capabilities

Škrabec sees the greatest long-term potential in a relationship that goes beyond traditional trade statistics. The strongest model, in his view, is based on complementarity.

“Slovenian companies can bring specialized technology, engineering expertise, project management and access to European know-how and financing. Kazakh companies bring local market knowledge, industrial capacities and strong regional connections,” he said.

That combination, Škrabec said, creates opportunities in “energy, water, railways, logistics, environmental technologies and industrial infrastructure.” There is also a regional dimension. According to him, there is a strong potential for joint ventures, localization and, eventually, expansion into third-country markets across Central Asia. For RIKO, this is particularly relevant because its model integrates technologies, financing and partners into complete project solutions.

Such a model could change the very definition of economic cooperation between Kazakhstan and Slovenia. Instead of asking only what one country can export to the other, businesses can begin to consider what they can build together and where those combined capabilities might travel next.

A Kazakhstan beyond resources

That question becomes even more important when Škrabec looks five to ten years ahead.

“I believe it would be a mistake to see Kazakhstan ten years from now primarily as a supplier of natural resources,” he said.

Resources will remain important, but in his view, the key question is how much value Kazakhstan can create domestically. He expects continued growth in manufacturing, energy, logistics, transport, digital industries and advanced technologies. The Trans-Caspian International Transport Route will add another layer to that transformation.

“The Trans-Caspian, or Middle Corridor, will also strengthen Kazakhstan’s role as a bridge between Asia and Europe,” Škrabec said.

But even the word “bridge” may ultimately be too narrow.

“The real opportunity is for Kazakhstan to become not only a transit and resource country, but a place where industrial value, technology and expertise are created,” he noted.

That is where he sees the strongest basis for European and Kazakh cooperation: European companies can contribute technology, engineering and investment, and Kazakhstan offers scale, location, resources and regional connectivity. The relationship, therefore, could evolve from a connection between markets into a partnership between capabilities.

The role of trust and of people

For Škrabec, however, economics alone cannot sustain a relationship over decades.

“I would add one more dimension: long-term partnerships are not built only through trade and investment. Culture and trust matter too,” he said.

This is not simply a philosophical observation. RIKO has already supported Kazakh cultural initiatives in Slovenia, including the Astana Opera’s Spartacus performance and an evening of Kazakh culture. The company is also developing an initiative for a memorial to Abai Kunanbayev in Slovenia. These efforts sit alongside a longer tradition of cultural diplomacy.

For the past 26 years, Škrabec’s Lions Club has organized an annual evening in Ljubljana dedicated to one country, presenting its art, cuisine, history, traditions, natural beauty and economy. RIKO has traditionally been the main sponsor. This year, the evening focused on Kazakhstan.

“The event takes place in the Slovenian capital, on one of Ljubljana’s most prestigious stages, and has long been regarded as one of the city’s leading social events,” Škrabec said.

He recalls the response to the Kazakhstan evening as exceptional. He also singled out Kazakhstan’s Ambassador to Slovenia, Altay Abibullayev, whose role went beyond formal diplomatic representation.

“Ambassador Altay Abibullayev proved to be an excellent host. At the end of the evening he presented me with a traditional Kazakh shapan (a coat). I received it as a great honor and a beautiful symbol of friendship between our two countries.” Škrabec said

It is a fitting detail in a relationship that Škrabec increasingly sees as being built on more than economic calculation. A representative office, a tender, a joint venture or a logistics project can create the infrastructure of a partnership. But people create memories.

And perhaps this is where Škrabec’s nearly four decades of experience matter most. He has seen the political map change, economies transform, and Astana grow from a very different place into the capital it is today. His assessment of Kazakhstan’s future is therefore not simply an investor’s forecast. It is also the perspective of someone who has seen how quickly a country can change when its ambitions, geography and institutions begin moving in the same direction.

For Kazakhstan and Slovenia, the next stage may be about turning that accumulated political goodwill into something more permanent: industrial partnerships, shared technologies, new transport links, local capabilities and, ultimately, a relationship in which economic cooperation becomes as natural as diplomatic dialogue.

As Škrabec put it, the most durable foundation is not trade alone, but “that combination of economic interest, cultural understanding and personal trust.”

World.title: Foreign Digital Firms Pay Kazakhstan Nearly $390 Million in Tax Since 2022
World.content:
ASTANA – Foreign digital companies have paid Kazakhstan 178.8 billion tenge ($390.2 million) in value-added tax since 2022, with annual collections rising more than fivefold over three years under the country’s so-called Google tax.

The figures show the growing fiscal contribution of international platforms serving consumers in Kazakhstan. They do not, however, directly measure the country’s total digital consumption or cross-border e-commerce, because the mechanism covers both digital services and goods sold through online platforms.

Kazakhstan introduced VAT rules for foreign internet companies, commonly known as the Google tax, in 2022. The mechanism requires international companies providing digital services or selling goods online directly to consumers in Kazakhstan to register and pay VAT.

Taxpayers include companies providing software, entertainment, gaming, education and other digital services, alongside businesses selling goods through online platforms.

How much did companies pay

As of Aug. 1, 133 foreign companies were registered as taxpayers, according to the State Revenue Committee of the Ministry of Finance, as reported by Kazinform.

Annual collections increased substantially through 2025. Foreign companies paid 10.4 billion tenge (US$22.7 million) in VAT in 2022, the first year of the mechanism. Payments increased to 24.3 billion tenge (US$53 million) in 2023 and 35 billion tenge (US$76.4 million) in 2024.

In 2025, the figure reached 57.6 billion tenge (US$125.7 million), more than five times the amount collected in 2022. Foreign companies paid 51.5 billion tenge ($112.4 million) during the first seven months of 2026, nearly 90% of the full-year amount collected in 2025.

Who are the largest taxpayers

The largest taxpayers illustrate the range of activities covered by the mechanism. The list spans physical goods, gaming, entertainment, software, communications and online education, underscoring that the mechanism extends well beyond online shopping.

In 2025, Singapore-registered Elementary Innovation Pte. Ltd., associated with the Temu marketplace, paid 13.3 billion tenge (US$29 million) in VAT. Apple paid 11.2 billion tenge (US$24.4 million), while Valve Corporation, the company behind the Steam gaming platform, paid 10.3 billion tenge (US$22.5 million).

Google contributed 7.3 billion tenge (US$15.9 million) and iHerb paid 4.9 billion tenge (US$10.7 million).

Netflix paid 353.9 million tenge (US$772,333), Spotify paid 293.1 million tenge (US$639,646), Zoom paid 183.2 million tenge (US$399,806) and Coursera paid 33.2 million tenge (US$72,454).

Expanding e-commerce market

The trend comes as Kazakhstan’s e-commerce sector continues to expand. Retail e-commerce reached nearly 3.8 trillion tenge (US$8 billion) in 2025, with marketplaces accounting for 86% of online retail sales, according to the Bureau of National Statistics. Together, these developments point to a broader shift in how Kazakh citizens purchase goods and access services, with both domestic and international digital platforms playing an increasingly important role.

The expansion of e-commerce has coincided with the widespread adoption of digital payments. Cashless payments account for 98% of transactions by number and 87% by value.

The tax receipts do not represent the total value of Kazakhstan’s digital consumption or measure cross-border e-commerce alone. Taken together with rising online retail sales, however, they indicate the growing presence of foreign platforms in the country’s consumer economy.

World.title: Almaty Museum of Arts Opens Exhibition Tracing Seven Decades of Kazakh Sculpture
World.content:
ASTANA – The Almaty Museum of Arts has opened a major exhibition exploring the development of Kazakh sculpture over seven decades.

The exhibition, titled “Müsinder: Sculpture in Kazakhstan from the 1950s to the Present Day,” opened on Sept. 8 in the museum’s Saryarka Hall and brings together more than 50 works by several generations of Kazakh artists, reported the museum’s press office. The project is curated by art historian Aliya Tiesenhausen and is part of the museum’s first-anniversary programme.

Among the artists represented are Kha­kimzhan Nauryzbayev, Isaac Itkind, Erkin Mergenov, Madina Zholdybek, Rysbek Akhmetov, Moldaqul Narymbetov, Yerbossyn Meldibekov and Aruzhan Zhumabek.

Rather than presenting a strictly chronological history, the exhibition examines how the language of sculpture has changed from the Soviet period to contemporary Kazakhstan. The works explore themes including the human body, memory, family, identity and social change.

The title refers to the Kazakh word “musin,” which can mean both “sculpture” and “human figure.” The human body therefore becomes a central element of the exhibition, allowing artists from different periods to reflect on society and personal experience.

The exhibition is divided into four thematic sections. One of them, “Game of Opposites?”, focuses on sculpture from the late 1950s through the early 1990s and examines the tension between officially accepted artistic practices and more individual approaches developed by artists in their studios. Works by Isaac Itkind and Erkin Mergenov demonstrate the emergence of more personal forms of sculptural expression during the Soviet period.

Later sections turn to contemporary approaches to the human body and its relationship with politics, culture, gender and personal experience. The exhibition thus connects works created under very different historical circumstances, highlighting changes in artistic materials, techniques and interpretations of the human figure.

According to curator Aliya Tiesenhausen, the exhibition presents sculpture as a “living artistic process” rather than simply a historical record. Soviet-era academic works are placed in dialogue with contemporary pieces to show how both artistic language and perceptions of sculpture have evolved.

“The history of sculpture is at the same time a history of society, memory, and the human being,” said Tiesenhausen.

The exhibition will run from Sept. 8 through May 2027. An illustrated catalogue accompanying the exhibition will be published in Kazakh, Russian and English, featuring scholarly texts by Tiesenhausen and art historians Valeria Ibrayeva and Alexandra Tsai.

The exhibition is also part of the Almaty Museum of Arts’ broader effort to study and present Kazakhstan’s artistic heritage. The museum, which opened in September 2025, was established as a major platform for Kazakh, Central Asian and international contemporary art.

In an earlier interview with The Astana Times, the museum’s artistic director Meruert Kaliyeva described its mission as combining the study and preservation of regional art with greater public access to international contemporary art. The museum was featured in an episode of The Astana Times exploring Almaty’s major cultural landmarks.

World.title: Kazakhstan Sets Out Priorities Ahead of BRICS Summit in India
World.content:
NEW DELHI – Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev is expected to participate in the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi on Sept. 12-13, with Kazakhstan seeking to advance cooperation in energy, critical minerals, transport connectivity and global water security.

India is hosting the summit under the theme Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability. BRICS is a group of eleven major emerging markets and developing countries of the world. They include Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and the United Arab Emirates, representing almost half of the world’s population and 40% of the global GDP.

Priorities of Kazakhstan, which joined the group as a partner country in 2025, were presented by Kazakh Ambassador to India Azamat Eskarayev at the BRICS Energy Partnerships for Progress and Prosperity diplomatic dialogue in New Delhi on Sept. 3.

Energy security was among the central topics of the meeting. Participants discussed traditional and renewable energy, new technologies, infrastructure, investment and critical minerals. Particular attention was given to resilient supply chains and emerging energy and transport corridors.

For Kazakhstan, the agenda closely aligns with its efforts to strengthen its role in Eurasian transport and energy connectivity. Eskarayev emphasized the country’s potential in traditional energy, renewable energy and critical minerals.

The discussion was not focused on a single project or agreement but on areas Kazakhstan intends to promote through the BRICS partnership.

Water initiative adds another dimension

Separately, Yeskarayev highlighted Tokayev’s initiative to establish an International Water Organization under the auspices of the United Nations.

The initiative calls for stronger international coordination on water resources and seeks to bring greater political attention to global water security. Kazakhstan has previously presented the proposal in other international forums, including the United Nations.

According to Aidar Kurmashev, head of the Asian Studies Department at the Kazakhstan Institute for Strategic Studies under the President of Kazakhstan (KazISS), the initiative could gain practical value if it is accompanied by cooperation on water technologies and management.

He suggested that Kazakhstan could develop pilot projects for arid regions involving satellite monitoring of water resources, digital irrigation management, wastewater reuse and specialist training.

“Kazakhstan could offer its territory for pilot projects involving Indian, Chinese and Emirati companies. Then the idea of an international water organization will gain a practical dimension, and potential partners will see specific facilities, technology needs and a possible financing model,” Kurmashev told The Astana Times.

From critical minerals to concrete projects

Kurmashev noted that in critical minerals, Kazakhstan should promote projects focused on domestic processing, component manufacturing and modern exploration technologies, Kurmashev said.

He emphasized that projects should have a clearly defined resource base, site, energy and water requirements, technology partner, potential buyer and financing model. The same approach should apply to transport and digital projects.

“Tokayev’s participation in the summit could help present Kazakhstan as an independent Eurasian participant with a practical agenda covering transport, energy, water and food security and technology,” Kurmashev said.

“The Indian context is also important. India’s chairmanship makes South Asia, sustainable supply chains and technological cooperation issues more prominent,” he added.

However, he noted that the value of Kazakhstan’s participation should ultimately be measured by what follows the summit.

“Political presence should be assessed by the continuation: whether there are bilateral agreements, responsible operators and projects with certain deadlines after the summit,” Kurmashev said.

BRICS as a tool for economic diversification

For Kazakhstan, BRICS can provide an additional platform for expanding economic ties beyond its traditional partners, particularly with major economies in Asia, the Middle East, Africa and South America.

The grouping was established in 2006 by Brazil, Russia, India and China, with South Africa joining in 2011. Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia and Indonesia have since joined as members.

Kazakhstan is not a BRICS member but became one of the group’s partner countries in 2025. It participated in the 2025 BRICS Summit in Brazil as a partner country.

According to Kurmashev, the partner-country format gives Kazakhstan flexibility to advance its interests without making BRICS an exclusive foreign policy platform.

“Kazakhstan has a dense network of bilateral and multilateral channels with Russia and China. These are the Eurasian Economic Union and the the Commonwealth of Independent States with Russia, the the Shanghai Cooperation Organization and Confidence Building Measures in Asia, the Central Asia-China format and regular high-level meetings,” Kurmashev said.

“Therefore, the additional value of BRICS lies primarily in reaching a wider audience. On the same platform, Kazakhstan gets access to the leadership and business circles of India, Brazil, South Africa, the United Arab Emirates, Indonesia, Egypt and other countries with which the intensity of economic contacts still varies,” he said.

Kurmashev emphasized that BRICS membership or partnership does not automatically increase trade. The grouping is not a customs union and does not create a common market or uniform tariffs.

Its practical value lies in bringing governments, companies and development institutions closer together, helping them identify partners and address barriers.

For Kazakhstan, the success of economic diversification should therefore be measured not simply by total trade with BRICS countries, but by increased trade with countries such as India, Brazil, Indonesia, the UAE, Egypt and South Africa, the emergence of new export categories and a broader investor base.

Kurmashev suggested that government agencies along with QazTrade, a state-owned agency aimed at promoting trade, develop individual country strategies, organize trade missions and support companies through the contracting process.

Can BRICS strengthen transport links with India?

Transport connectivity is another area where Kazakhstan sees potential for BRICS cooperation, although the grouping itself does not manage transport corridors.

The Trans-Caspian International Transport Route links Kazakhstan through the Caspian Sea, Azerbaijan, Georgia and Türkiye with European markets. For connections with India, the International North-South Transport Corridor, Iranian ports such as Chabahar, and the Kazakhstan-Turkmenistan-Iran railway offer potential links.

According to Kurmashev, a possible long-term route could connect India, Iran, Turkmenistan and Kazakhstan, with onward access through the Kazakh ports of Aktau and Kuryk to the Trans-Caspian route.

However, he noted that political declarations alone would not make such a route commercially viable. Stable cargo volumes would be needed to support regular container trains and shipping services, reduce empty runs and distribute fixed costs.

“At the BRICS Summit, Kazakhstan could propose preparing a pilot container shipment involving Indian, Iranian, Turkmen and Kazakh operators. Such a project could help identify actual transit times, tariffs and bottlenecks at each stage of the route,” he said.

At the same time, Azerbaijan, Georgia and Türkiye remain essential to the Trans-Caspian route, meaning key decisions on its operation would need to be coordinated outside the BRICS framework.

“Payments, insurance, sanctions risks around Iran and the number of transshipment points will remain important constraints. Therefore, BRICS can bring together interested parties, but the commercial viability of the route must ultimately be confirmed by carriers and shippers,” Kurmashev said.

World.title: Foreign Media on Kazakhstan’s Economic Transformation, AIFC and Rybakina’s Rise to World No. 1
World.content:
ASTANA — The Astana Times has selected articles from global media outlets covering Kazakhstan. This week’s foreign media digest highlights the country’s economic and financial development, sovereign wealth strategy and global ambitions, alongside Elena Rybakina’s historic rise to world No. 1.

Elena Rybakina becomes world No. 1 for first time after U.S. Open win over Zheng Qinwen

Women’s tennis has a new world No. 1. Elena Rybakina took the top spot from Aryna Sabalenka on Wednesday at the U.S. Open with a quarterfinal win over China’s Zheng Qinwen, 3-6, 6-1, 6-4. It is her first time at the summit of women’s tennis, reported The New York Times on Sept. 9.

“It’s a great achievement, and I feel like you will appreciate and think about it even more when you finish your career,” Rybakina said in a news conference, when asked about the milestone.

Kazakhstan’s AIFC says other countries are seeking to replicate its model

Kazakhstan’s financial hub says its model is attracting interest abroad as competition between financial centres intensifies, while limited market liquidity remains a key challenge, reported Euronews on Sept. 9.

For two days, Astana Finance Days 2026 brought together representatives of global financial institutions that collectively manage more than $26 trillion in assets, as Kazakhstan seeks to strengthen its position in the global competition for capital.

How Kazakhstan’s economic reforms have turned the tenge into the best-performing currency in Europe and Asia

EU Reporter published an article on Sept. 7 examining the tenge’s strong performance in 2026 and highlights Kazakhstan’s accelerating economic transformation, driven by foreign investment, diversification, digitalization, infrastructure development, and the expansion of its financial and technology sectors.

“The Kazakhstani tenge has become the best-performing currency in Asia and Europe in 2026, according to the Financial Times. Since the beginning of the year, it has appreciated by nearly 10% against the US dollar, outperforming all other currencies worldwide except for several currencies of Latin American and African countries. This performance has been underpinned by economic growth driven by the transformation of Kazakhstan’s economic model. The country is rapidly evolving from a commodity-based economy into a financial and technology hub for Central Asia, amid growing inflows of foreign capital,” reads the article.

Erlan Karin’s appointment links reform and national identity

The Times of Central Asia published an article on Sept. 1 about Erlan Karin’s appointment as Vice President of Kazakhstan.

“When President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev put forward Erlan Karin for vice president on Aug. 31, he called him ‘a genuine patriot’ with long experience in government. He also stressed Karin’s part in implementing major reforms, his grasp of long-term state strategy and his understanding of Kazakhstan’s prospects for socioeconomic development.

Karin has spent seven years in senior posts under Tokayev. He also has a sustained interest in a question that runs through the president’s agenda — how Kazakhstan can modernize while remaining connected to its own history and national identity,” reads the article.

From oil reserves to infrastructure: How Kazakhstan invests in future generations

EU Reporter released an article on Sept. 8 examining how Kazakhstan can transform part of its sovereign wealth from financial savings into long-term national capital by investing in infrastructure, healthcare, education, and other assets that can generate lasting economic and social benefits for future generations.

“Savings from the National Fund are already being utilized directly in the interests of future generations. Since 2024, Kazakhstan has operated the National Fund for Children program: every young citizen of Kazakhstan is annually allocated a portion of the fund’s investment income, and upon reaching 18 years of age, the accumulated funds can be used for education or housing improvement. This program has already entered the phase of practical asset utilization. Between February 2024 and Aug. 1, payouts were received by more than 338,000 young Kazakhstanis, totaling approximately $67.8 million. Meanwhile, the funds belonging to minors remain within the National Fund’s assets and continue to be invested until they reach adulthood,” reads the article.

Almaty and Astana set to retain Central Asia’s economic lead

Almaty and Astana are likely to retain their position as Central Asia’s leading economic centers, even as Tashkent and Bishkek record rapid growth and invest heavily in their future expansion. Kazakhstan’s two largest cities benefit from an economic scale, financial infrastructure and established business ecosystems that have been built up over decades, reported the Times of Central Asia on Sept. 7.

“Almaty and Astana benefit from an economic scale unmatched elsewhere in Central Asia. Kazakhstan alone accounts for more than half of the region’s GDP and roughly two-thirds of its inward FDI stock, according to TCA’s Central Asia Balance Sheet. That scale helps generate the fiscal resources needed to build and maintain the municipal infrastructure that supports business activity,” reads the article.

World.title: Kazakhstan Looks to New Players and Products to Drive Next Phase of Digital Finance, NBK Governor Says
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan has built the core digital infrastructure for its financial sector and is now entering a new stage focused on developing new products, attracting new market participants and creating innovative business models, National Bank Governor Timur Suleimenov said at the Central Asia Fintech Summit 2026 in Almaty on Sept. 11.

Speaking at the opening of the third annual summit, Suleimenov said Kazakhstan’s financial sector has already reached a high level of digitalization, with more than 90% of payments made without cash and most basic banking and government services available through digital platforms.

The summit, held on Sept. 11, brings together regulators, financial institutions, technology companies and experts to discuss the future of financial markets, digital currencies, artificial intelligence, digital assets, cybersecurity and other areas of fintech.

Suleimenov said the National Bank’s approach has evolved from simply digitizing its own operations to actively encouraging innovation across the financial market.

“We decided to change the approach altogether – instead of being the one who is pushed, to become the one who pushes the market,” he said, describing the regulator’s role as creating a “push” for the market and encouraging participants to move faster.

Kazakhstan builds digital financial infrastructure

Kazakhstan has established a national digital financial infrastructure. It includes biometric identification, interbank payments, the digital tenge and mechanisms designed to protect citizens and businesses from financial fraud.

The infrastructure has been expanded through successive stages, with the digital tenge entering industrial use in 2023, the National Anti-Fraud Center launched in 2024 and new interbank and QR payment infrastructure introduced subsequently.

The digital tenge is gradually being integrated into government financial processes, including public procurement, budget planning and the management of state funds. Suleimenov said the National Bank, together with the government, intends to increase the volume of digital-tenge operations to 2 trillion tenge (US$4.4 billion) over the next 12 months.

Suleimenov pointed to the interbank mobile payment system launched this year as one of the latest developments. The system includes transfers by phone number and a unified QR code. Since its launch on July 19, it has processed more than 20 million transactions worth around 400 billion tenge (US$888 million), according to the National Bank.

He described the high level of digitalization as a major achievement, noting that in many countries reaching 50–60% of non-cash turnover remains a challenge.

From infrastructure to products

The next challenge, Suleimenov said, is no longer primarily about building the technological “rails” of the financial system but about using them to create products that meet the needs of businesses and consumers.

During the opening plenary, moderator Vitaliy Volyanyuk, co-founder and CEO of Digital Business, asked Suleimenov to assess what the measures introduced by the NBK and other regulators had actually delivered and how Kazakhstan’s financial sector looks today.

Suleimenov described the sector as bank-centered but increasingly diverse, with the domestic financial system, the Astana International Financial Center and emerging digital-finance initiatives creating complementary opportunities.

“Briefly, the system is strong, highly capitalized and digitalized, and it has a huge future,” he said.

But Suleimenov stressed that infrastructure alone would not be enough.

“The second step is, of course, financial infrastructure, on which these solutions have to run. We are also creating that. But now, probably, the main step is creating products,” he said.

“We cannot and will not create the products ourselves,” he added, calling on banks, traditional financial institutions and new financial companies to work both together and in competition to develop new products and business models. The objective, he said, is to make access to financing, payments and cross-border transactions easier for both businesses and individuals.

Digital maturity remains uneven

The transformation, however, is not taking place at the same pace across the entire financial sector, Chair of the Agency for Regulation and Development of the Financial Market Madina Abylkassymova said during the summit.

Volyanyuk also asked about the readiness of smaller banks, insurance companies and other financial institutions for digital and AI transformation, rather than focusing only on the largest banks with significant technological and financial resources.

Abylkassymova said the agency had assessed the digital readiness of 94 financial organizations this year, examining process digitalization, data quality, infrastructure, cybersecurity, AI use and employee competencies.

“Banks remain the leaders, with almost 75% already using artificial intelligence. However, a gap remains between banks and other parts of the financial sector, particularly insurance and microfinance,” she said, stressing that digital transformation is not simply about introducing technology.

“It is also about the competencies of employees,” Abylkassymova added, arguing that digital and AI tools need to be embedded into the actual processes of financial organizations.

According to her, the agency is now developing a strategy for large-scale digitalization and further AI adoption across the financial sector. It has identified 1,200 specific measures and prepared individual development plans for the 94 organizations assessed.

Kazakhstan looks to export financial services

Suleimenov identified exporting Kazakhstan’s financial industry as another strategic priority. This includes helping domestic financial companies enter foreign markets and attracting international players that can serve global customers through Kazakhstan’s jurisdiction and financial infrastructure.

He said the country has a strong domestic financial jurisdiction alongside the Astana International Financial Center, which he described as an additional driver of competition and investment.

The next stage, however, will depend on whether market participants can turn the established infrastructure and regulatory framework into products that can compete both domestically and internationally.

“We have a strong foundation, but now we need the market to become more active – with new products, partnerships and business models that will allow us to fully use these opportunities,” Suleimenov said.

The Central Asia Fintech Summit 2026 brings together more than 120 speakers and experts. It focuses on the development of digital finance, including payments, digital assets, AI, cybersecurity, tokenization and anti-fraud technologies.

World.title: Kazakhstan Highlights Middle Corridor Growth and Digitalization at Batumi Forum
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan highlighted the rapid growth of the Middle Corridor and the need to accelerate its digitalization at the Georgian International Maritime Forum in Batumi on Sept. 7-8.

Kazakhstan Deputy Minister of Transport Zhanibek Taizhanov said freight volumes along the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR) rose 22% in January-August, while East-West transit increased 55%.

Digitalization drives seamless transit

Speaking at the panel session From Seas to Corridors: The New Geography of Global Trade, Taizhanov stressed the importance of integrating maritime, rail and port infrastructure to make international supply chains more efficient and resilient, the ministry’s press service reported.

He also presented President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s initiative to develop a digital map of transport routes, providing an integrated view of transport infrastructure, logistics chains and cargo flows along international corridors.

The Middle Corridor currently has a capacity of 6 million tons, including 182,000 TEUs. Measures to streamline logistics have reduced cargo delivery times from 38 days to 13-17 days, with a target of 10-12 days from China to ports in Georgia and Türkiye.

Kazakhstan is also advancing the Digital Trade Corridor, which enables online cargo tracking and single-window contracting. Its Tez Customs module has reduced transit customs processing from eight hours to 30 minutes, the ministry told The Astana Times.

Infrastructure expansion

The forum brought together government officials, maritime administrations, international organizations, port operators, logistics companies and industry experts.

Discussions covered port infrastructure, maritime cooperation, digital transformation, navigation and shipping safety, and applying the single-window principle in the maritime sector.

Discussions on the Middle Corridor also highlighted the need for further infrastructure investment. Speaking at the 5th International Forum on Freight Transport in the Black and Caspian Regions 2026 in Baku, World Bank Senior Transport and Logistics Specialist Luis Blancas said a new comprehensive report on the Middle Corridor is scheduled for publication on Sept. 27, Trend reported.

The report covers all nine participating countries and identifies 16 critical investment priorities worth around US$25 billion. More than three-quarters of the required investment is already underway, Blancas said.

The report is expected to provide a broader assessment of infrastructure needs as cargo flows between Asia and Europe continue to grow.

World.title: “Arresting a person in Georgia over their views on a 34-year-old war is a legal absurdity” – opinion
World.content:
Opinion on Giorgi Baramidze’s arrest

“Arresting someone over an opinion expressed in a historical programme about a 34-year-old war — especially when he has since apologised for the statement — is a legal absurdity,” said Tamta Mikeladze, director of the Social Justice Center, commenting on the arrest of Georgian opposition leader and former defence minister Giorgi Baramidze.

On 11 September, Giorgi Baramidze was arrested on charges of treason against the state, specifically sabotage. His arrest followed an interview on the programme “Birth of Georgia”, in which he said that at the beginning of the 1992–93 Georgian-Abkhaz war, the Georgian side had no prisoners because they were “shot”.

Tamta Mikeladze: “Arresting someone over an opinion expressed in a historical programme about a 34-year-old war — especially when he has since apologised for the statement — is a legal absurdity.

The prosecutor’s argument that the statement damaged Georgia’s international standing and image, offended the honour of war veterans and so on has no basis in criminal law. If specific individuals believed Baramidze had defamed them, they could have taken him to court in a civil case.

Claims that the statement could be used in international legal proceedings are also unfounded. There are no international legal proceedings concerning the war in Abkhazia, and Baramidze was not a decision-maker at the time. His words therefore could not carry the kind of weight that would affect any legal consequences.

Arresting someone for expressing an opinion – even if that opinion is unfounded, foolish, offensive or unacceptable – is therefore an unimaginable departure from the rule of law.”

Mikeladze also examines the alleged offence in detail and points to a mismatch between the charge and the statement, arguing that no remarks of this kind can legally constitute sabotage.

News in Georgia

World.title: One of Georgia’s opposition leaders, Giorgi Baramidze, detained on “treason and sabotage” charges
World.content:
Opposition figure Baramidze arrested in Georgia

Giorgi Baramidze, one of the leaders of the opposition United National Movement and Georgian former defence and interior minister, has been detained in Georgia.

Prosecutors searched his home before handcuffing him.

The detention stems from an interview Baramidze gave on the programme “Birth of Georgia”, in which he said that at the beginning of the 1992–93 Georgian-Abkhaz war, the Georgian side had no prisoners of war because they were “shot”.

On 7 August, the prosecutor’s office said it had opened an investigation into “treason against the state and sabotage” over the statement.

As of today, five former Georgian defence ministers are (!) in prison, while a sixth is facing criminal charges.

Giorgi Baramidze is now the seventh on the list.

What the prosecutor’s office says

Deputy Prosecutor General Amiran Guluashvili confirmed that Giorgi Baramidze was detained on charges of treason against the state, specifically sabotage. The charge carries a prison sentence of up to four years.

Giorgi Baramidze, one of the leaders of the opposition United National Movement and Georgian former defence and interior minister

The prosecutor’s office says its investigation found no evidence that prisoners of war were executed by Georgian armed forces or other participants in the conflict. It therefore described Baramidze’s claim as “baseless and fabricated” and said it was part of a targeted information campaign.
