According to the prosecutor’s office, Baramidze’s statement could damage Georgia’s international image, the reputation of its defence forces and the dignity of those who took part in the war. It could also undermine efforts to reconcile with communities affected by the conflict and rebuild trust.

The prosecutor’s office says Baramidze’s remarks harmed Georgia’s peace and de-occupation policy and obstructed the work of state agencies, including the Office of the State Minister for Reconciliation and Civic Equality, which is working to restore trust and cooperation.

The prosecutor’s office will ask the court to remand Baramidze in custody. The investigation is ongoing.

What Giorgi Baramidze said

During the programme “Birth of Georgia”, Giorgi Baramidze recalled the exchange of prisoners during the Georgian-Abkhaz war and said: “We had no prisoners. Our side did not take prisoners — they were shot.”

Baramidze’s statement drew a strong reaction from government officials. He later explained several times what he had meant.

He said he was referring to the very beginning of the war, when the Georgian side still had no regular, organised army and some fighters, driven by grief after losing loved ones in the fighting, sometimes did not take enemy combatants prisoner.

“During the first period, this was the situation: people whose mothers, fathers or other loved ones had been killed were so consumed by anger that they did not take prisoners during fighting and killed them instead. They had been driven to despair. This is the bitter truth about the early stage of the war, which I know because I was personally involved in prisoner exchanges,” Baramidze explained.

He said the situation later changed, with the Georgian side beginning to take prisoners, making prisoner exchanges possible.

Baramidze also says he was personally involved in the process, which ultimately helped secure the return of around 200 Georgian prisoners.

News in Georgia

World.title: Live from Gyumri, Armenia, in photos and videos
World.content:
Gyumri, Armenia, photos and video

Gyumri is the second-largest city in Armenia after Yerevan. The video was filmed during a journey from Georgia to Armenia, and the story follows this route.

As soon as you cross the Georgian border and enter Armenia, the road becomes mountainous. The plains and forest-covered mountains gradually give way to rocky slopes.

The road runs across the Ashotzk Plateau along the Akhuryan River gorge and around the Shirak Range. This is where Gyumri lies, at an altitude of more than 1,500 metres above sea level.

The air is noticeably cooler here, which is why both tourists and residents of the capital come here in summer.

Locals are particularly proud of their drinking water. It comes from mountain springs and is exceptionally cold and delicious.

Small drinking fountains can be found throughout the city. Locals call them “pulpulak”. They attract attention partly because of their distinctive designs, with no two fountains looking quite alike.

They are usually built from local stone — tuff or basalt — and decorated with national ornaments, crosses and various symbols.

There is also a tradition of building pulpulaks in memory of deceased loved ones.

A defining feature of Gyumri is its black stone. Almost all the city’s old buildings are made from local volcanic tuff.

Drinking fountain in Gyumri, Armenia. JAMnews photo.

In the city centre lies Vardanants Square. It was named in memory of the battle between the Armenian army, led by commander Vardan Mamikonian, and the Persian army in 450–451.

Vardanants Square in Gyumri, Armenia. JAMnews photo.

Churches of Gyumri

On either side of the square stand two churches: the Church of the Holy Mother of God, also known as the Church of the “Seven Wounds”, and the Church of the Holy Saviour.

The Church of the Holy Mother of God holds a special place in Gyumri’s history. During the Soviet period, when most churches in the city were closed and converted into warehouses or museums, the “Seven Wounds” Church remained one of the few still operating. It became a centre that preserved church traditions and a symbol of believers’ resistance.

Symbolically, the church courtyard contains a brass cross riddled with bullet holes. It commemorates the clergy who continued their service and supported believers during Stalin’s anti-religious campaign. Dozens of members of the Shirak Diocese clergy were arrested and executed.

Today, the bullet holes in the cross are clearly visible even from a distance. The names of clergy members who died during those years are engraved on its lower section.

On 7 December 1988, an earthquake almost destroyed the city in just 30 seconds.

The entire northern part of Armenia was affected. More than 27,000 people died, and 750,000 were left homeless.

A huge fragment of stone broke off the Church of the Holy Saviour in Gyumri during the earthquake. They left it lying beside the church. According to local residents, it serves as a reminder of that terrible day.

A bronze memorial, “To the Innocent Victims, the Compassionate Hearts”, was built nearby. The inscription appears on the monument in three languages: Armenian, Russian and English.

It depicts figures emerging from the rubble and helping one another.

The scale of the destruction clearly showed the difference in quality between older buildings and structures from the Soviet period.

Low-rise buildings in Gyumri made from traditional black tuff. JAMnews photo.

One- and two-storey buildings dating from before the Soviet era proved more resilient, while high-rise buildings constructed in the 1970s and 1980s were completely destroyed.

The tragedy fundamentally changed the city’s future development strategy. Based on the findings of seismologists and architects, Gyumri banned the construction of high-rise residential buildings.

The city returned to its historic style: low-rise, sturdy buildings made from local black and orange tuff.

Tourists often explore the city in these horse-drawn carriages, which are popular in Gyumri. JAMnews photo.

Gyumri, Armenia, photos and video

World.title: Armenian citizenship to become harder and five times more expensive under Interior Ministry draft
World.content:
New requirements for obtaining Armenian citizenship

The procedure for obtaining Armenian citizenship could change. If parliament approves the draft, obtaining citizenship will become not only more difficult but also more expensive.

The Interior Ministry proposes increasing the state fee for obtaining Armenian citizenship fivefold and the fee for renouncing it tenfold. Applicants will have to pay 250,000 drams ($690) to obtain Armenian citizenship and 1.5 million drams ($4,143) to renounce it.

The ministry has already published its draft on the electronic platform where legal acts are made available for public discussion.

The authorities justify the proposed changes by the need to “rethink” the institution of citizenship:

“In recent years, the number of people without a sufficient factual connection to Armenia has increased. These are people who have never visited the country or lived there for a significant period, but obtained Armenian citizenship for practical benefits, including when planning trips.”

The package of amendments includes not only changes to the state fees but also procedural changes. The government expects the amendments to take effect on 1 January 2028.

Between 1 January 2021 and 31 August 2026, 110,219 people obtained Armenian citizenship. Over the past 15 years, 250,000 people have obtained Armenian citizenship. Most of the new citizens did not live in the country permanently.

Those who renounce Armenian citizenship will not be able to regain it for five years

Applications to obtain or renounce Armenian citizenship will be submitted electronically. If necessary, applicants will then be able to schedule an appointment and submit their documents in person.

Under the new procedure, applicants must have legally resided in Armenia for the past five years to qualify for citizenship. They must also have spent at least 915 days in the country during that period.

Ethnic Armenians will face less stringent requirements. They will need to have legally resided in Armenia for the past two years and spent at least 366 days in the country.

A special commission within the Interior Ministry will verify ethnic background. Applicants will have to provide the relevant documents and archival records. The commission may also request certificates from religious or community organisations.

“People who have previously renounced their citizenship may apply to restore it only after five years have passed. They must also have lived in Armenia for at least 366 days during the two years preceding their application,” the draft’s explanatory note says.

Under the current legislation, people who have renounced Armenian citizenship can restore it without observing a minimum waiting period.

A presidential decree granting citizenship will take effect within one year of the applicant signing the oath. From now on, applicants will be able to take the oath only on the territory of Armenia.

If the authorities deny citizenship on grounds related to threats to national security or public order, the president’s decision cannot be challenged or changed through administrative or judicial proceedings.

The project aims to strengthen the standing and stability of the institution of citizenship

The authors of the bill say they have identified numerous applications to restore citizenship shortly after applicants renounced it. They cite the example of a parent who renounces citizenship to terminate their sons’ Armenian citizenship, allowing them to avoid compulsory military service.

The same person may then seek to restore their citizenship and regain the relevant rights and privileges. The amendments would make this impossible.

The authors justify the five-year restriction by arguing that the restoration of citizenship must not become a “situational mechanism”:

“Citizenship is not merely a formal legal status, but a long-term legal and political bond between the state and the individual.”

According to the drafters, the five-year restriction will promote:

“the stability of the institution of citizenship;

preventing its use for opportunistic purposes;

viewing citizenship as a long-term bond with the state”.

They stress that restrictions on restoring citizenship also apply in the Scandinavian countries, as well as in Germany, France and the United Kingdom.

Specialised commission to verify Armenian ancestry

The draft says that the system for making decisions on citizenship matters will also change. In particular, the interagency commission that reviews applications for the granting or termination of citizenship will be abolished.

The Interior Ministry considers that the commission’s work provides little practical benefit. It has almost never reviewed negative decisions or changed the administrative body’s preliminary position.

A specialised commission will be established in its place. Its task will be to verify applicants’ ethnicity, including their Armenian ancestry.

Until now, the authorities have based the verification of ethnicity solely on the availability of certain documents.

However, the Interior Ministry has concluded that applicants’ documents do not always provide a reliable basis for confirming Armenian ancestry. There have been cases in which people submitted forged or altered documents to take advantage of the simplified citizenship procedure available to ethnic Armenians.

According to the ministry, more than 70 such cases were identified between 2023 and 2026. The number of such incidents has also tended to increase each year.

“There were five such cases in 2023, 21 in 2024, 26 in 2025, and 19 in the first half of 2026 alone,” the Interior Ministry reports.

New requirements for obtaining Armenian citizenship

World.title: EPRC: Wildberries expansion poses significant risks for Georgia
World.content:
According to the Economic Policy Research Center (EPRC), the expansion of the Russian online platform Wildberries in Georgia poses significant risks for the country.

The centre makes this assessment in a new report examining the threats that Wildberries-related activities could pose to Georgian brands represented on the platform, consumers, Georgian banks and Georgia’s economic and financial system as a whole.

Wildberries is an online marketplace often described as “Russia’s Amazon”.

According to EPRC, at least eight Wildberries warehouses were put out of operation by Ukrainian strikes in late August 2026, while more than 20 facilities were damaged. During the same period, part of the company’s financial ecosystem, Wildberries Bank, was placed under international sanctions.

The centre says that, while Wildberries’ warehouse infrastructure in Russia became a target for Ukrainian drones and the company’s banking arm was placed on a sanctions list, Wildberries used Georgia and other neighbouring countries to expand its trading network and logistics capabilities.

EPRC predicts that, as a result, Georgia could become part of a regional infrastructure helping a company linked to the Kremlin and sanctioned Russian businesses reduce losses caused by the war and sanctions.

The report notes that Wildberries’ official infrastructure in Georgia includes warehouses, sorting centres and collection points. According to the company’s instructions, updated on 4 June 2026, Georgian sellers can choose a warehouse or sorting centre and review the conditions for accepting products, logistics rates, sorting times and delivery times to consumers.

According to EPRC, this indicates that the company’s activities in Georgia are no longer limited to collection points. Local infrastructure is also being used to receive, sort and subsequently deliver products. However, open sources do not currently confirm the existence of a large logistics centre in Georgia. A similar situation exists in Azerbaijan.

According to the report, information spread in September 2025 that local businesses had been given the opportunity to sell their products directly through the Wildberries platform.

EPRC also publishes what it believes is an incomplete list of Georgian brands available on the platform. The centre explains that finding a complete list is difficult because Wildberries does not allow users to search for brands by country of origin.

At this stage, the list of Georgian products and brands on the platform is believed to include Borjomi, Nabeghlavi, Natakhtari, Zedazeni, Gurieli, Kula, Badagoni, Chateau Mukhrani, Askaneli, Sarajishvili, MACH & MACH, ANOUKI and Aleksandre Akhalkatsishvili.

EPRC stresses that Wildberries operates as a marketplace. The presence of a particular product on the platform does not automatically mean that the manufacturer or an official brand representative is selling it directly. The product may be listed either by the manufacturer or by an independent reseller.

According to the centre, if an independent retailer sells the product, the brand may restrict those sales by protecting its intellectual property or using contractual mechanisms.

In EPRC’s assessment, Wildberries’ expansion in Georgia is no longer solely a matter of developing online trade. The centre identifies several major risks.

In particular, the report says Wildberries is linked to Russia’s trading and financial system, and its ties to the Kremlin have also been confirmed. The company’s financial arm, Wildberries Bank, has been placed under UK and EU sanctions. According to EPRC, the sanctions are linked to the bank’s role in financially supporting the military and the Russian authorities’ aggressive interests.

The centre also says the Wildberries platform is used to purchase goods needed by the Russian military, including military equipment and dual-use goods. According to EPRC, independent journalistic investigations have also confirmed this.

Against this backdrop, the report’s authors question the effectiveness of controls over the trade and export of such products in Georgia. In their assessment, this increases the risk that sanctioned goods or dual-use items could enter or be re-exported through the country.

EPRC pays particular attention to the development of Wildberries’ logistics capabilities in Georgia. The centre believes that, after a significant part of the company’s warehouse network in Russia was damaged, infrastructure outside Russia has become even more important to Wildberries. Georgia could therefore become part of the company’s regional diversification network.

The report also describes the growing integration of Georgian businesses into the Wildberries system. Products from Georgian brands are already sold on the platform, and Georgian entrepreneurs can join it as direct sellers. EPRC believes this creates both reputational and potential financial risks for companies in the future.

According to the centre, Georgia’s financial sector is also at risk. Wildberries Bank came under UK and EU sanctions in 2026, while 5% of the bank is also owned by the sanctioned Russian bank VTB.

EPRC says that the fact that customers in Georgia pay for purchases on Wildberries using Georgian bank cards means that the local banking sector must comply with the sanctions regime and carry out additional transaction checks. According to the centre, after sanctions were imposed on Wildberries Bank, the National Bank of Georgia shifted responsibility to individual financial institutions, explaining that each bank must assess the risks of violating or circumventing sanctions independently.

In EPRC’s assessment, given these circumstances, the development in Georgia of infrastructure linked to a sanctioned financial institution, a business close to the Kremlin and a platform used to supply the Russian military cannot simply be viewed as foreign investment or the expansion of retail trade.

The centre suggests that if Wildberries continues to expand in Georgia without state oversight or proper customs and financial monitoring, and Georgian companies and banks deepen their cooperation with the platform, the country could become part of an economic and logistics network that helps Russian businesses continue operating amid war and international sanctions.

EPRC believes that such a process could have long-term economic and reputational consequences for Georgia.

EPRC on the risks posed by Wildberries in Georgia

World.title: Georgian Legion commander on former prosecutor general: ‘He is following directives from Russian intelligence services’
World.content:
According to a statement by Mamuka Mamulashvili, commander of the pro-Ukrainian Georgian Legion, former Georgian prosecutor general Otar Partskhaladze, who recently took command of a unit fighting on Russia’s side, is following directives from Russian intelligence services. Mamulashvili also said Partskhaladze’s value as a military figure was zero.

The Georgian Legion is a volunteer formation established in 2014 after Russia invaded eastern Ukraine. In 2016, the Georgian Legion officially joined Ukraine’s 25th Motorised Infantry Battalion. It is now subordinate to the Main Directorate of Intelligence of Ukraine’s Defence Ministry. The unit includes Georgian volunteers as well as fighters of other nationalities. It currently has around 2,000 members. In 2023, Russia’s Interior Ministry added Georgian Legion commander Mamuka Mamulashvili to its wanted list.

According to Mamulashvili, Otar Partskhaladze will try to draw ethnic Georgians living in Russia into his adventure — the war against Ukraine. However, his chances of success are doubtful, as very few Georgians fighting on Russia’s side are seen on the front line, and most of them have already been killed.

Former Georgian prosecutor general Otar Romanov-Partskhaladze, who is fighting on Russia’s side, told Russian pro-Kremlin media that members of the Georgian Legion are “war criminals” and will face prosecution under Russian law. Earlier, on 7 September, it became known that Partskhaladze would lead the international “St George” unit, which was created to take part in the war against Ukraine.

Mamuka Mamulashvili: “Partskhaladze will get a response. He will realise that he made a serious mistake by launching a campaign against the Georgian Legion.

No unit, not even Ukrainian ones, has faced the kind of pressure the Georgian Legion has endured. We are one of the oldest units, even compared with Ukrainian volunteer formations. Russia does not like the fact that so many Georgians are fighting on Ukraine’s side. That is why Russia has been fighting us for more than 12 years, both informationally and physically.

Since they failed to destroy the Georgian Legion physically, they have now tried to create a counterweight by forming another Georgian unit that supposedly will fight on Russia’s side. In reality, this is an attempt to discredit Georgia and bring it under the same sanctions that Russia faces. To do this, they are using people with Georgian surnames who live in Russia and who make all sorts of absurd claims that the Georgian Legion should be tried under Russian law.

In 2022, Russia designated the Georgian Legion as a terrorist organisation. This is hardly surprising, as the Georgian Legion has inflicted enormous damage on the Russian Federation. We can see that their disinformation machine has become much more active. Attempts to kill us physically and attacks have also increased. I have personally been attacked seven times and have survived three attempts to poison me.

Partskhaladze is following directives from Russian intelligence services because his own value as a military figure is zero. I doubt that this man knows which end of a weapon fires. Most likely, he was ordered to finance and create another battalion. He will then try to draw people with Georgian surnames who live in Russia into this adventure. I do not know how successful he will be, because over these 12 years I have encountered very few Georgians on the front line — and those I did encounter were already dead.

The battalion will most likely consist of Russians, with a few Georgian-speaking people who will claim that the unit is mainly made up of Georgians.”

Commander of the Georgian Legion on former prosecutor general

World.title: Mzia Amaglobeli: ‘All it takes to avoid asking the regime for pardon is self-respect’
World.content:
“I don’t need advice to avoid apologising to an aggressor or asking the regime for a pardon. A sense of self-respect is enough,” political prisoner Mzia Amaglobeli writes in response to a statement by Shalva Papuashvili, speaker of the parliament of Georgia. At a briefing on 9 September, Papuashvili called prisoners of conscience “prisoners of Brussels’ shamelessness”.

The publication Batumelebi published Amaglobeli’s letter.

Mzia Amaglobeli: “The briefing in parliament was a display of shamelessness and nothing else. The regime has no morals. They do not even want to take responsibility for the unjust verdict that, in the name of Georgia, sent us to prison and branded us dangerous criminals.

They point the finger at Brussels and European diplomats. Shame on them. I don’t need advice to avoid apologising to an aggressor or asking the regime for a pardon. A sense of self-respect is enough.

If two years in prison is not humiliating enough, it will not be difficult for you to come up with something else if you want to keep me behind bars.

Power and state institutions are in your hands.

As for me, I will wait for international justice. I will wait for the day when the European Court of Human Rights examines the legality of the charges against me and the sentence imposed on me for slapping someone.

And you wait too, Mr Papuashvili. The European Court will examine the fairness and legitimacy of the repressive laws you have adopted, as well as their compliance with the Constitution and democratic processes.”

What Shalva Papuashvili said

On 9 September, commenting on the situation of political prisoners and prisoners of conscience, Shalva Papuashvili said they were “prisoners of Brussels’ shamelessness”. Papuashvili also spoke specifically about convicted journalist Mzia Amaglobeli, claiming that the court had given her the lightest possible sentence.

“Under Georgia’s Criminal Procedure Code, a lesser sentence is possible only through a plea agreement. That is what both the law and practice provide. A plea agreement was offered to her. It required only one thing: for Mzia Amaglobeli to acknowledge that what she had done was a crime and that her conduct had been wrong.

Mzia Amaglobeli is a prisoner of the shamelessness of those ambassadors who sat in court, looked her in the eye and effectively told her: ‘Do not plead guilty. Stay in prison.’ It is also the fault of those who awarded her completely unjustified prizes, including the European Parliament, thereby encouraging her not to admit that attacking a police officer is a crime,” Papuashvili said.

Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the well-known publications Batumelebi and Netgazeti, is the first female journalist in Georgia to become a prisoner of conscience.

Authorities arrested her in January 2025 in the city of Batumi during a protest after she slapped the head of the local police, Irakli Dgebuadze. The incident followed a confrontation between protesters and police, which the officers had provoked.

On 6 August 2025, Batumi City Court sentenced Mzia Amaglobeli to two years in prison. The court rejected her lawyer’s request to change her pre-trial measure.

Mzia Amaglobeli responds to the speaker of parliament

World.title: Armenia’s Anti-Corruption Commission did not open proceedings against Pashinyan
World.content:
Commission rejects case against Pashinyan

The Corruption Prevention Commission refused to open administrative proceedings against Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan. Commission members said the complaint contained no “obvious signs of violations of the code of conduct”.

Semyon Babayan, head of the human rights NGO Public Informant, had asked the commission to assess the prime minister’s alleged “violations of the code of conduct”.

“Pashinyan’s public rhetoric and the wording he often uses grossly violate the legally established integrity system and the ethical standards that public officials must follow,” the applicant said.

He presented the commission with 11 such examples. One of them was the word “immoral”, which the prime minister used to describe the Catholicos of All Armenians.

According to the human rights activist, “it insults the feelings of believers and violates the requirement for religious neutrality”.

However, the commission found that the wording remained within the permissible limits of freedom of expression.

For a long time, Nikol Pashinyan has demanded that Catholicos of All Armenians Garegin II step down. He claims that the Catholicos has broken his vow of celibacy and has a daughter. The prime minister also believes that the Catholicos has links to foreign intelligence services and follows their orders. On 24 August, Nikol Pashinyan called the Catholicos “immoral” while speaking in parliament. He also referred to the Patriarch by his secular name, Ktrich Nersisyan. He has used this name for him since launching his campaign to reform the Church. In protest, opposition MPs banged on their desks every time the Catholicos’s name was mentioned. “Your Catholicos is immoral. If you are not bothered by the fact that the man who heads the Mother See is sexually active, then keep banging your desks as much as you like. There is no other way to have a child — even in the Church. There is only one way to have a child: sexual intercourse,” Pashinyan said.

Commission says the word “immoral” falls within the bounds of political speech

The commission commented on the use of the word “immoral” against the Catholicos, citing case law from the European Court of Human Rights. It stressed that political speech enjoys a broader scope of protection.

Commission members assessed the prime minister’s wording as falling within what is permissible in the context of political debate:

“The use of exaggeration, generalisations and even shocking or striking expressions is characteristic of political speech during political debates — in this case, a speech delivered from the parliamentary rostrum.”

They also noted that, according to the European Court of Human Rights, freedom of expression covers not only positive and favourable statements, but also those that may “offend, shock or disturb”.

The Corruption Prevention Commission therefore concluded that the prime minister’s statement should be considered in the broader context of political debate.

The decision also gives the meaning of the Armenian word “պիղծ”, which Pashinyan used, citing academician Eduard Aghayan’s Explanatory Dictionary of the Modern Armenian Language. It notes that the word primarily means “unclean, immoral, vicious”, while in a religious context it means “heretical, unacceptable, ungodly”.

As for the statement “your Patriarch is immoral”, commission members found no attack on the faith or a religious group. In their view, Pashinyan made an “assessment of the alleged conduct” of a specific member of the clergy:

“Pashinyan’s statement sought to criticise not the person, but a specific phenomenon — namely, the alleged violation of the vow of celibacy.”

The commission also stressed that the word “immoral” carries a negative connotation but “does not cross the line into vulgarity or profanity”. Its members also found no calls for violence or threats in Pashinyan’s speech.

According to the decision, the prime minister’s speech was “predominantly critical in nature, as is characteristic of political debate”.

What other violations did the human rights activist identify?

Semyon Babayan also told the commission about 10 other “serious violations” that he believes the prime minister had committed:

“Violation of the principle of separation of powers: a public statement that ‘there is no judge who would not do what I tell them to do’, which directly undermines the independence of the judiciary and trust in democratic institutions.

Use of offensive language: using crude, street-level rhetoric in public against opponents or citizens — conduct that is clearly incompatible with the ethics expected of a senior public official.

Unsubstantiated assessments and ‘back-of-the-envelope estimates’: arbitrarily citing percentages related to corruption and bribery, such as 70% or 100%, without referring to official or verified factual data.

Erosion of public trust: using threats and divisive rhetoric from a high state platform, which contributes to the spread of intolerance.

Threats to ‘smear [people] across the asphalt’: publicly calling for the use of force in a personalised and punitive manner, outside the framework of legal procedures.

The phrase ‘whimpering judges’: humiliating members of the judiciary and systematically discrediting the institution.

Statements that citizens would be ‘brought to their knees’ because of their political views: entrenching a culture of communication based on force and a commanding tone that is unbecoming of a statesman.

Segregation of fellow citizens by labelling them ‘persons of Armenian origin’: violating the principle of national unity and artificially dividing society.

Showing preferential treatment towards members of his own team: violating the principle of equal integrity standards for the sake of political expediency.

Erosion of the integrity and image of a public official: maintaining a marginal, sarcastic and aggressive tone in public debate, undermining the duty of a public official to set an example of appropriate conduct.”

The commission found no signs of an obvious violation in any of the examples cited.

Commission rejects case against Pashinyan

World.title: Azerbaijani gymnasts win silver medal at World Championships (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 13. Azerbaijani gymnasts achieved a successful result at the World Aerobic Gymnastics Championships, held in the Spanish city of Pamplona from September 11 to 13, the Azerbaijan Gymnastics Federation said.

Representing Azerbaijan in the mixed pairs event, Madina Mustafayeva and Vladimir Dolmatov delivered a confident performance in the final and won the silver medal, finishing just 0.1 points behind the winners.

The Azerbaijani pair, who are European champions, scored 19.050 points in the qualification round to advance to the final. Based on the results of their final performance, the Azerbaijani gymnasts took second place on the podium.

More than 350 gymnasts from 38 countries competed in the prestigious event, which brought together the world’s top aerobic gymnasts.

World.title: Rhythmic gymnastics grace show concludes in Baku (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 13. From September 10 to 12, the Baku Olympic Sports Complex witnessed a combination of grace, agility and love for gymnastics, the Azerbaijan Gymnastics Federation said.

For three days, every moment in the arena was filled with a special atmosphere: the excitement of the young gymnasts stepping onto the big floor for the first time, the determination of junior gymnasts to perform every element flawlessly, and the fierce competition among young gymnasts who fought for medals until the very end.

Each performance reflected a unique aspiration, every movement embodied tremendous effort, and every medal told the story of a long journey. The gymnasts’ graceful movements on the floor, the harmony between the elements and the music, and their belief in victory created a special atmosphere at the Baku Olympic Sports Complex throughout the three days.

During the competition, spectators also showed great interest in the gymnasts’ performances. Fans who filled the stands watched the routines with keen interest and greeted successful performances with applause. The performances of the youngest gymnasts won particular sympathy from the audience, while the applause throughout the arena added to the dynamic and enjoyable atmosphere of the competition.

On the final day, the competition continued with performances by junior gymnasts. Junior gymnasts born in 2014–2015 competed in two groups in the one-apparatus program. This was followed by the award ceremony for the all-around winners in this age category.

Gymnasts in the youth category, born in 2011–2012, also demonstrated their skills in the one-apparatus program. The all-around winners in this category were presented with awards.

In the afternoon, the group exercise competitions got underway. The youngest participants, born in 2016–2018, performed with the ball, while the junior gymnasts, born in 2013–2015, performed with the ribbon. At the conclusion of the competitions, the all-around winners in both age categories were awarded.

Thus, the three-day competition featuring gymnasts from different age categories came to an end. The winners and medalists of the competition, which was marked by grace, agility and determination, took to the podium and received their medals at the Baku Olympic Sports Complex.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s trade turnover with BRICS members and partners reaches about $72 billion in 2025
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 13. President of Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said at the ongoing BRICS summit in New Delhi that Kazakhstan’s trade turnover with BRICS member states and partners reached about $72 billion in 2025.

“Possessing significant industrial, transit and technological potential, we intend to diversify our trade, economic and investment ties with all BRICS countries. As the chair of the Eurasian Economic Union, Kazakhstan advocates expanding economic cooperation with BRICS and advancing efforts to conclude a free trade agreement with India. As a reliable supplier of key raw materials, our country contributes to ensuring global supply security. We see significant opportunities for developing partnerships in deep processing in the energy sector, critical minerals and agriculture, with particular emphasis on technology transfer, knowledge exchange and joint investment. In addition, we have significant potential for jointly implementing large-scale infrastructure projects, including those of international importance. The New Development Bank could consider financing commercially viable projects in all BRICS countries, including Kazakhstan,” Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said.

The President of Kazakhstan said that strengthening transport connectivity would help unlock this potential and give impetus to overall economic growth.

“As one of Eurasia’s key transit and logistics hubs, Kazakhstan seeks to accelerate and make cross-border transportation more predictable by developing its railway network, ports and digital infrastructure. Last year, the volume of transit cargo transportation through Kazakhstan approached 40 million tons. Our long-term goal is to increase this figure to 100 million tons per year. Overall, our transit network already handles up to 85% of overland freight transportation between China and Europe. As part of the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, Kazakhstan serves as a link between Asia and Europe across the Caspian Sea. Further synergy between this key transport route, the Belt and Road Initiative and the North-South International Transport Corridor will help create a more integrated and resilient Eurasian transport network. In this regard, I welcome India’s proposed BRICS Framework Programme for Cooperation in Logistics and Supply Chains, as it could contribute to developing practical cooperation within the BRICS Plus framework,” Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said.

World.title: EU Special Representative makes post about visit to Azerbaijan
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 13. EU Special Representative for the South Caucasus and the crisis in Georgia Magdalena Grono has made a post on her X page about her visit to Azerbaijan.

"Concluded another series of regular consultations in Azerbaijan, where I met with Foreign Minister Bayramov, as well as with Presidential Advisers Hajiyev and Amirbayov in Baku on 10 September. We discussed EU's support to the Azerbaijan-Armenia bilateral peace process, including humanitarian aspects related to legacies of past conflict, as well as connectivity and regional co-operation efforts. On 11-12 September, I joined for the first time a visit organised by the Azerbaijani authorities for the diplomatic community to former conflict-affected areas in Karabakh and East Zangezur regions to get acquainted with the situation on the ground. We had the chance to engage with local authorities, former IDPs and media representatives. This visit also included various sites of cultural and religious heritage, such as mosques and churches. Deeply diverging views and narratives persist, for instance on origins of some sites and would need to be addressed between Azerbaijan and Armenia to also overcome this aspect of past conflict as part of their broader reconciliation efforts. Acknowledgement of outstanding legacies of past conflict and suffering on all sides would be paramount for this. Following exchanges with Azerbaijani counterparts, now looking forward to my upcoming meetings with Armenian officials and civil society representatives tomorrow in Yerevan," the post said.

World.title: Russian strike on Ukraine-Poland border shows war at Europe's 'doorstep'
World.content:
Fresh Russian strikes in close proximity to NATO sites have stoked fears among some European leaders that the war between Ukraine and Russia is spilling across borders.

A Russian attack on a truck near Ukraine's border with Poland was confirmed by Polish and Ukranian officials on Sunday.

The attack marks the latest strike to hit areas near NATO nations as Moscow and Kyiv intensify their long-distance strikes to try to shift momentum in the war.

A Russian drone struck near the Ukrainian-Polish border in the small town of Yahodyn, Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said, which is only 2km from Poland.

"Russia's barbaric strikes at the Ukraine-Poland border in Yahodyn are not just a continuation of its attacks on our state borders," Mr Sybiha said on X.

"This is Putin's terror 'knocking' directly on the doors of the EU and NATO. Russian barbarians are at your gate, dear partners," he added.

Polish border guards said that the Dorohusk-Yahodyn crossing point had briefly stopped working after the attack around 800 metres from Poland, but that the crossing had since resumed operations.

Fears the Russia-Ukraine war is expanding

Lithuania also briefly closed Vilnius airport on Sunday, local time, in response to a possible sighting of a drone, prompting NATO to summon at least one fighter jet, the National Crisis Management Centre said.

Lithuania later said the sighting turned out to be a flock of birds.

Russia resumes strikes on Kyiv after weekend ceasefire It came as Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin held an hour-long phone conversation about talks between their envoys in recent days.

The air alert was lifted and the airport reopened within 38 minutes, after the NATO jet made a visual identification, Lithuania's National Crisis Management Centre said.

"On initial radar readings, marks left by birds and drones can be similar," it added in a statement.

Military drones straying into the airspace of Finland, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania are stoking concerns that the war in Ukraine is spilling over into NATO's northern borders with Russia.

Transport sites near Ukraine-Poland border targeted

In a separate statement, Ukrainian Railways said that in Volyn — another region bordering Poland, — a drone attacked the locomotive of a passenger train just 2km from the Polish border.

The company said no-one was injured.

A passenger train in Lutsk was also hit in a Russian drone strike over the weekend. (Reuters: supplied )

Ukraine operates several border crossings with Poland, through which a significant proportion of the military and humanitarian aid from its allies is delivered to the country.

Russia's Defence Ministry said it had targeted infrastructure facilitating military cargoes from Europe in Western Ukraine.

Ukraine is dependent on trade and arms shipments from across the Polish, Romanian and Moldovan borders.

Russia has begun targeting Ukraine's border crossings with its Western allies in recent weeks, as part of a growing campaign by both sides to erode the other's economic infrastructure more than four years into Russia's invasion.

Putin told the war in Ukraine must end

In India, where Russian President Vladimir Putin had been attending the BRICS summit, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that both Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping had offered help brokering a peace settlement, Russian state news agency TASS reported.

Last month, at a summit in Kyrgyzstan, Mr Modi told Mr Putin that the war must end, one of several calls for peace by leaders of nations that have traditionally strong relations with Russia.

Narendra Modi (left) has told Vladimir Putin that the war must end. (Pyotr Kovalyov via Reuters)

Last month, Kazakhstan's President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev publicly told Mr Putin that he should halt the conflict along the front line, which has remained largely static this year.

Russia has ruled that out, saying Ukraine should pull back to leave the industrialised eastern Donbas region in Moscow's hands, something Kyiv has said it will never do.

Both Brazil and China, themselves founding BRICS members, have called for a resumption of peace talks.

TASS cited Mr Peskov as saying that Mr Putin had informed Mr Modi of the situation "on the ground" in Ukraine, and that Russia had not ruled out resuming three-way talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States in October.

Ukraine strike nuclear power plant in Russian-held territories

Overnight, hostilities showed no signs of letting up.

In the Russian-held part of Ukraine's southeastern Zaporizhzhia region, the head of Russia's state nuclear energy company Rosatom accused Ukraine of striking fuel trucks close to the Zaporizhzhia nuclear power station, Europe's largest.

Russia currently controls the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant in southern Ukraine. (Reuters: Alina Smutko)

The Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant has been controlled by Russia since March 2022, and remains close to the front line.

A Ukrainian military spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Russia, Ukraine to halt strikes on capitals during peace talks Vladimir Putin and Volodymyr Zelenskyy have agreed to halt strikes on their respective capitals.

In Russia itself, the mayor of the city of Nizhnekamsk, in the Volga River region of Tatarstan, said that "civilian and industrial" targets in the city had been struck by Ukrainian drones, causing at least two deaths and several more injuries.

Mayor Radmir Belyaev did not clarify which targets had been struck, but the city hosts a major oil refinery which has been attacked in the past.

Ukrainian authorities did not immediately comment on the strike on Nizhekamsk, but did say they had struck another refinery in the southern Krasnodar region.

ABC/Reuters

World.title: Cowboys back in the saddle as Alice Springs Rodeo returns
World.content:
The dust was flying and cowboys were hitting the dirt as the Alice Springs Rodeo returned after a year out of the saddle.

More than 2,000 spectators in total visited the arena at Blatherskite Park on Saturday, watching competitors take on bucking bulls and horses, while some of the youngest riders tried their luck on poddy calves.



For Aileron Bush Club secretary James Christian, the response showed how much the event had been missed.

"It's electric," he said.

"People are really glad to have a rodeo back on here in town.

"There's people from all different parts of society here, all cheering … they're enjoying the spectacle."

James Christian says the rodeo brought the community together. (ABC News: Chris Murrkarany Fitzpatrick)

Mr Christian said the event drew organisers and competitors from across a huge stretch of the Territory.

"The committee comes from probably a diameter of about 1,000 kilometres," he said.

"We've all converged on Alice Springs to put on this show.





[ Young competitors took part in horse and poddy calf events. (ABC News: Chris Murrkarany Fitzpatrick) "But it takes the whole community to help make that happen."

Young riders take their turn

Among those preparing to enter the arena was 10-year-old Lucy Muenstr, who was competing on the poddy calves.

She said she was more excited than nervous about getting into the arena.

"It's pretty fun," she said.

"You can just watch everyone fall off, and that, and it's just funny sometimes — but it's not funny if someone hurts themselves."

Ten-year-old Lucy Muenstr was excited to take on the poddy calves. (ABC: Chris Murrkarany Fitzpatrick)

Another young rider, 12-year-old Ollie McKay, had travelled 300 kilometres and was also hoping to leave with a buckle.

"I enjoy it, and it's just, like, the fun and the feel," he said.

"I just like riding and just like the cattle and all that."

For a cowboy veteran, 41-year-old rider Garyshane James, who has competed in rodeos for about 25 years, seeing another generation taking part was an important part of the event.

"Kids that get here — amazing young fellas getting in and having a go and keeping the cowboy spirit going," he said.

"Rodeo was our key to get out and see our mates."

Garyshane James has competed in rodeos for about 25 years. (ABC: Chris Murrkarany Fitzpatrick)

Three competitors taken to hospital

The dangers of the sport were also on display.

Three competitors were taken to hospital after being injured during the rodeo and were reported to be in a stable condition and recovering.

Three competitors were taken to hospital after being injured during the 2026 Alice Springs rodeo. (ABC: Chris Murrkarany Fitzpatrick)

Rodeo announcer Ricky J. Morrison said injuries were an accepted risk for many competitors.

"The cliché saying for rodeo is it's not if you get hurt, it's when," he said.

"If you do it long enough, you're going to get hurt."

He said the difference in size between riders and bulls made the risks clear.

"When a cowboy weighs anywhere from 50 to 100 kilos, and the bulls weigh anywhere from 450 to 600 kilos … you're probably going to come out second best sometimes," he said.

Rodeo announcer Ricky Morrison (right) says getting hurt is an accepted risk of the sport. (ABC: Chris Murrkarany Fitzpatrick)

Animal welfare concerns remain

While the crowd cheered on the competitors, not everyone was tipping their hat to the rodeo.





Di Evans has written numerous papers on rodeo for the RSPCA (Supplied: RSPCA) RSPCA Australia senior scientific officer Di Evans said the organisation remained opposed to rodeos because of concerns about the animals involved.

"We oppose rodeos on animal welfare grounds because of the high risk of pain, injury, fear [and] stress," she said.

Dr Evans said behaviours including head tossing, showing the whites of the eyes and excessive salivation could indicate distress in bucking animals.

" Great for a spectacle, but not so good for the animals. "

She acknowledged rodeos could provide social connections and contribute to the identity and economy of regional communities, but argued those benefits could be achieved in other ways.





Sam Webb pocketed $3,000 after winning the Open Bull Ride and shoot-out. (ABC: Chris Murrkarany Fitzpatrick) "If there's other ways that people can … connect with this culture and this focus without harming animals [and] display these skills through another way," she said.

Sam Webb cleans house

In the end, the competition produced a clear winner.

Territory cowboy Sam Webb, 38, won the Open Bull Ride before taking out the final shoot-out, earning $1,500 for each victory and pocketing $3,000 in total.

Mr Webb said there was no secret to his success.

"It's just like a hard day at work," he said.

"You work hard, you get the results.

"I was due for a bit of money."

He said he was never worried about taking on the bull that ultimately delivered his win.

"That's the fella I wanted, the big red fella," he said.

Mr Webb said beyond the competition, the rodeo offered something less tangible but no less valuable.

"It just brings the community together, brings everybody together," he said.

"It's a time to meet and greet and have a good time."

After the hiatus in 2025, organisers have described the rodeo as a "peak success" and hope to get back in the saddle again next year.

World.title: Kangaroos survive Blues scare to keep AFLW record alive
World.content:
Ash Riddell racked up 39 disposals as North Melbourne survived a scare to keep its record AFLW winning run rolling with a 10-point victory over Carlton.

In other results on Sunday, Melbourne defeated Port Adelaide 11.8 (74) to 2.11 (23) at Casey Fields, Richmond beat St Kilda 9.4 (58) to 6.7 (43) at Windy Hill, Sydney got past cross-town rivals GWS 13.9 (87) to 8.8 (56) at Henson Park, and Fremantle downed Essendon 5.7 (37) to 3.4 (22).

In front of more than 3,500 supporters at Arden Street, a boilover was on the cards after the Blues kicked back-to-back goals against the breeze in the second quarter to take a three-point lead.

The match was still in the balance in the dying minutes, with Carlton's Lily Goss having the chance to close a 10-point deficit to four after taking a mark 35 metres out.

But not realising there was a player behind her, Goss played on and was immediately tackled, with the moment proving Carlton's last chance to fire a shot as the Kangaroos held on to win, 4.9 (33) to 3.5 (23).

Riddell was unstoppable throughout, while Jasmine Garner (30 disposals, five clearances, one goal) was also a significant contributor for the victors.

The Kangaroos have a 5-0 win-loss return this season.

They have won a record 32 straight matches since drawing with Geelong in round two of 2024.

Riddell said her team embraced the challenge thrown down by the Blues.

"We love it, and we had that against Brisbane a couple of weeks ago," Riddell told the Seven Network.

"We get excited by that. You could see the girls smiling as they came in at three-quarter time. We want that challenge, so it's great."

Although Carlton dropped to a 4-1 win-loss record, the strong display against the Kangaroos has fuelled their belief.

"We would have loved to have won, so we're a little bit disappointed, but also super proud," said Blues captain Abbie McKay following her 27-disposal, five-clearance effort.

"We lost by [53 points] last year, so it shows we're really growing as a team.

"We're here to win, and we're here to win a grand final. Although we lost, it shows we're improving."

Riddell was everywhere in the first term on the way to 15 disposals and four inside 50s.

Goals against the breeze to Nell Morris-Dalton and Lila Keck thrust Carlton into a shock lead early in the second term, but a 40-metre set-shot from Tahlia Randall followed by Blaithin Bogue's goal on the run ensured the Kangaroos entered the long break with a nine-point advantage.

Randall suffered a scary moment in the third quarter when she hyperextended her left elbow, but she was able to return after receiving treatment.

The stand-out moment of the third quarter was a two-bounce, tackle-busting effort from Carlton speedster Goss that helped set up a goal to Erone Fitzpatrick.

Garner's late major ensured the Kangaroos headed into three-quarter time with an eight-point lead, and there were no goals scored in a frantic final term.

AAP

World.title: Screen time to be capped for NSW students to improve results
World.content:
Students in NSW public schools will be limited to as little as 15 minutes of screen time per day, under guidelines announced by the state government.

The 15-minute limit will apply to students from kindergarten to year 2.

Students in years 3 and 4 will have up to 30 minutes of daily classroom screen time, increasing to 45 minutes for years 5 and 6.

The guidelines will become mandatory from 2028. (ABC News)

The guidelines will be introduced next year, but will not become mandatory until 2028.

Education Minister Prue Car said children needed to get back to basics, including using pens and paper.

"There's just too much screen time for our young people in our school system," she said.

"We want to make sure that at school it's not the default, that the default is pen and paper."

Screen time limits will be more relaxed for high-schoolers, with digital learning allowed to make up 25 per cent of a subject's coursework for years 7 to 10.

Students in years 11 and 12 will be able to spend half their class time on digital devices like laptops and tablets.

Ms Car says there is too much screen time in schools. (ABC News: Nick Dole)

Raising standards

The state government said the screen time limits were designed to arrest a "worrying trend" of falling academic results.

Ms Car said according to the OECD's Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA), Australian students were nearly twice as likely to spend more than two hours a day learning using digital devices than the OECD average.

Global results show Aussie students' struggles Australian students have recorded their lowest-ever scores in maths and reading in international testing, but improved on their science results.

Last week, PISA data also showed reading and mathematics scores for15 year olds in NSW were going backwards.

"There's no doubt the two are linked, and they're linked around the world," Ms Car said.

Education secretary Murat Dizdar said while technology would continue to play an important role in classrooms, imposing screen time limits would help students concentrate.

"It's about backing in the research and evidence that our own students and our teachers are telling us around avoiding distractions in the learning process."

Digital detox a 'relief' for students

While mobile phones have been banned in all NSW classrooms for several years, some schools have recently been trialling their own limits on other forms of screen time.



Chatswood High School principal, Robin Chand, said since paring back the use of digital devices, staff had noticed an improvement in students' handwriting and engagement.

"I know that this will be welcomed by students because students directly tell me that they feel relieved at times when they are working directly with pen and paper and their course books," Mr Chand said.

"When screens go down, relationships go up.

"And the relationships that are the most important in our classroom are relationships between the students and their teachers," he said.

Mr Chand says that "when screens go down, relationships go up". (ABC News)

Seventeen-year-old student, Archie Newman, said learning with hard copy books, pens and paper had allowed him to slow down and think more deeply, without the temptations of a laptop or tablet.

"I was someone who could get distracted so easily with digital technology," he said.

"And [now] the emphasis on handwriting is allowing me and my learning experience to be maximised."

World.title: 71yo motorcyclist dies after hitting pothole on highway
World.content:
A motorcyclist has died after hitting a pothole on the Western Highway in Victoria's south-west this afternoon.

Victoria Police said emergency services were called to the Western Highway in Trawalla after reports that a motorcycle had struck a pothole and lost control at around 12:50pm.

The rider, a 71-year-old Ballarat man, died at the scene.

"The exact circumstances surrounding the crash are yet to be determined and will be investigated," a Victoria Police spokesperson said.

All westbound lanes were closed on the Western Freeway between Windermere and Beaufort.

It comes just days after a new report from Victoria's auditor-general found almost half of Victoria's road network is in poor condition and crumbling faster than the government can repair it.

Victoria Police has urged anyone with dashcam footage to contact Crime Stoppers.

World.title: 'Can't get boy's face out of my head': Witness retells Sydney carjacking
World.content:
A bystander who attempted to protect two children during a pursuit and carjacking in Sydney's south-west, described the moment a man allegedly lunged at him with a knife.

About 3pm on Saturday, police were called to carry out a welfare check on a 36-year-old man in Lakemba, but he fled in a vehicle with two children, who police confirmed were his sons.

Officers engaged in a short pursuit through the Campsie area, which they said was called off due to the "manner of the man's driving".

The car crashed in Lidcombe at the intersection of Parramatta Road and Bombay Street. (ABC News)

The car crashed at the intersection of Parramatta Road and Bombay Street at Lidcombe, about nine kilometres away, where members of the public attempted to intervene after the father got out of the car with the boys.

Nicholas Karagiannis was driving along Parramatta Road when he came across the crash scene.

While rendering assistance to the driver, the 46-year-old said he heard bystanders yell, "He's getting away" and "He's got children".

Mr Karagiannis said he chased after the man, who was allegedly attempting to enter other vehicles while armed with a knife.

Witness Nicolas Karagiannis. (ABC News)

Instinctively, Mr Karagiannis said he wanted to make sure the two boys were okay, but "everything happened so fast".

"He had a knife in his hand, he did not look well," he said.

" I can't get that boy's face out my head. "

Video shows Mr Karagiannis and several other men attempting to subdue the father in the middle of a busy road.

At one point Mr Karagiannis managed to grab one of the young boys "but the boy wanted to go back".

"They were just crying …in shock, my heart bleeds for those kids," he said.

Mr Karagiannis said he pleaded with the father to let the children go to no avail.

A woman was thrown out of a black Cerato. (ABC News)

In the video, the man appeared to bundle the boys into a black Kia Cerato, and moments later the female driver is forcibly thrown from the car.

Police said he allegedly threatened the woman with what they described as "a small black knife".

"I just did what I think anyone else would do in that situation [when] you see a guy with a knife and two young boys," Mr Karagiannis said.

The children, aged between five and seven, suffered minor injuries and were expected to be released from hospital on Sunday.

Second altercation

Inspector Mark Wakeham said a member of the public had unsuccessfully tried to remove the keys from the Cerato's ignition, sustaining a laceration to his hand as the father sped off with the two children inside.

The vehicle came to a stop on the M4 near the overpass of Greystaynes Road before being approached by members of the public, including an off-duty police officer, Inspector Wakeham added.

Bystanders this time managed to restrain him before police arrived.

Police praised the actions of bystanders who tried to help. (Supplied)

Inspector Wakeham described their actions as "incredibly brave".

" They did a wonderful job and we'd like to thank members of the public for assisting us with this case. "

He ruled out the incident as an act of kidnapping.

The man remained under police guard in hospital on Sunday where he was charged with three offences, including aggravated robbery with wounding, police pursuit and reckless wounding.

In the afternoon he appeared in court from hospital via a video link.

He did not apply for bail with the matter adjourned until September 24.

World.title: Broncos, Titans win to wrap up NRLW regular season
World.content:
The Brisbane Broncos have thrashed the Warriors to hit peak form before the finals, while the high-flying Gold Coast Titans beat the Newcastle Knights to wrap up the NRLW regular season.

The Broncos, defending premiers, put in a stunning seven-try second half on Sunday in a club-record 52-18 victory at Brisbane's Langlands Park.

Meanwhile, the Titans' 32-20 win in Newcastle stretched their unbeaten streak to 10 matches. They had already secured second place on the ladder behind the undefeated Sydney Roosters.

The Broncos finished the regular season in third place.

They were too classy for the Warriors, who ended a disappointing season with a fifth straight loss.

Roosters remain perfect in NRLW The Roosters come home strong to secure a second straight unbeaten NRLW season as they look to rectify last year's grand final stumble.

The New Zealanders came out of the blocks firing, but the Broncos scored first via Kerri Johnson, before former Brisbane premiership winner Gayle Broughton crossed for the visitors.

Broughton laid on another try with a deft kick for winger Tysha Ikenasio and the Warriors looked set to head into the break with a lead.

But Broncos centre Deleni Paitai scored her first NRLW try with 10 seconds left in the half to give her side a 12-8 advantage.

The Broncos extended their buffer just four minutes into the second half when Chelsea Lenarduzzi powered over.

Tries followed to Paitai, Tamika Upton, Georgia Bartlett, Julia Robinson and Lauren Dam, before Warriors centre Stacey Waaka stopped the rot.

Waaka stretched her try-scoring streak to seven matches, and Jasmin Huriwai added another for the Warriors prior to Robinson scoring her second for the Broncos.

Teagan Levi scored a double in the Titans' win over the Knights. (Getty Images: Scott Gardiner)

In Newcastle, Mercedez Taulelei-Siala opened the scoring for the Knights inside two minutes.

But the Titans' response was almost immediate when Phoenix-Raine Hippi scored.

Laikha Clarke made it two tries in two minutes for the Titans, but once the match settled into an arm wrestle, it was Sienna Yeo who scored a neat individual try for the Knights to lock up the scores.

Teagan Levi scored next for the Titans to continue her stellar debut NRLW season, before Evania Isa'ako touched down to give Gold Coast a 20-10 lead at the break.

Fane Finau revived Newcastle 10 minutes into the second half with a tackle-busting solo effort, but the Titans came back six minutes later through Indie Bostock.

From the ensuing kick-off, the Titans marched up the field, and Levi brushed off three would-be defenders to score her second try.

Isa'ako sealed her double minutes later, and while Taulelei-Siala scored with eight minutes to go for Newcastle, it was too little, too late.

AAP

World.title: Funding for prostate cancer charity redirected to McGrath Foundation
World.content:
Tens of thousands of men are diagnosed with prostate cancer in Australia every year.

Martin Fisk is one of them.

"I was experiencing extreme fatigue that I couldn't work out why, so I went to the GP and she ordered a bunch of tests," he said.

" Then I got the phone call that nobody wants to get. "

It was a diagnosis Mr Fisk had been dreading; both his father and father-in-law died from the disease.

He is now receiving a combination of hormone therapy, radiation and drug treatments — all tracked and monitored with regular biopsies, tests and scans.

Martin Fisk's father and father-in-law both died from prostate cancer. (ABC News: David Sciasci )

A specialist prostate cancer nurse helps to coordinate this vital yet complex care, while supporting Mr Fisk and his family in Canberra.

"I'm having three different treatments, they each have side effects, but they also interact with each other, and [my nurse] is across all of that," he said.

"When I have a symptom I can't explain, I can go to her."

'Specialist knowledge built over many years'

Prostate cancer accounts for 17 per cent of new cancer diagnoses, with one in five men at risk.

Prostate Cancer Foundation Australia (PCFA) provides specialist nurse positions in hospitals around the country, mostly funded by the federal government.

"We have many men in touch with us who are telling us they're alive today because of the support they received by prostate cancer specialist nurses," said PCFA director of nursing Sally Sara.

Sally Sara says some nurses have already told the foundation that they are looking for other positions. (ABC News: Daniel Taylor )

But federal funding for PCFA's nursing program will be moved to the McGrath Foundation from July next year, part of a wider shift to an "all-cancer" model.

"We have had a number of nurses in our network already approach us to tell us that they are looking for alternative positions," Ms Sara said.

" I have grave concerns for men out there in the community who are dependent on this specialist level of care. "

PCFA CEO Anne Savage says the foundation has "no issues with McGrath", but the change risks losing expertise built over time.

"[The nurses] are not interchangeable with the McGrath all-cancer service," she said.

"Their specialist knowledge, trusted clinical relationships, and deep understanding of prostate cancer have been built over many years."

Move towards all-cancer model

The government says the funding change is a continuation of its "all-cancer" model which has brought multiple disciplines into the McGrath Foundation.

In a statement, Special Envoy for Men's Health Dan Repacholi told the ABC that the transition would be planned to ensure patients "continue receiving care".

"Existing nurses will have the option to move across to McGrath, keeping their location, experience and patient relationships wherever possible," he said.

"If a nurse chooses not to transition, McGrath will recruit someone to fill that position."

In a statement, Dan Repacholi said the same level of funding for prostate cancer nurses would be maintained under the changes. (ABC News: Laurence Curson)

Last month the federal government announced that $46.5 million over five years — the equivalent to 60 full-time positions — would be moved to the McGrath Foundation.

The McGrath Foundation was founded in 2005 by former Australian cricketer Glenn McGrath following the death of his wife Jane from breast cancer.

Prostate cancer support groups Michael Platts panicked when he was diagnosed with prostate cancer. Now he wants to help others break through the stigma around the condition.

After initially raising money for breast cancer nurses, it now provides care for all cancer types.

It's developed the McGrath Model of Care which the foundation describes as "a national, evidence‑based framework shaped by real‑world nursing experience".

In recent years the Labor government has shifted its funding for 14 types of cancer from a range of individual charities and foundations to McGrath, representing tens of millions of dollars.

Mr Repacholi said the latest change "maintains the same level of funding", and all the money being moved to McGrath would be used for dedicated prostate cancer nursing.

He said that nurses wouldn't lose their specialist skills or practice.

"It's not a funding cut. The contract's simply moving from PCFA to McGrath as part of the national all-cancer nursing model," he said.

Foundation to pursue 'every available avenue'

PCFA says it will pursue "every available" avenue to protect its nursing services, including "parliamentary scrutiny and examination of our contractual and legal rights".

"This is not a dispute about funding, this is about the standard of care and the survival of Australian men impacted by prostate cancer," Ms Savage said.

Through fundraising and corporate sponsors, PCFA provides an extra 24 full time nurse positions beyond the 60 funded by the Commonwealth.

"The PCFA will retain responsibility for those positions, honour its existing agreements and continue raising funds for specialist prostate cancer nursing," Ms Savage said.

Ms Savage says the change to the "all-cancer" model risks losing nursing expertise that's been built over time. (Australian Story)

Despite being in the midst of his treatment, Mr Fisk is himself now raising money for prostate cancer, with more than $16,000 raised at last count.

Mr Fisk spent much of his working life in the community and charity sector, including running the mental health organisation Menslink for more than a decade, and is no stranger to raising money for charity.

He is taking part in PCFA's annual Long Run campaign, with funds raised going towards the specialist nursing care like he and his family are receiving.

"We have people from all over Canberra and, in fact, all around the world chipping in and donating with some amazing messages of support," Mr Fisk said.

"They make me cry, but they also make me a bit stronger to go out and help more people if I can."

Martin Fisk (centre) takes a walk with this wife Sandra Fisk (left) and friend Zebunnissa Khan (right) at Lake Burley Griffin. (ABC News: David Sciasci )

Mr Fisk says support provided by his nurse for his mental health has been just as important as his physical health.

"Having a cancer diagnosis and cancer treatment is a scary journey. [My nurse] is able to be there alongside [us]," he said.

"I want to make sure [nurses] are available not just to me, but for all the other prostate cancer patients that are coming in the future."

World.title: ‘Humans make mistakes’: Insurer offers discount to self-driving car owners
World.content:
BusinessConsumer affairsGeneral insurance ‘Humans make mistakes’: Insurer offers discount to self-driving car owners Elias Visontay September 14, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Self-driving cars have successfully developed to a point where a major insurer believes they reduce the risk of collision enough to warrant offering some owners using the technology cheaper insurance premiums. Most Australians may not realise they’re already sharing the road with self-driving cars or have full confidence in their safety, but on Monday Zurich Insurance said it will offer discounted premiums to drivers who insure a Tesla that uses Full Self-Driving (FSD) Supervised mode. Tesla’s self-driving in action. Janie Barrett/Cormac Lally The Tesla drivers will be deemed less risky policyholders after early-stage data reviewed by Zurich’s underwriters showed there was lower accident frequency for drivers using the futuristic technology. The underwriters formed the view that the automated trips using FSD were safer than human-driven journeys. FSD mode – which requires a human’s constant supervision to legally operate – became available for owners of certain newer Model 3 and Y Teslas in Australia about 12 months ago, allowing those who pay a $149 per month fee to let their vehicles drive them around.



The technology relies on eight cameras fixed on the car that provides a 360-degree view, which feeds information into a neural network navigation software that processes more than one million pixels of visual data every millisecond to determine how to steer, accelerate, brake and change lanes to navigate to a user’s pre-entered destination. If no destination has been set, the car continues driving straight ahead, while sticking to its lane. Drivers using FSD must be paying attention to the road, with an internal camera monitoring their retinas to ensure they are not distracted and are ready to intervene and take over control should the car make an error. If the car detects that the supervising driver’s eyes are distracted or their hands are holding anything and not otherwise ready to grab the wheel at any moment, a warning will be issued. The car will automatically pull over and deactivate the self-driving option for the rest of a trip if a supervising driver is repeatedly caught failing to pay attention or have their hands free. By requiring supervision to operate, Tesla’s FSD is classified as a Level 2 Advanced Driver Assistance System under Australia’s road rules, with the human behind the wheel considered legally in control of the vehicle. Supervising drivers can intervene to re-take control at any time, whether by choice to redirect or pull over, or if prompted due to issues with the car’s sensors.





During a test drive conducted by this masthead this week, FSD’s handling of roundabouts was smooth, with the car swiftly slowing to respond to hazards and pedestrians during a drive across Sydney. However, the car’s navigation system became confused at times, including when driving through recently updated lane changes off Sydney’s Harbour Bridge. At one point, it attempted to exit using a bus-only lane, and another time it did not recognise a school zone 40 km/h speed limit. Tesla’s Full Self-Driving (Supervised) mode in action. Janie Barrett The inclusion of FSD as a risk rating factor is a first in Australia. Zurich believes it is just the second globally to take the step. Zurich would not specify the exact discount would be in price terms for FSD users. The offer of cheaper insurance comes at a time of surging costs for motorists, with premiums jumping by about 50 per cent between 2019 and 2025.



“As vehicle technology and driver behaviour continues to evolve at an extraordinary pace, it is critical that we continue to innovate alongside this change”, said Alex Morgan, Zurich’s head of general insurance. Related Article Driverless cars ‘You can tell I’m not steering’: Self-driving Teslas hit Australian roads “Humans make mistakes. They get tired. They can be distracted. It’s not that the machine is perfect, but it does appear to be true that on average, across the population and over time, it makes fewer of the mistakes that humans do,” Morgan said. “It should be noted that self-driving technology helps to solve a lot of problems associated with driver error. It does not, however, do much to solve the problem of a tree branch falling on your roof in a storm, a shopping trolley being pushed into your passenger door, hail smashing your windscreen, or your vehicle being stolen,” he said. Thom Drew, Tesla’s Australia director, said the company was pleased to see insurers beginning to recognise the safety benefits of automated driving. “FSD [Supervised] is making driving significantly safer, and it’s encouraging to see ... this [insurance] benefit and reflecting the reduced risk for Tesla owners.”



The reporter tested FSD on a vehicle loaned by Tesla. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.
