Camojojo's original Hibird feeder has long been a reliable model in my testing stable, unique for its ability to run on both 2.4-GHz and 5-GHz Wi-Fi bands—almost all smart feeders are 2.4-GHz only (learn why below)—and last year saw the debut of an upgraded model, the Hibird Pro. The update has built-in solar panels, an option for pole mounting, and supposedly improved AI identification, though it still frequently misidentifies even common birds in my West Coast backyard as East Coast species. The app is not as streamlined or user-friendly as Birdfy's or Birdbuddy's, but it's still easy enough to navigate, with options for changing video length (default is 10 seconds) or viewing in slo-mo. Video is the default media type it saves, though this is 4K Ultra HD. Without a subscription, you can't search past videos by bird, and cloud storage is capped at 5 GB over 60 days, though the feeder does come with a 128-GB SD card. You'll also get “smarter” chats with the app's AI Q&A function, “Dr. Bird,” and the ability to share across two devices with a subscription ($45 year/$4 month).

Tech.title: Try These 3 iOS 27 Safari Settings to Get More Out of Apple’s Browser
Tech.content:
At Apple’s recent hardware event, the software powering its foldable iPhone Duo stood out, with translucent Liquid Glass effects and vertically stacked icons. But you don’t need to snatch a folding smartphone to reap the benefits of Apple’s iOS 27 updates.

When iOS 27 leaves beta on Monday, Siri AI’s standalone app and smartphone search integration will likely be the most immediately obvious change for many iPhone users. But it’s worth digging even deeper to uncover helpful additions to key apps, like Apple’s Safari browser, as well as revamps to underutilized apps, like Shortcuts.

The version of Safari available in iOS 27 looks fairly similar to the last iteration, with a few key updates tucked away in the settings. These Safari features are powered by Apple Intelligence, which requires an iPhone 15 Pro or newer (they're also available on iPadOS 27 and macOS 27).

Notify Me

Photograph: Courtesy of Apple

If you’re shopping online and want a quick price-drop notification, you can use the “Notify Me” feature to scan a webpage on a certain cadence and look for changes. First, head to the page you want to track and tap the three-lined hamburger menu icon in the top right corner of Safari. About halfway down, you’ll see this option listed.

“Safari can let you know when a website updates the content you’re interested in,” reads the feature’s description. Here you’ll find an open text box where you can describe what change in content you want Safari to scan for, as well as how often you want it to check.

For example, my couch is broken, so I’ve been eyeing a few different replacement options. I have two final contenders from CB2, but both are out of my price range. So, I set up a “Notify Me” for Safari to scan the pages each day for a significant discount. Whichever one goes on sale first will likely be what I decide to get, and now I don’t have to refresh the pages manually every day.

While many other browsers have similar shopping features, like the price-tracking bell in Google Chrome, I appreciate how this feature stretches beyond just buying stuff. You can also use Safari to scan for ticket drops, privacy policy changes, and other content updates.

Describe an Extension

Photograph: Courtesy of Apple

If you’ve experimented already with the “Describe a Shortcut” feature for iPhone automation, then “Describe an Extension” for Safari will seem familiar. It's located under the same settings menu as the “Notify Me” tool, just a little further down.

Tech.title: Best Indoor Garden Systems I’ve Been Testing All Year (2026)
Tech.content:
Gardyn Home 4.0 (9/10 WIRED Recommends) was one of the easiest indoor gardens to assemble and set up out of the box; it also yielded the most dramatic success of any of the brands I tried. Flowers, kohlrabi, thyme, and even a whole cauliflower all thrived in this pipe-based, front-light system with room for plants to grow up, out, and every which way.

Seeds arrive in proprietary pods called yCubes, and each Gardyn purchase comes with your choice of yCube sets: “Salad Lover,” “Budding Florist,” or “Chef Faves.” I've tried both “Budding Florist” and “Chef Faves,” and my favorite is the latter; it has an interesting variety of everything from breen and Tokyo bekana greens to Thai basil and miniature sunflowers.

Though Gardyn recommends starting the yCubes in the company's add-on $80 nursery, I've germinated plenty of yCubes right in the system just fine. (Make sure you don't add nutrients until they sprout. If you're germinating yCubes later on, when nutrients are already in the system, you can just use a shallow bowl with loosely tented plastic wrap placed on the Gardyn's base.) The seeds arrive tucked in mineral wool, snug in their little yCubes that slot into larger cups ("yPods") that fit into the pipes. When the Gardyn waters the plants, the yPods fill with nutrient-infused water, and the plants' roots grow right into the water.

Part of what makes the Gardyn foolproof is the subscription app add-on, “Kelby,” which monitors your plants via attached sensors and cameras. It delivers customized watering and lighting schedules, as well as maintenance suggestions via AI (which an anonymous source told me is basically OpenAI's ChatGPT with an overlaid prompt). This subscription adds an additional $259 a year to the base purchase price, though it includes a certain number of credits per month—depending on whether you have the Home or Studio model—to order new yCubes. There's a free 30-day trial for Kelby, but you can definitely still use the Gardyn without it, relying on manual light and watering controls. Also, there have been some recent privacy concerns with Kelby, which makes me more apt to do away with it altogether (more below).

Once a month, the base needs to be emptied and scrubbed. Every few weeks, the roots need to be checked for root rot and growth outside the yPod, examined for whether it's time to prune, and/or tucked back in if they've wandered too far. This maintenance is admittedly a bit laborious, and if you do not do it consistently, you will be very sorry when it's time to clean the Gardyn and prepare it for its next planting. (Ask me how I know!)

I now have two Gardyns, a Home 4 and a Studio 2, which is smaller and holds fewer pods. Aside from some non-sprouting yCubes (which the company will replace upon request), I have no major complaints about Gardyn's system. Though I will note that the plants in the Studio have been overall less lush than the Home, due to the Studio having one light bar rather than two—this is why my primary recommendation remains the Home. I also like that Gardyn offers a Vacation Mode, which adjusts the lighting and watering to slow growth and minimize maintenance tasks while you're away. Also note that Gardyn is now FSA- and HSA-eligible.

NOTE: Throughout the spring and recently on July 2, 2026, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency released advisories regarding vulnerabilities in Gardyn Home and Studio devices. These security weaknesses could have allowed someone to take remote control of a Gardyn device, access plant photos, and obtain personal information such as names, addresses, phone numbers, and email addresses. Gardyn claims these vulnerabilities have been remediated with the most recent firmware update and advises customers to ensure their Gardyns are internet-connected and running firmware version 619 or later. If you think your device may have been compromised, email [email protected] or call 844-4-GARDYN. For more information, see Gardyn's Security update for Gardyn Home and Gardyn Studio.

Tech.title: Coway Airmega Halo Review: Is Your Air Really Clean?
Tech.content:
Overall, it delivers on most of its promises, but I ran into some problems during field-testing that made me question its sensor, and I wish it had more transparency with pollutant levels.

Photograph: Molly Higgins

Simple Design That’s Maybe Too Simple

The Halo is only 9.7 pounds, making it lightweight and portable as far as air purifiers go, but it doesn't have accessibility features like a top handle or wheels for easier moving. It has a small cutout in the back to grip, but because I have an upper-limb disability, moving it was awkward—I essentially had to hug the purifier to maneuver it, since I don't have large hands that can easily grip the inlet.

The purifier's cylindrical design with a 360-degree air-intake structure draws in polluted air from all sides, making for fewer spatial constraints and more options for placement around the home. The inside of the machine uses Coway's HyperVortex filtration system, which is an aerodynamic fan and duct design that Coway states is “inspired by eagle wings and golf ball dimples.” It uses wing blades to stabilize airflow, along with aerodynamic blades for powerful airflow for the generator fan and dimples to reduce air resistance for smoother air intake.

Setup was extremely easy—I just needed to unscrew the bottom, remove the filter from the plastic protective covering, screw the bottom back on, and plug it in. There's no need for a Wi-Fi connection, no app, and no remote. I started testing air purifiers earlier this year, and I've found I actually like having a connected remote, or better yet, an app that allows me to monitor air quality and adjust settings from afar. This model had neither. I also appreciate getting transparent numbers of pollutant levels directly from the machine rather than relying on colored lights, but this machine had the latter.

Tech.title: AI Agents Are Thirsty for Power
Tech.content:
Welcome back to Power Play! Each week, senior writer Molly Taft tackles a topic around this midterm season’s biggest issue: data centers. If you’ve got a question or thought for the column, feel free to shoot Molly an email at [email protected] or reach them securely on Signal at mollytaft.76.

“What on earth are they building all of these data centers for?” an exasperated friend asked me recently.

They’re not the only one asking: We got several similar questions on our recent data center livestream. It’s a really reasonable thing to wonder about. After all, if AI is already making all these breakthroughs, why are tech companies taking on billions of dollars of debt and constructing some of the biggest power plants in the world to build even more data centers?

The answer isn’t to help the average user search for recipes or look up places to visit on a vacation; simple chatbot queries are an increasingly outdated way of thinking about how AI works. Now, AI is all about agents—there’s no official definition, but roughly speaking, agents are large language model-based systems designed to make autonomous decisions to execute a task—and the shift towards them is part of what’s driving Silicon Valley’s power buildout.

“Rather than asking an AI chatbot a simple question and answer, these agents can give themselves hundreds of small prompts based on a user’s original question,” says my colleague Maxwell Zeff, who writes the weekly Model Behavior newsletter. “For example, if someone asked an AI agent to build them a website, it might run for hours to build out features, re-prompting itself dozens of times in the process to build different web pages, menus, and datasets that power the thing.”

Tech.title: With a Better Understanding of Physics, We Could Predict Volcanic Eruptions
Tech.content:
The original version of this story appeared in Quanta Magazine.

In the summer of 1991, Pinatubo, a volcano in the Philippines, self-destructed. The eruption started on June 12, and three days later it culminated in a tremendous explosion. By the time pyroclastic flows—incandescent avalanches of molten rock and gas—tumbled down its sterilized slopes, Pinatubo’s peak had been obliterated and replaced by a 2.5-kilometer-wide chasm.

The eruption killed more than 800 people, mainly because roofs, weighed down by rain-saturated ash, collapsed. But it could have been so much worse: About 250,000 people, across multiple cities and a sprawling US Air Force base, lived in the volcano’s shadow. When Pinatubo started convulsing and belching steam in April of that year, scientists from the US and the Philippines deployed an array of instruments that tracked the volcano’s inner tumult.

“We didn’t know much about that volcano, and so there was this really rapid geological assessment. And the assessment said, ‘Oh, crap, when this thing erupts, it only erupts big,’” says Mike Poland, current scientist in charge at the US Geological Service’s Yellowstone Volcano Observatory. “And that became the basis for a forecast.”

By early June, ash and lava were escaping Pinatubo’s flanks, and an evacuation was ordered, just a few days before the cataclysmic hammer fell. It was, in other words, a very close call.

Those scientists saved countless lives, but their forecast was more of an educated guess than it might have appeared. It was nothing like a weather forecast; they couldn’t say with anything resembling certainty that on June 12 an explosive eruption was going to occur, nor could they predict the evolution of that eruption.

With very few exceptions, this imprecision is true of all well-monitored volcanoes. But volcanology, as a field, has made great leaps since Pinatubo blew its top. The instrumentation is more advanced, machine learning has made interpreting data far more efficient, and scientists have a much better understanding of the magmatic plumbing that drives volcanism. That’s prompted me—as a professionally trained volcanologist who now writes a lot about the field—to wonder: How close are we to forecasting volcano behavior the way we forecast the weather?

Tech.title: 10 Best Standing Desks Worth Buying in 2026
Tech.content:
Tips and Frequently Asked Questions Is a Standing Desk Worth It? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron New research shows that while standing desks can potentially mitigate some health risks by limiting your sitting time, standing too long isn't all that great and can increase the risk of cardiovascular disease. I reached out to Anne-Kristina Arnold, a kinesiology expert and senior lecturer in the Department of Biomedical Physiology and Kinesiology at Simon Fraser University. She says the results from this recent study “illustrate how challenging some of this epidemiological research is." “To say standing workstations are good for everybody in every situation all the time is never going to flow,” Arnold tells WIRED. "There are so many variables, so many varied kinds of work we do—we're varied in our body sizes, in our fitness, in the shoes we wear. It's really hard to be able to say definitively that standing workstations are good. The research is mixed." Switching from sitting to standing doesn't solve all problems, and standing too long can cause its own problems. If you want to work with a standing workstation, Arnold recommends to use it in the standing position for 20 minutes per hour. If you have a normal desk, get up and move every 15 to 20 minutes. However, there's no definitive guideline. “The standing workstation isn't necessarily the answer—getting up and walking is better,” Arnold concludes. —Julian Chokkattu Electric vs. Manual Standing Desks AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Our guide here focuses largely on electric standing desks, which have motors in the legs to smoothly move the table up and down. However, we have a few manual standing desk recommendations, too. If you're planning on switching up how you work a few times every day, an electric desk will simply be more convenient. However, if you just want to be able to adjust the height of your desk and won't be changing it all that often, then maybe look at manual standing desks. They're often cheaper. How to Properly Stand and Sit With a Standing Desk AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron The same ergonomic rules you follow when sitting at a workstation apply when you're standing. When your elbows are at a 90-degree position, you want the desk keyboard to be elbow height. Your monitor should be at eye level (a good rule of thumb is the top of your monitor should meet your eye), and if you're using a laptop, you should keep it angled with a laptop stand for a more ergonomic typing position. Be sure to adjust your office chair appropriately to the floor before adjusting the height of your desk. Watch Your Wires! AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Cable management is exceptionally important when it comes to standing desks. After setting up your standing desk, make sure you keep an eye on every single wire that's connected to something on the desk when you start raising the desktop. Otherwise, funny things start to happen: wires come undone, or scoot light objects off the desk. WIRED reviewer Julian Chokkattu has unboxed and set up many desks over the years, and yet he still made a rookie move. As he was raising a desk, he didn't realize his Ethernet cable was taut, and it broke cleanly off the back of his PC when the desk reached a certain height. Welp. As for me, I'm a naturally distracted person, and so I need to tack my cables down or suffer grievous consequences on the regular. Keep an eye on the wires. Keep an eye on stuff near the wires. If you're not careful, you can even accidentally knock art off your wall. —Matthew Korfhage How We Test AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron I and other members of WIRED's Reviews team test standing desks in our own homes and in our own home offices. We use desks for months at a time (even years, in some cases), jotting down every flaw we see over the course of that time and noting any highlights. We look at building materials, motor noise, motor speed, preset options, cable management, and ease of use—and of course, the simple intangibles like aesthetics. We gauge the difficulty of the assembly and setup, as well as the difficulty of disassembling or moving each desk. Desks are a solid investment, and so we expect a desk to be with us for years, perhaps longer than we live in a city. And so we also look at both the length of the warranty and the service reputation of each company. Sometimes a small detail can take on outsized importance when using a desk over long periods, whether the existence or nonexistence of a grommet, a rounded edge, or a bolt that gets a little wobbly over time. That's why WIRED's Reviews team believes in the value of long-term testing, and why we do so in our own home offices. This long-term testing also means it's not easy for our small team to test every single desk out there, as these are bulky, big pieces of furniture and the setup is fairly involved. This means you may see a few missing brands in this guide, but we're always testing and adding more desks. —Matthew Korfhage

Other Standing Desks to Consider

Photograph: Nicole Kinning

Ergodriven Tempo Automatic Standing Desk for $629: It was only a matter of time before desks got “smart,” right? This Tempo from new-ish company Ergodriven is designed to automate the process of standing or sitting, with a Cruise Control function that will encourage you to change position during the day by, well, automatically doing so. A “wiggle” will alert you when the desk wants to change position, which you can override manually if you're eating lunch or in a meeting. A sensor will register your presence, so the desk won't move when you're away. WIRED contributor Nicole Kinning found that this all works as promised—as does a little app that registers “achievements” like standing time. But note the desk, while sturdy, is also a bit heavy, and a slight cosmetic crack formed early on the rounded edge. The 16-year warranty provides a bit of assurance.

Photograph: Nicole Kinning

Luxor Compact Electric Standing Desk for $200: The Luxor is a no-nonsense standing desk that does exactly what you expect and takes up minimal space. It’s perfect for students, small apartments, and anyone who needs a compact, budget-friendly setup. At 23.5 inches deep, the tabletop is shallow enough to fit into tight corners or shared spaces. The electric lift moves steadily at an inch per second, whisper-quiet, and the 154-pound weight capacity can handle a laptop, monitor, and a few textbooks with no sweat. The lift mechanism is exposed underneath, so you’ll want to leave some legroom when at sitting height. —Nicole Kinning

Simple Height Adjustable Desk for $850: The Simple Height Adjustable Desk lives up to its name. Assembly is straightforward and cable routing is tidy thanks to an integrated channel that keeps everything corralled. The T-shaped legs slide into a bracket instead of screwing or locking into place, which feels a little ambiguous, but once it’s upright, the desk is solid and sturdy. In practice, the desk became everything I needed. It’s smooth, quiet, and spacious, with four height presets. The laminate top is durable and forgiving—ideal if you’re like me and regularly forget that coasters exist. There are no fancy gimmicks, which is exactly the point. It's a dependable, fuss-free desk that prioritizes function over flashy. —Nicole Kinning

Photograph: Nicole Kinning

Eureka Ergonomic Opal Standing Desk for $2,250: WIRED contributor Nicole Kinning was a big fan of the, well, opaline looks of the Eureka Ergonomic Opal standing desk. It's a sturdy, milky-toned, downright fancy-looking pillar of vaguely art-deco luxe: beaded cabinets on each leg, gold hardware, marbled top, integrated drawer, hooooooey! It all makes for a quite distinctive aesthetic, and setup is a bit tricky given the heft of the desk. But unlike most standing desks, this one is outfitted quite beautifully as a full workstation, with roomy cabinets in each leg and a drawer offering ample storage. Just be sure to put grips on the bottom; it slid around on Kinning's hard floors like a curling stone, she noted. Once it's in place, bask in the stateliness. It's the rare standing desk where she could see herself writing a Great American Novel.

Autonomous Desk Pro for $600: The standout feature here is the new Desk AI, a separate control attachment that tracks your standing habits along with environmental factors like air pressure and quality, temperature, humidity, and noise. In theory, it’s meant to help you work smarter, but in practice, it mostly flags things you can’t control from the desk itself. If it came with an air purifier or fan to manage these conditions, then we’d be talkin’. Still, it’s a fun and techy bonus on an otherwise reliable desk.

Photograph: Nicole Kinning

Vari Solid Wood Electric Standing Desk for $829: Even though it’s solid wood, this desk never felt too precious for everyday use. Made from FSC-certified lumber, the desk is heavy and stable, even at standing height on carpet, and the motor is impressively quiet and subtle when adjusting. The ComfortEdge feature turned out to be more helpful than reviewer Nicole Kinning expected; over long typing sessions, it noticeably softened where my wrists meet the desk, a nice upgrade to a standard desk’s hard, squared-off edges. Yes, the solid wood Vari is on the pricier side, but it feels justified if solid wood and long-term durability matter to you. If they don’t, consider the traditional version.

Boulies Magvida for $760: The Boulies Magvida advertises its best feature in the name itself. This midsize desk (55 x 28 inches) is known for its EMO system, a magnetic organization setup built beneath the desktop. Instead of drilling holes or fiddling with brackets, you just snap accessories, like a cable tray, hooks, and silicone straps, into place. The add-ons feel premium and the magnets don’t budge, and there’s an optional magnetic drawer that’s also handy. Add in memory presets, a child lock, anti-collision detection, and simple color options and you’ve got a clean, clever setup.

Herman Miller Jarvis Bamboo Standing Desk for $1,325: As someone who spent years hunching over keyboards, obsessive research led WIRED reviewer Simon Hill to the Jarvis Standing Desk (now owned by Herman Miller), which has served him well for six years. With a contoured bamboo top, handy optional extras to tuck wires out of sight, and a responsive control panel for easy height adjustment (including presets), this is an excellent standing desk. The only weakness is that it wobbles slightly at higher levels. The newer touchscreen OLED control unit is not as reliable as the original, so opt for the programmable controls.

Room & Board Lincoln Desk for $5,399: Few standing desks can lay claim to true elegance. But Room & Board's Lincoln desk—designed in collaboration with design firm Gensler—is an exception. This is a dignified, sturdy, wobble-free electric standing desk that'd fit in with an executive office or a well-appointed home, made with solid wood and available in walnut, maple, cherry, ash, or oak (with a rye, salt, or charcoal stain). You can configure the desk to have integrated drawers on the left, right, or on both sides if you choose the larger 72-inch size. There's even a drawer in the center! This is what privilege looks like, where standing desks are concerned. The price is commensurately high, though take note this included white glove delivery and assembly. Also take note that the thickness of the desktop means only some clamps will mount onto its girth. This monitor arm mount will work, but for some mounts, you might have to directly screw it to the desktop. All in all, this is a gorgeous standing desk that doesn't look anything like a standing desk, but with a few quirks and a high price.

Staples Union & Scale Electric Standing Desk With Micro Movements (UN62092) for $513: Staples' house brand, Union & Scale, makes some of WIRED reviewer Julian Chokkattu's favorite affordable office furniture, and its standing desk is no exception—though at this middle price range, it didn't keep pace with Branch's reasonably priced desks. Still, this was easy to put together, and while the white desktop is not much to look at, the dual motors do the job. He liked the control panel, which has dedicated buttons for moving the desk up and down, as well as two height presets. He also didn't see any wobble, though the collision sensor could stand to be more sensitive. There's a cable tray at the bottom back of the desk to route cables, but there's sadly no grommet to pull them through. The Micro Movement mode moves the desk up and down over time to reduce fatigue and encourage movement, but it might be more distracting than useful.

Beflo Tenon Premium for $3,998: While incredibly expensive (and heavy!), WIRED contributor Henri Robbins found the hardwood smart desk both sturdy and well-designed. Assembly was straightforward, and once the desk was up and running, Robbins found all of the features (touchscreen controls, a built-in power strip, audio passthrough, and LED lighting) to work well, and in convenient locations. The touchscreen controls are intuitive (iOS-like), and features like a sit/stand timer and phone connectivity provide additional functionality. The desk supports over 200 pounds of stuff even when moving, and the height-adjustment motors will temporarily disable if they overheat, instead of risking damage to the desk. The table also looks fantastic, and a multitude of first-party accessories let you customize the desk to your specific needs. The largest issue with this table is the noise. While in no way loud, it was certainly more audible than the “whisper-quiet” descriptor Beflo uses in its marketing. Besides that, the lighting color adjustment had some difficulties creating specific colors using the built-in touchscreen, and the audio cable was too short to reach a desktop computer on the floor, even at the lowest height. However, the Tenon is still a great, if pricey, option to consider.

Herman Miller Spout Sit-to-Stand Table for $3,275: Herman Miller's Spout Sit-To-Stand Table is lovely to look at. Like the Branch Four-Legged Desk, it looks like a normal desk with four legs, giving it a luxe look. Those motors in the legs rise smoothly, and it’s easy to raise and lower the desktop to my preferences with the button on the right. The motor does have a high hum to it, and WIRED reviewer Nena Farrell found it loud enough that she'd hesitate to use it when her husband is on a call in the same room, but not so loud it would disturb her son if he were sleeping a room away. Bizarrely, it doesn’t have memory presets, but it's pretty easy to just adjust the desk each time to sitting and standing heights. You can add a cable tray underneath the desk each time to organize cords, but it costs extra. The only other item built into the desk is a single slim center drawer perfect for pens and notebooks. It comes in three desktop sizes and three finishes: laminate white, veneer walnut, and veneer ash. You can also customize the base color, with seven different colors ranging from your classic black and white to a gentle blue and olive green. While it’s gorgeous to look at and works well, Farrell found it disappointing that such a high-priced desk doesn’t have presets and uses veneers rather than real wood.

FlexiSpot E7 Pro for $400+: Standing desks can get pricey, but FlexiSpot routinely offers similar functionality at a lower price. At first glance, the E7 Pro looks much like the Herman Miller Jarvis, but look closer, and you discover the entry-level option has a shallow 23-inch desktop, the control unit feels a bit cheap, and it emits a high-pitched whine in operation. WIRED reviewer Simon Hill had some issues fitting larger power adapters in the cable tidily, and the desk can get wobbly when fully extended. But, even when fully configured, the E7 Pro is cheaper than many rivals. Minor flaws aside, it is a perfectly decent standing desk.

Inbox Zero 47-inch Adjustable Electric Standing Desk for $196: This desk has every feature you'd expect to need at the price range less than $200, wrote former WIRED reviewer Martin Cizmar. There are rolling casters so you can not only move the desk up and down, but also shake it all around. The desk's electric controls have presets but also allow you to fine-tune the height for typing or Zooming. The split top that makes it easier and cheaper to ship doesn't hurt the performance, but is less pleasant visually, and the little motor works audibly hard (tshunk, tschunk, tshunk) while raising the desktop. Based on three months of testing, it's a decent budget standing desk with casters, but if you can spend a little more, you'll probably be happier with something else.

Standing Desk Accessories

Branch Clamp-on Power Photograph: Julian Chokkattu

Branch Clamp-on Power for $89: This simple and elegant clamp attaches to your desktop and adds three AC outlets, a USB-C, and a USB-A, so you don't have so many wires running down to the ground.

LumeCube EdgeLight 2.0 for $150: Why have a lamp take up valuable desk space when you can clamp the lamp to your desk? These task lights from LumeCube are great for illuminating the desktop and even your face during late-night Zoom calls. You can adjust the color temperature and the brightness.

BenQ ScreenBar Lamp Photograph: Julian Chokkattu

BenQ ScreenBar Lamp for $139: Alternatively, you can place these ScreenBar lamps over your computer monitor, and it will light up your desktop, no clamping required. The ScreenBar Pro also has a motion sensor, so when you leave your desk, the lamp will turn off, and it will light up when you're back. You can adjust the brightness and color temperature, and an automatic setting makes it adjust these controls based on the room's ambient lighting.

Secretlab Premium Footrest for $89: WIRED reviewer Julian Chokkattu been using this footrest for several years, and it's excellent. The plush memory foam is cushy and a nice respite for Chokkattu's feet, and it's easy to clean with a vacuum and a damp cloth. It hasn't shown much wear despite years of use.

Monoprice Single Monitor Adjustable Gas Spring Desk Mount for $84: WIRED reviewer Julian Chokkattu has tested a few of these WorkStream arm mounts for years, and they've reliably done the job. You can adjust the tension with a hex key and move the monitor around to your desired position. Just make sure you don't go over the recommended weight load with a big and heavy screen.

Mount-It! Dual Monitor Arm for $280: This heavy-duty monitor arm holds up my ultrawide monitor and my vertical monitor, both of which have BenQ Screenbar lamps on top, along with my webcam. It handles the weight with no effort, and the clamp is accommodating enough to even work with the 5-inch Room & Board standing desk. There's RGB lighting throughout, but it's not bright enough to splash onto the wall, so it's a little pointless, noted WIRED Reviewer Julian Chokkattu.

Harber London Professional Desk Mat for $239: Keep your desktop protected with a large desk mat like this one. I've used several mats from Harber London over the years, and this latest model is the favorite of WIRED reviewer Julian Chokkattu. The pebbled leather is supple and soft, and the mat stays put. It's easy to clean as well.

Avoid These Standing Desks

Corsair Platform:6 Desk Photograph: Julian Chokkattu

Corsair Platform:6 Desk for $1,400: Where do I start? I liked Corsair's standing desk because it's spacious, has a fun pegboard design to mount your tchotchkes, and even has an interesting rail system that lets you mount and slide things across the desktop, like your monitors. Unfortunately, several months after mounting two monitors on the included dual-monitor arms, this rail system has tilted forward due to the weight. (I'm also not the only one to experience this.) It doesn't help that I never really found this rail to be all that useful. The standing function works well, and you get two presets, but sometimes the little screen would throw me an error message “rE5.” Pressing and holding the down button resolved it, but none of these are issues anyone should deal with considering the crazy-high price. That's the real problem. It's just so expensive, and the five-year warranty feels like a slap in the face. This model is still listed for sale, but as out of stock last time we checked. —Julian Chokkattu

Marinamantra ‘Flow’ Sit-to-Stand Desk for $1,149: I had high hopes for this one. A desk that lets me sit crisscross applesauce while I work?! Sold. But the reality didn’t live up to the pitch. When I unboxed the desk, several screws were scattered loose in the box. That set the tone for a desk that eventually worked, but often misbehaved, sometimes refusing to move up and down. That said, I do like the cord management lip and the clever Velcro covers that keep cables and hardware neatly tucked out of sight. Unfortunately, none of that matters much if I’m spending more time flipping it over and poking around underneath the hood than actually using it. —Nicole Kinning

Tech.title: The Anti-Woke Right Can’t Figure Out How to Stop ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’
Tech.content:
Rockstar Games’ best-selling Grand Theft Auto series wasn’t often accused of political sensitivity during its legendary run from the late 1990s through the early 2010s.

In fact, parents and activists denounced the franchise for exposing children to a seedy world of sex, violence, crude humor, and wanton crime. Elon Musk even claimed that he couldn’t get into the last installment, GTA V, because he was mortified to play as a character who shoots police officers.

But times (and moral panics) change. In the 13 years that fans have waited for Grand Theft Auto VI—finally out on November 19—the American right-wing grievance machine has drifted from fears of impressionable kids turning to a life of larceny to concerns that they will grow up “woke.” And despite knowing very little about the forthcoming game, the agitators of the latter movement have decided it must amount to a stealth campaign to poison the youth with depictions of gender equality, LGBTQ acceptance, and racial diversity. (Rockstar did not immediately return a request for comment.)

Since the height of Gamergate in 2014, an angst-ridden subset of male gamers have maintained a paranoid vigil against what they see as the creeping influence of women and LGBTQ developers in the gaming world. Between the feverish anticipation for GTA VI and the various delays of its release date, they’ve had ample opportunity to foment a preemptive backlash to what is sure to be a massive hit, not unlike the failed furor over supposedly “woke” elements of Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey.

“GTA 6 is a humiliation ritual for all male gamers,” an X user with the handle @Wokenessisevil complained on Tuesday, sharing a clip of the game’s two lead characters, Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, who are in a relationship that evolves based on the player’s choices. In the scene, Lucia, the series’ first mandatory female protagonist, asks Jason to pick an outfit for her and expresses mild annoyance when he seems more or less indifferent to the options she presents.

Tech.title: Sony Will Pay Out $7.85 Million in PlayStation Store Credit. How to Claim Part of the Settlement
Tech.content:
You may be eligible to claim part of an upcoming $7.85 million settlement payout if you’re a PlayStation customer who lives in the US. The case centered on an allegation that Sony “unlawfully eliminated competition and monopolized the market for (its) digital games” by discontinuing the sale of game-specific vouchers that allowed PlayStation owners to buy digital games from other online retailers.

The class-action lawsuit Caccuri v. Sony Interactive Entertainment alleged that Sony’s actions caused “consumers to pay more for certain digital games than they otherwise would have paid on the PlayStation Store.” It alleges that this action is a violation of antitrust laws, as it forces PlayStation customers to buy from a single storefront at an inflated price.

Put simply, the lawsuit alleges that Sony limited the sale of digital games on other marketplaces, funneling customers into its own PlayStation Store. Some of these games include PlayStation exclusive titles, such as The Last of Us, as well as third-party games, like Mass Effect Trilogy and Resident Evil 4.

The lawsuit was initially settled in 2024, but the settlement was rejected twice during the approval process — most recently in July 2025 (PDF), when the presiding judge said the proposed plan “[did] not provide an estimated recovery or a range of potential recovery for class members.” The approval process was reinitiated in April.

Sony denied any wrongdoing or that settlement class members were damaged by its actions, and the court has not decided if the company violated any laws. Despite this, the court has preliminarily approved the $7.85 million settlement payment, subject to the court’s final approval hearing.

The settlement website is live now. The hearing is scheduled to take place on Oct. 15, and it’s meant to confirm the settlement sum, allocate up to 25% of the funds for attorneys’ fees and create a plan to distribute the rest of the money to eligible class members.

If you fit all of the criteria to be part of the Sony PlayStation game-voucher settlement, you’re automatically a class member in this lawsuit and will be able to collect a portion of the settlement money — added directly to your PlayStation Network account wallet — sometime after the final approval hearing.

Gamers who have deactivated their PlayStation Network accounts can apply for the settlement payment by sending qualifying purchase information to the email address info@PSNDigitalGamesSettlement.com. Customers with deactivated accounts will receive cash payments instead of PSN account accreditation.

The option to opt out of the settlement to retain your right to sue Sony separately in regard to its game-voucher sales practices closed on July 2. A written request to the court opting out of or objecting to the settlement had to be received by then; otherwise, you will remain part of the settlement class.

Who can be part of the Sony PlayStation settlement?

Not every PlayStation owner is automatically eligible. The money is reserved for those who purchased a digital game through the PlayStation Store during a period after Sony ceased its sales of game-specific vouchers for alternative online storefronts.

In order to join, you must meet the following qualifications:

Be a living individual human being in the US or its territories. Have purchased one of the eligible digital games (PDF) through the PlayStation Store between the period of April 1, 2019 and Dec. 31, 2023.

Affected individuals are automatically part of the settlement class and will receive their compensation through their PlayStation Network account wallet, subject to approval at the final hearing, the date and time of which could change. Any updates will be posted to the settlement website.

How much will the Sony PlayStation settlement pay?

It’s unclear how much each settlement class member will receive, though we know affected parties will automatically receive compensation in the form of PlayStation account funds.

Up to a quarter of the $7.85 million settlement will be used to pay attorneys’ fees, taxes and other administrative costs. The remaining settlement money will be administered equally to every settlement class member. Settlement class members will likely see a couple of dollars added to their PlayStation accounts once the funds are fully allocated.

Tech.title: The Latest Weird Thing to Play Doom Is the Mapped-Out Brain of a Fruit Fly
Tech.content:
Doom is such a simple, beautifully designed game that it can run on all sorts of weird things, from pregnancy tests to potatoes. Weird things can play it, too. In an effort to eternally one-up itself, the community has now gotten a map of a fruit fly’s brain to play the 1993 first-person shooter.

It started with Google, which partnered with HHMI Janelia Research and other collaborators to map the brain and central nervous system of a male fruit fly. This mapping, which is weirdly beautiful, contains 11,700 types of neurons and 166,000 neurons overall, breaking the record for the most complex neuron mapping ever done.

The research is pretty cool: It involved taking very thin slices of a fly’s brain and body, imaging them and using AI to combine the millions of 2D images into 3D neural shapes. Google says that “knowing the structure of the brain allows neuroscientists to understand the mechanisms behind brain function.”

Now, make it play Doom

The game is played frame by frame, letting the fly’s simulated brain determine its next move based on what it sees. Doomfly

It turns out that knowing the structure of the male fruit fly brain can also help modders and developers teach it how to play Doom. A few days after Google dropped its fly brain research, software engineer Alex Wormuth created a simulated fly brain using Google’s map and then set it loose to learn how to play the pioneering FPS.

The process is quite complicated. Each frame of the game generates 3,335 brightness inputs and 811 R8 color inputs. These inputs are fed into the simulated fruit fly brain, which contains 25.6 million connections. These inputs hit specific neurons based on what the frame shows, and that information is used to determine which controls the fly uses. This process repeats each frame the game runs.

It even works with pain. Wormuth says that nonfatal damage targets the PPL101 dopamine receptors, which control hunger and aggression in real fruit flies.

You can watch the fly’s progress in learning how to play Doom on Wormuth’s Doomfly website, which also shows sensory input, neural activity and other metrics so you can watch the simulated fly brain work in real time. If you swap to the 3D view, you can watch the fly shoot demons.

Flying high with other games, too

Doom isn’t the only game that a simulated fly brain is learning how to play. Developer Jessica Paquette set up a similar neural network with the fly’s brain to learn how to play Super Mario 64, while mechanistic interpretability researcher Lyra Bubbles made another one learn how to play Beat Saber.

A few days later, X user David began teaching it how to do an escape room, and another, Shashank Jain, taught it how to play soccer. Wormuth came back a couple of days later and gave the fly brain $100 worth of bitcoin to trade to see what it would do. X user Simba made the fly brain deploy its own cryptocurrency token on Robinhood.

The fly brain experiment is going to have a lot more impact in neuroscience in the long run, but for at least the next few weeks, don’t be surprised if you see headlines about a fruit fly brain learning how to do other random stuff, like creating real fonts that you can download right now or putting it in music videos and letting it dance.

Tech.title: Before You Get That Phone Deal, Double-Check Bill Credits and Installment Plan Details
Tech.content:
With phone prices climbing higher than ever, it’s no wonder most people turn to carrier financing to buy a new phone. Not only can you spread out your payments over time, but cellular companies often offer enticing deals to win customers over, especially if you’re switching to a new provider. Depending on the deal, sometimes you can even get your new phone for free.

But those deals can be a little confusing, and involve caveats and rules that aren’t always clear. Very rarely is a discount given without a catch. You might also come across terms like “bill credits” or “trade-in credits” that you don’t fully understand.

If you want to know what these terms mean or other details, like what happens if you decide to switch carriers midplan, read on as we walk you through what you need to know before accepting a new carrier deal.

This article was made possible in part by T-Mobile. It was written and edited independently without partner oversight.

What is carrier financing?

Wireless providers often have financing deals for new phones, versus paying for a new device upfront. Sarah Tew/CNET

Simply put, instead of paying up front for a new phone, carrier financing lets you pay for the phone over time through an installment plan. So, for example, if a phone is $1,200, you can spread the cost over 24 months, which translates to just $50 a month. That’s a lot easier for most people to manage.

It’s worth noting that you will still need to pay upfront costs, like activation fees and taxes on the new phone, whether you’re on an installment plan or not. Sometimes carriers do offer deals that let you spread that out over time. T-Mobile, for example, has the Equipment Installation Plan Flex 36 that will spread out the payment of the device, fees and taxes over 36 months, making the initial cost zero. That said, you still need to qualify for the plan, and depending on your credit, you could have to pay interest on top of that.

One particular downside of carrier financing is that it locks you into that carrier for an extended period (usually two to three years). This means you can’t use your phone with another carrier during this time. If you want to end your agreement with the carrier, that will usually result in early termination fees, or ETFs.

Being stuck with a carrier-locked phone is sometimes bad news if you travel a lot and want to use international eSIMs, which only work with unlocked phones. Otherwise, you’ll have to use your carrier’s international data plan, which can be more expensive.

What are trade-ins and bill credits?

It might be time to trade in that old iPhone and get bill credits toward the cost of a new one. James Martin/CNET

When shopping around for new phones, you might see the words “bill credit” or “trade-in credit” advertised by a carrier. For example, a carrier might offer a trade-in credit of up to $1,000 if you trade in your existing iPhone for a new one. Then they might say that the trade-in credit will be paid to you as 24- or 36-month bill credits.

What does all of that mean? First, let’s talk about that trade-in credit. Not all phones will be eligible for one. Often, the carrier will only give a trade-in credit for newer phones. The newer the device, the more trade-in credit you will get. So that out-of-date iPhone 11, for example, probably won’t be worth very much, if at all.

It’s also worth looking into what else is required for you to get that trade-in credit. Sometimes carriers will only offer the trade-in credit if you 

Let’s say you agree to the terms and the carrier offers you that $1,000 trade-in credit. Here’s where bill credits come in. If the carrier says the trade-in credit will be paid over 36 months of bill credits, it means that $1,000 will be paid off over the period of 36 months. You won’t get a lump sum of that $1,000 credit instantly, and the credits you do get can’t be cashed out and can only be used toward the amount of your phone bill.

But let’s say you don’t have a phone to trade in at all. You could still save some money if you don’t mind switching carriers. Sometimes carriers will offer to pay for your device as an incentive to switch over to their company. Again, device payments are often applied as bill credits spread over a 24- or 36-month period.

What happens if I pay off my plan early?

The iPhone Duo is Apple’s most innovative and expensive phone. Patrick Holland/CNET

You can certainly pay off the remaining balance on your phone if you don’t mind paying the upfront cost. However, be warned that you’ll also forfeit any remaining credits you received for the device you traded in. You could also forfeit any other discounts that you agreed to upon signing up for the plan. Be sure to read through the early payoff rules before deciding to pay off your phone ahead of schedule.

What if I want to switch carriers?

Switching wireless providers can have its advantages, but consider the cost, especially if you haven’t completed any device installment plans that you have. AT&T/Verizon/T-Mobile/CNET

If you want to switch carriers while you’re in an existing installment plan, you might have to pay ETFs to end your current agreement. However, most major carriers like T-Mobile, AT&T and Verizon will offer carrier-switching incentives where they’ll pay your ETFs for you. Bear in mind that there’s often a cap on how much of the ETF they will cover. The payment is also often in the form of bill credits.

You can take advantage of carrier deals when choosing this route. T-Mobile, for example, has a five-year price guarantee that locks in the price of text, talk and data for at least five years. AT&T is also attempting to draw new customers with a modular Build-A-Plan that lets you customize your plan according to your budget. Verizon recently introduced Simplicity, an unlimited phone plan that usually costs $45 a month, but is just $30 a month for new customers who bring their own number.

Tech.title: Apple’s New iPhone Duo Folds Horizontally, Like a Passport
Tech.content:
If you’re used to the vertical flip opening of phones like the Motorola Razr, or still fondly remember snapping your vintage not-so-smart cellphone open and shut, think different. The just-announced folding iPhone Duo opens horizontally, like a book, and its size and fold direction make it reminiscent of a paper passport. The much-anticipated phone was revealed Wednesday at Apple’s latest event.

While it wasn’t confirmed until this week, the folding phone was the worst-kept secret in tech, with hundreds of articles reporting that it was on the way. And it joins a crowded field of foldable phones, with key players including Samsung, Google and Motorola, and Chinese brands like Honor, Oppo and Huawei. But as CNET’s Abrar Al-Heeti notes, Apple’s entry into the fray is expected to nudge foldable phone designs forward.

Al-Heeti notes that the iPhone Duo is compact, and Apple says it’s the thinnest iPhone ever when opened. The phone has a 7.6-inch display on the inside, a 5.4-inch outer display, and will come in two colors, star white and night sky.

Foldable phones typically have visible creases where the phones fold in half. CNET Director of Content Patrick Holland notes that this is an issue preventing some shoppers from buying foldable phones, but he says the crease is “nearly nonexistent” on the iPhone Duo. He says it will be interesting to see whether the crease becomes more pronounced as the foldable phone ages, as it has with all other foldable phones.

Tech.title: Today’s NYT Strands Hints, Answers and Help for Sept. 13, #924
Tech.content:
Looking for the most recent NYT Strands puzzle answers? CNET publishes daily answers and hints for The New York Times Mini Crossword, Connections, Connections: Sports Edition and Strands puzzles.

Strands is like a word find game, but without the list of words to find. Sometimes I see the theme and begin recognizing the answers right away. But for those times when I can’t seem to manage this, there’s a loophole: Strands lets you make as many words of four or more letters as you want. For every three of those words you find, the puzzle will highlight one of the answers. You’re still going to have to unscramble that answer, though, which can be very tough.

I go into depth about the rules for Strands in this story.

James Bond fans, this puzzle might be one for you. You’ll recognize the theme as the words start to fill in. Read on for hints and all the answers.



Hint for today’s Strands puzzle

Today’s Strands theme is: Top secret.

If that doesn’t help you, here’s a clue: 007.

Clue words to unlock in-game hints

Your goal is to find hidden words that fit the puzzle’s theme. If you’re stuck, find any words you can. Every time you find three words of four letters or more, Strands will reveal one of the theme words. These are the words I used to get those hints, but any words of four or more letters that you find will work:

COUNT, COUNTER, PURE, GREY, TANG, GNAT, RATE, SOLE, RATER, STEER, CRED, CREDIT, RECOUNT

Answers for today’s Strands puzzle

These are the answers that tie into the theme. The goal of the puzzle is to find them all, including the “spangram,” a theme word that reaches from one side of the puzzle to the other. When you have all of them (I originally thought there were always eight, but learned that the number can vary), every letter on the board will be used. Here are the nonspangram answers:

MOLE, AGENT, ASSET, PLANT, OPERATIVE, COUNTERSPY

Today’s Strands spangram

NYT/Screenshot by CNET

Today’s Strands spangram is UNDERCOVER. To find it, start with the U that’s four letters down on the far-left row, and wind down and then across.

Toughest Strands puzzles

Here are some of the Strands topics I’ve found to be the toughest.

#1: Dated slang. Maybe you didn’t even use this lingo when it was cool. Toughest word: PHAT.

#2: Thar she blows! I guess marine biologists might ace this one. Toughest word: BALEEN or RIGHT.

#3: Off the hook. Again, it helps to know a lot about sea creatures. Sorry, Charlie. Toughest word: BIGEYE or SKIPJACK.

Tech.title: BlizzCon 2026: New Starcraft Shooter, Diablo 5, World of Warcraft Forever
Tech.content:
In a packed, rowdy BlizzCon main hall, the game developer finally confirmed the rumors: We’re getting a shooter set in the Starcraft universe. The game is titled simply Starcraft.

All we saw was a brief teaser that showed the rise and sudden fall of an elite soldier. Still, Starcraft (the game) is the first major news from Starcraft (the series) in a decade, when Starcraft 2’s Nova Covert Ops campaign pack was released. The announcement of the franchise’s return rocked the enormous main hall at BlizzCon.

I grew up playing the original Starcraft, spending late nights in custom games with friends, so I’m interested to see whether (and how) Blizzard can revitalize the franchise.

The game is planned for a 2030 launch, a full two decades after the release of StarCraft 2.

Diablo 5 announced, alongside Netflix series

In 2029, Sanctuary will finally fall. Players will fight to take it back in Diablo 5.

In a dark and hazy main hall, Blizzard Entertainment showed a short teaser revealing Diablo’s return at the BlizzCon opening ceremony. For the series’ 30th anniversary, Diablo announced plans to drag players deeper into the darkness than they’ve ever seen. Diablo 5 will show us what happens when the Lord of Terror finally takes over the world.

According to Diablo devs, the game will explore the question of what you must become to save a world that has already fallen.

The past two Diablo games spent about a decade in development, so the announcement of the next entry is earlier than expected. We just wrapped the Mephisto storyline, and here comes Diablo announcing his (eventual) return.

In the meantime, there’s still more planned for Diablo 4, which released its Lord of Hatred expansion earlier this spring. Blizzard will add the Amazon class — a returning favorite from Diablo 2 — via a class pack next year. It’s not a full expansion, but it gives players the opportunity to explore the Skovos Isles, home of the Amazons, as one of their own.

Blizzard CEO Johanna Faries also announced that an animated Diablo series is coming to Netflix and hinted that there may be more planned for other franchises sometime in the future.

World of Warcraft is forever, and Forever comes in November

The rumored “Classic plus” is coming to Blizzard’s flagship MMO. Titled World of Warcraft Forever, the game will funnel new content to players while preserving the feel (and level cap) of vanilla WoW.

WoW Forever will add three new zones, overhaul several existing zones, drop 1,000 new quests into the game alongside nine new dungeons, two new raids and a new Skyborne race.

Perhaps most surprisingly, the beta for WoW Forever opens on Thursday, and the game is set for a launch in less than two months, on Nov. 4.

Over in contemporary WoW, the latest expansion, Midnight, is entering the next phase of its story. Blizzard showed us a new cinematic that raised the stakes in ways that, as a non-WoW player, I frankly didn’t really follow, but it looked momentous.

We also got a tease for the next expansion, The Last Titan, which will conclude the Worldsoul trilogy of expansions that began with 2024’s The War Within.

Alongside a 3.0 update to Warcraft 3: Reforged, a remaster of the classic real-time strategy game, Blizzard is releasing a new Forsaken Kingdom campaign, launching today.

Overwatch finally reworked Roadhog and Sombra (again)

Blizzard’s hero shooter had its big moment earlier this year, when the game announced 10 new heroes for its 10th anniversary, plus a new, ongoing story that has spanned everything from cinematics to in-game map changes. The game’s BlizzCon announcements weren’t as big as those of other franchises, but there were still some surprises tucked away.

We got our first look at Doctrine, a vampire-inspired support hero who will join the roster in season 5 next month. Doctrine is playable this weekend in a hero preview before joining the roster permanently in October.

The game is also adding a new escort map, set in the Icelandic prison that contained Doctrine before Doomfist and his crew of ex-Talon members broke him out.

A new support hero and a new map were expected. What really made me shoot forward in my seat was the announcement that hero reworks are starting to come through — and longtime damage hero Sombra is switching roles and becoming a support hero.

Sombra’s been a tough nut to crack for Overwatch, often overpowered at the highly coordinated pro level, and annoying to both teammates and opponents at the casual level — largely due to her ability to go invisible and quickly teleport across the map. She’s already been through four reworks by my count, and the devs seem to make smaller-but-still-substantial tweaks to her kit every six months or so. As a longtime support player and Sombra-enjoyer (which I will not apologize for), I’m very excited for this change.

Roadhog’s also getting a rework, although he’s staying within the tank role. Like Sombra, he’s a hero who’s been a longtime annoyance for players, due largely to being balanced around a hook ability that can quickly combo down non-tank heroes.

Hearthstone announces next expansion, new class coming next year

Blizzard’s card battler is taking players back 10,000 years in the past with the upcoming Reign of the Black Empire expansion, which adds a new “assemble” keyword allowing players to smush two minions’ text boxes together. It’s also getting a new Journey feature that will be a dedicated home for events, story content and limited-time events.

In March, the game will also add its first new hero in six years: the monk. Blizzard didn’t say much about the new class, but I’m sure we’ll hear more about it over the course of BlizzCon.

New content for Heroes of the Storm

Heroes of the Storm is getting a new hero for the first time in six years. Xal’atath from World of Warcraft is joining the roster later this month. The multiplayer online battle arena has been largely in maintenance mode since 2022, though still receiving periodic balance patches. Whether the new hero marks the start of more dedicated support for the game likely depends on how much interest it generates.

This is a developing story and will be updated as Blizzard releases more information.

Editors’ note: Adam Benjamin’s travel costs for BlizzCon were covered by Blizzard Entertainment. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

Tech.title: Meta Pulls Invasive AI Prompts After Mother Reveals Feature Scraping Family Data
Tech.content:
Meta is putting out yet another bad-publicity fire, saying it has fixed an issue in which its Meta AI software could suggest prompts to users that would collect and reveal personal information, including about children.

The controversy started from a Sept. 2 Instagram video posted by parenting and lifestyle blogger Kalie Robins, who goes by kontheinside. In the video, Robins discussed a prior video post of herself singing in a car with her daughter in the backseat. Below the published video, Robins revealed how Meta AI posed a series of invasive prompts, such as “Who’s the child passenger?” and “Where does Kalie Robins live?”

According to Robins, when she clicked on those automatic questions, the AI tool pulled information from her past posts, piecing together private details about her life, including her location. The AI also drew on other profiles, such as her mother’s account, and even accessed data from a photo she claimed had been deleted years ago.

Robins said in the video: “I did not understand posting separate innocent pieces of our lives over years could mean an AI could sit there and assemble all those breadcrumbs into information about my minor children in seconds.” The video went viral, drawing thousands of comments and more than 308,000 likes as of this writing.

‘The issue was never just one photo’

A Meta spokesperson told CNET in an email that it has since “fixed” the issue, and that Meta AI will no longer suggest inappropriate, personal questions on users’ posts. The company admitted the feature missed the mark and stated that the tool is only meant to help people find more information using data users already have access to.

The response from Meta, which was also shared with other outlets, wasn’t sufficient for Robins. In a subsequent Instagram post on Sept. 10, she said she was glad that the company acknowledged the problem, but that she still had questions. “What exactly was fixed? What safeguard failed in the first place? And what protections are now in place when Meta AI encounters information involving a child?”

Even if Meta AI no longer suggests intrusive personal prompts, the feature can still make suggestions based on information the software can access, such as publicly available text, images from the web or previous posts on social media by users like Robins.

Meta also denied Robins’ claim that its AI accessed a photo deleted years ago. Instead, Meta told CNET that the photo of Robins’ kids was deleted right before the video was made, and a temporary bug briefly kept it visible.

In an email to CNET, Robins said that regardless of what happened with the deleted image of her kids, the larger concern remains. “The issue was never just one photo — it was the AI compiling information about my kids from multiple sources,” Robins told CNET. According to Robins, Meta has not contacted her directly or apologized.



Just the latest Meta privacy problem

Adding to the hundreds of comments posted on Robins’ Instagram account have been news stories on sites like Futurism, where the story was first widely publicized. Business Insider reported that what happened to Robins is prompting some parents to urge others to stop posting images of their kids online.

“This is creepy!” said Cathy Pedrayes, who posts frequently on social media about scams and dark-web trends.

Meta has faced multibillion-dollar settlements and court judgments this year over how its technology affects children, including addiction and creating environments where they may be vulnerable to exploitation.

Meta has also been facing criticism of its Meta smart glasses, particularly the facial recognition technology it has been developing.

Recently, the tech giant started rolling out its Muse AI agents, which it markets to users seeking more customized AI experiences through personal assistants.

Tech.title: CNET Readers Were Right About the iPhone Duo. But There’s One Thing They Got Wrong
Tech.content:
Apple’s “Surprise and Shine” event has officially wrapped, and all of the answers for the CNET Group’s Big Guessing Game are in.

The contest was held across CNET, Lifehacker, Mashable, PCMag and ZDNET. In three rounds, readers predicted what Apple would unveil this year. Each correct answer earned one chance in a drawing to win the latest Apple Watch. Here’s a rundown of all the answers we learned on Wednesday and a recap of the first and second rounds.

Tim Cook and John Ternus didn’t appear at the ‘Surprise and Shine’ event together

Most (71%) contest participants expected Apple’s new CEO John Ternus and former CEO Tim Cook to appear together at the event, but they didn’t.

Instead, Cook opened the event with the introductory video shot on an iPhone, then passed the scene to Ternus saying, “That’s your guy. That’s your opener.” Then Ternus appeared and kicked off the event.

Wednesday marked Ternus’ first Apple event as the company’s CEO. Cook has become the company’s executive chair.

Apple unveiled two new iPhone models

Half of CNET’s respondents (50%) expected three new iPhone models, but Apple unveiled two — the iPhone 18 Pro/Pro Max and the foldable iPhone Duo.

That lineup indicates the possibility of a split launch, where we see more models in the iPhone 18 series lineup announced in the coming months and early 2027, when we could see the iPhone 18 base model.

The iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,199 and the 18 Pro Max at $1,299. Both are available for preorder starting today.

The new foldable iPhone costs $2,000

CNET readers’ guesses about the price of Apple’s foldable iPhone, officially named the iPhone Duo, would cost an average of $1,847.

The iPhone Duo costs $1,999.99. So if you answered $1,999 or $2,000, you’re correct. The iPhone Duo stands out with no crease when open and a lightweight thin design. But the four-figure price tag is still more than what US adults are willing to spend — CNET’s survey found that US adults interested in the phone are only willing to spend an average of $781.

New Apple Watch Ultra 4 is in the fall lineup

Close to 3 in 4 (74%) contestants expected to see an Apple Watch Ultra 4 this week, and sure enough, Apple released the latest model at Wednesday’s event. The Ultra 4 starts at $800. It has new Audio Intelligence features to hear the previous 15 seconds of a conversation when you press a button and low-battery modes to track workouts.

Apple also announced the Apple Watch Series 12, which costs half as much ($400) as the Ultra 4 and has increased processing power with a new S11 chip, as well as a new bronze finish. Both new watches are available for preorder.

Apple’s ‘One More Thing’ moment was the iPhone Duo

As expected, Apple brought back “One More Thing” as a way to reveal one final product that would wow us. Most CNET readers seem fairly certain that the foldable iPhone would be it, and they were right.

The guesses were closely followed by a new Home hub (14%), but Apple didn’t announce one at the September event. Some CNET readers also expected smart glasses (8%), but those will likely be unveiled later in 2027 due to rumors of “bumps” in development. And even though Apple announced the AirPods 5, it wasn’t the tech company’s final ah-ha moment.

Looking back at rounds one and two

The CNET Big Guessing Game had two previous rounds, in May 2026 and July 2026, when we asked readers to make predictions about Apple software and devices, respectively.



Most of our round one questions about software were answered at Apple’s WWDC event in early June, and now we can resolve the final one.

New CEO John Ternus did not make an appearance at WWDC.

The only remaining round one question left to answer at the September Apple event was whether or not the Apple Watch would add a dedicated AI health coach. Although the new Health app for the Watch has plenty of coaching features, we determined that the final answer was no.

Most of the round two questions, which focused on Apple devices, weren’t settled until Wednesday’s event.

The final question of round two was a freebie (any reasonable answer was marked correct) about what you’d like to see change about the iPhone. Readers’ most popular request — a lower price — hit a blocker on Wednesday as Apple announced it was boosting the price of its latest Pro and Pro Max iPhones by $100.

We will be contacting our grand-prize winner via email this week, so please keep an eye on your mailbox if you entered the contest. While you’re waiting, now’s the time to catch up on everything Apple released on Wednesday, rewatch the event and stay tuned to see if you won the CNET Group’s Big Guessing Game.
